As a disclaimer, I read this because I saw S.J. Maas' gushing review on this book... I should have known better, seeing how I felt after reading Throne Of Glass. No use crying about it now, it's not like I'll get those hours of my life back. 
 I'm so torn on this... It started off great and hit the skids right at three quarters through the book. Then, it redeemed itself at the end. I predicted almost everything that happened in the book, which is extremely annoying. I also found myself skipping through parts (which is something I NEVER do) because it was getting too wordy. Another thing that irritated me was the music that was interwoven throughout the book. Come on, how the hell did the main character know all those songs? She was ten when she was taken and I don't think they played any music after that point in her life. That was never elaborated on and it just felt forced. It was a weak way of making the book feel more real. It was a great premise, but (mostly) weak follow through. The bright spot of this book to me was the supporting cast of characters. They were very well-rounded and felt real. Ruby? Her characterization was hit or miss. I liked her personality/development through a majority of the book, but she hit the skids right when the plot of the book did. My last major gripe was the world Bracken laid out. It felt... unrealistic. I know I'm supposed to suspend my imagination when reading fiction, but a lot of world building she did (with the economy, abandoned cars, hotel rooms.... etc.) was weak if you put some thought to it. 
 Every time I think I have found something that comes close to The Hunger Games, I have my heart broken. I will read the sequel to this, but I don't think I'll be reading this book more than once.

Well....Long story short I got a bruise on my head because of The Darkest Minds. I mean its amazing but reading on the top bunk of the bunk bed sitting upright wasn't the best way to read it. One second your reading and everything is going smooth and then you turn the page and.... 
 BAAAMMMMMM. 
 You jump and your heart starts racing because of the turn of events.(in my case I hit my head on the ceiling)!! And let me tell you I hadn't expected half the book to go the way that it did. So I pretty much damaged the top half of my head....oh well i can't be the only one. 
 Back to the matter at hand. Alexandra Bracken has quite literally written one of the best books i have ever read. 
 Lets just say the only reason i'm not happy about this book is that the second one doesn't come out for a couple of more months. Other than that It was an awesome read.

I stayed up until 4 am reading this, it was that good. Unfortunately it's part of a trilogy (DAMN YOU ALL YA NOVELS EVER), which I didn't realize and now I have to wait until Fall 2013 for the next one.

This came fairly highly rated but it was not worth the time. It's a midling book with little character development or depth. The premise is interesting but really only highlights the blandness of the plot. Also, one character forces himself on another by telepathy and it's not addressed as rape, which really irritated me. Girls need to know that they are not at fault and they did not deserve unwanted attention instead of it being described as another trauma... Overall, disappointing.

I'll be upfront and admit that I could not finish this book. Aside from the amazing first few chapters, it goes downhill from there. I couldn't manage to care about the characters or their motivations. And there was hardly any plot to speak of. Great story concept, very weak execution.
3.5 stars

Its not even that bad, just so unoriginal and predictable and boring. Could't the author have done a bit more to explain some things? Why did some kids develop powers after the disease, and why is the government afraid of them? And even with that I felt the author could have done more with the world and characters she created. 
 I need to stop reading YA for a while.

The first few chapters kept me interested, but about the time Ruby met up with the trio, I lost interest. I wish Alexandra Bracken had really embraced the darkness of the story she was presenting. It just never felt quite dark enough. Ruby was whiney and boring. Liam and Chubs were also pretty bland. Zu was easily my favorite character, and there wasn't even enough of her. There was too much happening, but at the same time, there wasn't enough going on. I know that doesn't seem to make sense, but it does to me. I really liked the whole X-Men vibe with all of the powers, but ultimately, this book was pretty boring and not as dark and gritty as I would have hoped. One of my biggest pet peeves is when an author chooses a difficult subject matter to tackle, but instead of fully committing to the horror of said subject, they water it down to make their book more accessible. And I feel that that was done here. Honestly, this book came off as bad dystopian fanfiction most of the time. I don't know if I'll continue with the series. I've heard the books get better with each installment, and that some of the characters I complained about experience major growth later. I might consider picking up the second book, but definitely not anytime soon.

1. Predictable. 
 2. Boring female lead. 
 3. Unexplained disease that killed most children and gave the rest superpowers.

Ok, here's the deal- we have RFID chip technology now. Like in real time. We used it in livestock and force owners to chip animals sold across state line or taken to fairs. YOU can't tell me those kids wouldn't have chips embedded in theirs hips. Sorry dude. They totally would. And then this whole book would have been seriously harder to write because there aint no hiding from "the man". Watch the bbc's the last enemy if you doubt me. You won't sleep for a week- 
 So the problem is. . . The book was pretty good- but not a viable distopian- sans mythology companant-adventure. The character was decent but I think enclave was better- and it had zombies! Everything is better with zombies. Right? You know I'm right. And that micheal vey book gets around big gov tracking because they are a private funded group- all hush hush. 
 And then she just does something even she knows is stupid just because??? No, not buying it. I see it is to launch second book, but for reals- would not have happened. Idk, just not distopianly (yes I just made that word up) savvy enough for those of us who have already read a crap ton o books. But if you don't read a ton, and are blissfully ignorant of everything xfiles' lone gunmen tried to warned us about, then you will be like "awe this book is great". The rest of us have to settle for a book that is a decent enough read through while waiting for the next installment of throne of glass, or raven boys. Or, swoon, the crown of embers. Ah, we all need a hector. Am I right ladies? You know I am.

3 - 3.5 Stars 
 The concept was interesting, and so were a few (very few) characters, but the main character Ruby was just so dumb and weak that it was hard to enjoy the story. Also, this didn't really "ignite me", which sometimes can happen even though a book is really good.. It then takes me a bit longer to get into a story. 
 It started out very interesting but somehow got kind of boring during the middle... the premice of the IAAN and the camps was a very interesting concept, but I felt like we threw away some great potential here... maybe we'll see more of that in Never Fade. 
 I do like Chubs, he is funny and intelligent and Zu was kinda cool, too. Apart from these two, all the other characters were rather boring and cliche. What is it that you all see in Liam? 
 The ending with Ruby and Liam surprised me as well. 
 I'm definetely reading the second one (Never Fade) because this still has potential, but I don't see how this is the "best book ever". Reminded me of a lot of other franchises like x-men (kids with superpowers) or even TMI (mild spoiler: I'm talking about the character constellation of Liam - Ruby - Clancy... that was soo Jace - Clary - Sebastian, just that Jace and Sebastian are strong, well-developed, solid characters and Liam and Clancy aren't) 
 The cover and the cover of Never Fade are beautiful though! Also, props for the title: "the darkest minds". That's a pretty cool title. The writing was also solid IMO. 
 That's pretty much all there is to say about it for me...

This book is not the average dystopian story but I have to admit, I got pretty lost. And not just the first time around. The second and the third as well. I quit the book half way through the fourth time. I do have to give the credit that you will never read another story quite The Darkest Minds.
I did not finish this book because it was very boring and lacking in character development and the plot was not very exciting.

Aside from the typos (I got the over them), there's a great story line, a different plot from other fantasy novels & it keeps you guessing. There's no actual love triangle (thankfully, those were getting old to read in other books) & the ending was a surprise. Actually looking forward to book number 2 & seeing the writing advance from here. Three stars for the grammatical errors or it would've been 4. Not perfect but definitely not boring. Good read.

** spoiler alert ** 
 Vorweg mochte ich sagen: Das Buch ist auf keinen Fall ein schlechtes! Wenn ich das irgendwie neutral betrachte, kann ich mir bestens vorstellen, das viele Leute es mogen werden. Es hat ein ganz interessantes Setting und auch die dustere Stimmung ist mal etwas anderes. Leider konnte ich mit dem Buch absolut nichts anfangen. Es kommt wirklich selten vor, dass ich einem Buch 1 Stern gebe, wenn es nicht wirklich grottenschlecht war. The Darkest Minds konnte mich aber weder packen, noch begeistern und der einzige Grund, warum ich es zu Ende gelesen habe ist einfach, weil ich das mache. Ich breche Bucher grundsatzlich nicht ab. Das habe ich noch nie getan. Ich denke mir immer wieder, dass es vielleicht noch eine Wende oder Uberraschung geben konnte, die mich uberzeugt, aber nein: Dieser Roman ist einfach nichts fur mich gewesen und irgendwie tut mir das auch leid, weil sehr viele nur Gutes daruber zu sagen hatten. Das ist schon, freut euch! xD 
 Kurz und knapp meine Meinung: 
 1) Der Einstieg ist schwer, verwirrend und ja, auch, wenn es ein "Fantasybuch" ist, so hab ich viel an den Erklarungen gezweifelt. 
 2) Die unsinnige Gewalt in diesem Buch hat mich sehr gereizt. Es gibt einfach zu viele Stellen, an denen die Bosen bose sind, um bose zu sein. Sicher ein dystopisch angehauchtes Buch muss schreckliche Dinge vorweisen konnen, aber dann doch bitte begrundet. Misshandlung von Kindern ohne Sinn und Verstand finde ich echt scheisse. Klar, man konnte damit argumentieren, dass die Leute den Kids wehtun, bevor die Kids den Leuten dort wehtun, aber ein ziemlich seichtes Argument. 
 3)Yay, es ist mal wieder Flucht-Zeit! Wie sollte es auch anders sein, reisst Protagonistin Ruby aus und wir durfen eine ellenlange Flucht miterleben. Es gab kein Ziel fur die Charaktere, weshalb ich hier mal wieder das absolute Crossed-Feeling abbekommen habe. Hin und her, vor und zuruck und noch mal eine Runde im Kreis. Doppel Yay! 
 4) Ruby. Hass. HASS. Sie ist eine weinerliche, unsichere und totunglucke Prota. Klar, sie hat viel durchgemacht und bis zu einem bestimmten Grad fand ich alles nachvollziehbar, vielleicht interessant, aber im Grossen und Ganzen, hatte ich sie am liebsten mit meinen Handen erwurgt. Mich hat ihr Charakter extrem wutend gemacht. Ich hasse Bucher, die ich hasse, weil ich die Charaktere hasse. Meh -.- 
 5)Der Plot uberhaupt. Krafte hier und Farben da und blablabla...ich habe immer noch nicht verstanden, warum die anderen uberhaupt bei Ruby geblieben sind. Zur Holle aber auch! O.o Im Grunde geht es darum, herauszufinden, warum die Jugendlichen "Superkrafte" haben und wo die Grenzen gezogen werden konnen. Fur mich echt nichts neues. 
 6) Noch mehr Gegenspieler. Es gibt gefuhlte 100 Organisationen, die sich hier miteinander verfeinden und alle die Kinder mit ihren Kraften fur ihre Zwecke missbrauchen wollen. Nice one. Es wurde immer unubersichtlicher, wer was weshalb tut und das keine der Gruppen auch nur ansatzweise mal miteinander kommuniziert war seltsam. 
 7)Zu. Cooler Nebencharakter. Danke dafur. 
 8) Das Ende? Hatte mich schocken sollen, aber ich weiss ja nicht...ich kenne das inzwischen aus 5 anderen Bucher und daher war es eben nicht mehr DIE WENDE DES JAHRTAUSENDS... 
 Was soll ich noch sagen? 1 = Did not like it. 
 I DID NOT LIKE IT. Sayonara!

OMG A MUST READ MUST READ!!! The story is sooooo good! I found it similar in some parts to the fifth wave. I CANT BELIEVE RUBY ! She erased herself from Liam 3 my heart just about broke into a million pieces right there, I can't wait for never fade to come in the mail! (So much for a pre order tbh)

I loved this book. It was different and well written. The characters. Oh how I absolutely loved the characters. A huge factor in how much I enjoy a book is how I respond to the main characters. The four Ruby, Liam, Chubs, and Zu were amazing. They went through so much, and they're just children. Don't look at me, I have a lot of feels about these characters. 
 The end of this book absolutely broke me. Seriously. If you need me, I'm just gonna be sat here in the corner, attempting to pick up the shattered pieces of my poor little heart. Ugh, why do I do this to myself? I get emotionally attached, and then when it doesn't turn out how my brain thinks it should, I end up sobbing incoherently about fictional characters. This is only the first book. I hope this isn't setting the tone for the rest of the series, because I don't think I can take it. Really though, whatever happens, this book was great and I can't wait to find out what happens next!

It's about two and three-quarters stars, not quite a three. So much to say here, this will contain some spoilers caution! First of all I purchased this book new and I rarely do that, second-hand and book swap is the way I roll! So let's just say there was quite a bit of hype built up for me. The very first chapter held much promise, I was pleasantly surprised the author Alexandra Bracken didn't dive into a : meet girl, girl likes this and doesn't like this, she is yay tall with blue eyes, etc. it jumped right into the action. But very quickly this "action" just continued to be events rapidly unfolding without any real further explanation as to why and how. It was so vague I couldn't understand a lot of pieces until they were explained much deeper into the book. Now I understand when enticing plot details are left waiting to be unraveled by continuing the story, but this was so poorly executed it did nothing to heighten the books appeal. When she meets Liam, Zu and Chubs, I liked how Bracken didn't have boy and girl gushing over each other right away. There was some real great similes of emotion throughout the book, in fact, even if a lot of it was so cheesy I didn't realize I ordered a plate of nachos. I'm surprised I could even read the part when Ruby put her feet on top of Liam's and they slow-danced next to the fire due to my constant eyerolls. Seriously, is he a love interest or her fucking dad? And Chubs bad-cop roll? Ugh, I...ugh. This was so ridiculously unnecessary, so over the top, so laughable, I just can't get over how predictable and weak his bad attitude was. 
 A lot of others have mentioned a lack of sexual-awakening exploration. Male and females separated for all of their pubescent lives suddenly driven together? There could have been so much potential for awkward, funny, eye-opening reading. There was a small glimpse of that when Ruby tried to shave her legs in the shower, and realized she was sixteen and wrestled with feelings of self-pity and doubt. I liked this part, it was a true glimpse of what the story should have been more like. I feel there should have been more interpersonal struggle, more feelings of confusion and a sense of loss in independence. There was too much other useless fluff that didn't match what I think the original idea of the story is. Children separated from everything and learning to become adults in a scary world. Which brings me to my next point: never in a thousand years would parents willing give up their children, especially to something so vague as an idea of rehabilitation. Sure powers can be scary and overwhelming, but it would never change thousands of bonds of love between mothers and children. Especially if other children were inexplicably dying? An even fiercer attempt to protect them would have evolved. Not a single person would have realized this would have been an extinction of humanity if they continued to execute and punish the only remaining children of their future? That being said, apparently no other country on the planet was having this power development, oh no, only the grand US of A.... Very believable. 
 So the first part of this book was a big wah-wah sobfest. I rolled my eyes so much I couldn't decide if this book or Insurgent was worse (and that was a god awful book). But once they arrived at the camp, it took a much more interesting turn. The other childrens' descriptions of Clancy? I thought it was a reincarnation of Jesus, haha, it was hilarious. I really liked the fact that this wasn't a cookie-cutter love triangle, there was some initial attraction on Ruby's part but I'm glad she didn't "fall for it." 
 Now someone please explain to me this universal taboo that all Young Adult seems to share in a strict lack of sex. Sure there's violence, grief, death, and an absurd masochism in the female lead being both clumsy and prone to get beat up (*coughstephaniemeyerscough*), but sex, such an integral part of growing up, ESPECIALLY in a book like this where genders have been separated, I just don't understand why it's so hush-hush. Teenagers have raging hormones, there will be at least some interest in sex and exploration. I'm not claiming this for all teenagers, but I feel that there is a sad omission to a subject that is both real and integral to growing up. They cuddle and feel each others' heartbeats....it's morning and they wake up. Slow dance next to the fire, look into each other's eyes...unfinished chapter turns into the next morning. Sure there's room for imagination, and maybe some things are better left implied than said, but when it drives me crazy with "did they do it or didn't they?!?" Vagueness is then Detrimental. This brings me to Clancy's mindfuck of Ruby. Did he end up physically raping her or not? I'm still confused about that part because I feel it could be very important to later decisions made in the book. 
 Twist at the end? I didn't see that coming and actually really enjoyed the not so happy ending. This book leaves enough to either be a stand alone, or the first installment. Sadly there are so many fallacies and parts that have a definite plug-into-the-equation feel that I really really struggled with it overall. It was disappointing, it wasn't dark at all, and I think so much potential was wasted.
Loved this but the ending KILLED me

I haven't loved a sci-fi/dystopian book this much since I read Angelfall back in October. The Darkest Minds is kind of similar to The 5th Wave but oh so much better. It had everything: lovable and diverse characters, kick-ass action, and also a super cute (albeit frustrating and tear-worthy) romance. The beginning was a little slow, but about 50 pages in things started to pick up and I couldn't stop reading. It's definitely not a heart-touching and/or meaningful read, but fun and engaging all the same. 
 p.s. THE ENDING OH MY GOD NOOO WHY

reference_books.title: Under the Wide and Starry Sky
reference_books.review_text: Just okay

reference_books.title: Truly Madly Guilty
reference_books.review_text: The premise of the story sounded promising - during a typical neighborhood bbq attended by three couples and three children, something happened to one of the children. But the author sure took her own sweet time getting to that event. I started getting frustrated that it was taking so long to find out what actually happened while we got caught up on the backgrounds of the various characters. But I liked how she alternated narrators and events. There were some chapters that told what happened the day of the bbq and others that took place before and after that event. And I liked the way the story ended - not all the ends were tied up, but it felt right for the characters.

reference_books.title: American Housewife
reference_books.review_text: Dark short stories about unusual housewives, sometimes only tangentially. I'm not a huge fan of short stories in general, but many of these were unusual and interesting.

reference_books.title: At the Water's Edge
reference_books.review_text: I wasn't sure I wanted to read another book set during World War 2, but this one was interesting from the beginning. The three main characters were unlikable from the very beginning - and the two men were still unlikable at the end - but Maddie grew quite a bit. They set off from America to find the Loch Ness monster - partly on a lark, but mostly so Ellis could redeem himself in the eyes of his father, who'd tried to find it years before (and whose adventure ended in embarrassment). The events at the end of the book tied up all the loose ends too conveniently, but the book as a whole was very enjoyable.

reference_books.title: Look Again
reference_books.review_text: 4 stars? 5 stars? I couldn't decide. I was hooked right from the beginning, and even though there was a little too much (cliched) romance between the main character and her boss. I liked her. Once I read that the author was a single mom - like the protagonist - it make more sense. I feel that someone who reads more mysteries would have seen the twist near the end before it happened, but I didn't :)

book_a.title: The Swans of Fifth Avenue
book_a.user_review: The story was fascinating - socialites in Manhattan in the 1950s. I kept looking online to find information about the "swans" who were Truman Capote's good friends, and it was interesting to see how the author incorporated real-life events into her novel. By far the most interesting part of the book was when Capote's short story about the women was published. He'd been listening to their secrets for years, and he used them all - then he was surprised that they were hurt. Understandably, they felt betrayed, and they shunned him completely - not taking his calls or accepting his excuses. The part of the novel leading up to this, though, could have been trimmed considerably. While I enjoyed reading about life in Manhattan at that time, the author went overboard with details about shopping, parties, clothing, and social events.

sample_reviews.review_text: This book has some amazing reviews and I can't help but think, am I reading the same one? I expected a fun read about Truman Capote and the women he loved to gossip about. I made it to page 50 and decided not to dedicate any more of my life to the overwritten and boring prose.

Thanks to Random House and Netgalley for an advanced copy of this book. 
 Well I DNF'd at 20%. I was giving Melanie Benjamin one more try after the disappointment of the Aviator's Wife. She's just not for me. So many words and so little story. Basically in 20% I got that Truman Capote was a deceptive fame-monger who couldn't be trusted and a lot of descriptions of clothes and places. Meh.

A semi-fictional account of Truman Capote and his "swans", the rich, beautiful and influential women of New York. Capote collected stories from his "friends" which he eventually used in a short story exposing them all, even the one woman he actually cared for, Babe Paley. 
 This book sent me into a Google / Wikipedia black hole, looking up all of the characters and their tangled relationships. 
 While the book was a swift read and had a few entertaining sections, it wasn't particularly moving. It only scratches the surface of these relationships and gives only the highlights of events that actually happened. 
 If anything, I was left with the reassurance that relying on beauty, fame or money to sustain you will always lead to loneliness. That and I would like to read more Capote.

Best friends are for telling your secrets but be careful who you trust. Set among the glittering world of the socialites of Manhattan the story transports you to the world of Truman Capote were friendship can go hand in hand with betrayal in the name of 'art'.

Disappointing. 2.5 stars. A lot of light chatter about socialites, all revolving around one mag article Capote wrote. Not satisfying in terms of character development. Loved the cover art, but should have stopped there c

As a fan of Truman Capote's work I couldn't wait to dive into this book. A fun read if you are interested in the New York socialite scene, or find interest in stories about what people will do to be a part of the in crowd. Lovely descriptions of what goes on behind closed doors with the seemingly perfect wives of wealthy men. Truman was as unbearable as I expected, but the author did a good job of providing more to his character simply by including information about his childhood and life behind the scene. Overall I really enjoyed this book. Gave it 4 stars instead of 5 simply because there were some parts that lagged a bit too much for my taste.

This was interesting, as a piece of Americana in the elite socialites of the 50s and 60s, big money, and Truman Capote, but I struggle with fiction from reality. I like to know where the line is and these books inevitably leave me wondering too much. Fans of high society, fashion, gossip columns, etc. will undoubtedly like this, but for me it probably stops at just interesting.

Long time readers of this blog may have gathered that I am a bit of a fan of novels which include well known literary figures. The Swans of Fifth Avenue deals with the friendship between Truman Capote and society icon, Babe Paley. 
 Set primarily in the 1950s and 1960s the novel tells the story of the close friendship between Truman and Babe. The book is filled with the glitz and glamour of life for the wealthy at that time. Champagne is flowing and shopping for fine clothes is what these women live for. Fascinated by the beautiful Babe and the other wealthy women (the swans), Truman soon attaches himself to the group, gossiping with them and playing the part of friend and confidante. 
 This novel posits that Truman's friendship with Babe was more sincere than that he shared with the other women. Perhaps one of the most enjoyable facets of the story is the inner struggle of Babe; a woman who was born and raised to be a beautiful object on the arm of a man, but who longs for something more meaningful. For a time, at least according to the book, Babe's friendship with Truman provided this. 
 But as the years wear on Truman's life takes a turn, his previous successes all but history as he struggles with alcoholism. The writer ends up committing the worst betrayal possible; using the secrets he has learned from the swans in his own work. 
 Full review: http://www.katejwilson.com/2016/01/bo...
Interesting look at that time period. Very small on story.

Brilliantly executed fictionalized account of Truman Capote and his "Swans", the moneyed style makers of New York City in the mid-twentieth century. Heartbreaking and evocative, this was a gorgeous imagining and well worth a read.

I thoroughly enjoyed listening to this book. I loved being enveloped in midcentury NYC with Truman Capote and his swans. While I was familiar with Capote I really didn't know very much about this time of his life and his place in society. This was a fascinating look at the rick and famous of this glamorous era. 
 I'm sure this book benefited from being consumed in audio rather than print. The narrators did a great job bringing Truman to life.

This is a fictional story based on the real people who were Truman Capote and the group of high society women in Manhattan who were his closest friends ("Swans"). The course of their relationship parallels the changes happening to New York society from the 1950's to the 1970's. Very enjoyable read.

I ended up enjoying this story though it was a struggle. There were times that I was frustrated by the total lack of insight into these characters, though that may well have been the point of the story. While the fashion icons of days past had style, grace and sophistication, unlike those of today unfortunately, they proved that money doesn't buy happiness. I enjoy reading about accomplished women. None of these women, with the exception of CZ Guest and perhaps Pamela Harriman, were shown to have accomplished anything beyond their presentation and I don't buy that creating a visually envious life is enough for anyone's soul. And while they all had sadness in their lives and most hard childhoods, who doesn't had sadness. Perhaps I would have enjoyed reading some of their charitable activities, what they did to help others. I'm assuming they did something given the enormous wealth they possessed. But this book does not include that information. I hated all of them, including Truman. We are all flawed, and that I accept, but reading about individuals guided only by their needs to fulfill their narcissistic needs is difficult to tolerate. I love fashion; I love art; I love beauty. This book had that, but the characters were presented as being one-dimensional.
I was looking forward to reading this book but I found the characters boring and the plot sluggish. So sluggish that I couldn't finish it. Needless to say but I didn't care for it.

The Swans of Fifth Avenue is historical fiction based on the life of Truman Capote and his relationships with members of the NYC social elite. The book begins when Truman meets a group of socialites he refers to as his "swans." At the center of this group is Babe Paley, perhaps Truman's closest friend throughout his life. 
 Throughout the book we catch glimpses into what might have happened during events in history, such as Truman's famous Black and White Ball, the publication of In Cold Blood, and the infamous unfinished last novel that was published in excerpts and caused a rift between Truman and his NYC society friends. 
 Note: I received a free ARC of this title in exchange for an honest review.

Oh, so boring. I should have guessed so from the blurb (which I deliberately don't read, so I deserve it I guess). A book about "the glamour and perfumed and smoky atmosphere of New York's high society". 
 I don't like socialites, I don't like books about socialites, I don't find them entertaining, I don't find them interesting. I don't care about Truman Capote and Babe Paley. And the book is filled with tales about them and about Truman's beloved swans, the society women who were his best friends. 
 I wonder how the life of these people looked interesting to them. I would definitely find a job or a hobby. How can you wake up late, lunch, shop, and gossip all day long. I have no clue. 
 Book full saccharine and very boring. 2 generous stars.

I enjoyed previous books by Melanie Benjamin but found this book to be very poorly written. The book traces the close friendship between writer Truman Capote and socialite Babe Paley until a scandalous short story written by Capote exposes personal information about Babe and destroys their friendship. There were constant exclamation marks (almost like reading the diary of a 6th grade girl) and all of the characters were shallow and concerned with appearances but also had penetrating psychological insight into their motivations and flaws. I normally enjoy historical fiction about real people but this was dull and pointless.

I tried to get through this book, but I gave up on it about a hundred pages from the finish. I'm fascinated by Truman Capote, but reading about him in this book was not enjoyable. It was hard to like any of the characters except Babe, but even there I just could not take another page of this book. I'm not usually harsh in my reviews but I just really didn't like this one.

2016 368 pages 
 a gossipy account of New York high brown ladies during the 60's. Truman capote names them the swans because of the beauty and stature. Truman writes about all of them, unlocking fury for the secrets he told of their private life. 
 I found this interesting. Melanie wrote Aviator's wife. after reading that, I did not like Mr. Lindberg. After Swans, I did not like Capote either. Man hater? interesting writing, but a bit confused.

I could not finish this book, a re-imagining of events involving Truman Capote and the uber socialites he palled with, such as Babe Paley. He betrayed them in 1975 by publishing a "tell all" article in Esquire Magazine. 
 This book was simply tedious and sad. Also I was listening to the audio version, and I didn't care for either reader (Cassandra Campbell and Paul Boehmer). She is overly breathy and imho mispronounces too many words and he was just "meh." I probably could overlook their performances if the writing was better but oh well.

Interesting concept - tells stories of Truman Capote's interactions with Manhattan's most elite society ladies, especially Babe Paley, whom he dubs his "Swans." I think I liked it, but I wouldn't read it again. Entertaining, but sad. Interesting commentary on the emptiness of fame, money, and notoriety.

My low rating is because I really and not a fan of character based novels. They are not my typical read unless super good. I just finished a great page turner and the lives of NY socialites seems "Oh Hum".

This was a guilty-pleasure I picked up from the discharge pile at the library while I was working. "A book about the friendship between Truman Capote and Babe Paley? Why the hell not?" It was fun to read about the icons of my childhood/teen years. Like Melanie Benjamin, I grew up in the suburbs of a small city. I didn't exactly relate to most of my peers, and instead of reading "Seventeen" and "Cosmopolitan", I'd read "Vanity Fair", "Vogue" and my Dad would pick me up copies of French "Vogue" at this newsstand in the city. I had pictures of Babe Paley mixed in with the requisite (for me) pics of Katharine Hepburn and Susan B. Anthony on my folders and locker, and I wished I could go back in time and attend Capote's Black and White Ball. So this was a bit of nostalgia for me. But mostly, it was a bittersweet experience, because the people I looked up to and the things I aspired to when I was sixteen are so different from what I'm all about as an adult.

The Swans of Fifth Avenue by Melanie Benjamin is a 2016 Delecorte Press publication. I was provided a copy of this book by the publisher and Netgalley in exchange for an honest review. 
 I'm in the same boat as the author when it comes to my memories of Truman Capote. I remember him in "Murder by Death", and have very vague memories of his making the rounds on the late night talk shows, pretty much making a fool of himself. But, later in life, I grew curious about Truman's early life, his creation of the 'true crime novel' with "In Cold Blood", and what led to his massive celebrity, and ultimately his downfall. 
 I watched the movie "Capote" as well as the lesser known "Infamous" and read Gerald Clarke's biography. However, none of these works truly delved into Truman's intimate relationships with the 'Swans" since the focus was either on years he spent working on "In Cold Blood' or on his unorthodox southern upbringing and his friendship with Harper Lee. This book only skirts around these elements of Truman's life, only reminding us of his bitterness and hurt over his mother's abandonment of him, the one person he longed for and longed to impress more than any other. 
 This story is a work of fiction, and is dedicated to "Breakfast at Tiffany's, to the perfect and best dressed icon of fashion, Babe Paley, and the relationship Truman shared with Babe, and her "Swans". 
 "The best time to leave a party is when the party's just beginning" - Diana Vreeland 
 I was immediately caught up in the magic and glamour of the fifth avenue crowd, the behind the scenes look at the lives of Slim Keith, Babe Paley, Marella Agnelli, Gloria Guinness, and Pamela Churchill Hayward Harriman. 
 All these ladies lived within the confines of high society rules and demands, never daring to stray too far off course. Marriage wasn't about love, it was about money, power, and position, and business. There were divorces, affairs, and betrayals, but their lives were as dull as a butter knife until Truman Capote waltzed in and turned everything on its ear. He brought with him a certain charm and grace, and drew the stuffy high society crowd into his web quite seamlessly, making them wonder how they had ever gotten along without him. He cajoled, and romanced these ladies, offering them a shoulder to lean or to cry on. But, while he was attentive to them all, I have no doubt Truman really did love Babe and of course she loved him. 
 'Languid, Lovely, Lonely; the swans arched their beautiful necks and turned to gaze at him as he stood rooted to the shore, his feet encased in mud. They fluttered their eyelashes, rustled their feathers, and glided over to their leader, the most beautiful of all. There was no sound save the sigh of their graceful bodies drifting across the water. Watching from the shore, wringing his hands, willing himself still for once, even as he had a childish urge to hop first on one foot, then the other, he was filled with the old fear; that he wasn't good enough, brave enough, handsome enough, tall enough-------- 
 Enough. 
 Still, he hoped, he dreamed, he waited; holding his breath, he fixed his gaze on the most dazzling of them all, the lead swan. Like he was making a birthday wish, he blew his breath toward her and her alone, praying the wind would catch it and carry it to her, a prayer. As she bent her lovely head toward the other swans, she was seen to listen gravely, as if this was a most solemn rite; as if there was no other topic in the world that needed her attention, no wars and deaths and treaties and dilemmas. Only this, his happiness. The other swans whispered, whispered; one hissed, but he could not tell which it was. Then they broke ranks; into a preordained formation, and perfect arc surrounding their leader, who remained utterly still, her head bowed in reflection. Then she raised her head, turned, and looked at him, still standing on the shore. They all turned to look; the swans, with one choreographed movement, beckoned to him with their blinding-white wings that were arms, he saw for the first time. Arms as white as snow leopards; whiter than pearls around the swans' fragile necks. The lead swan did not beckon. But her eyes, those dark glittering pools of unfathomable loneliness, never left his as his feet took wing; as he skimmed the surface of the water, not a swan, no never would he be one of them, and even then he knew it. He was a nymph, a hovering dragonfly- a sprite, landing among the swans with a burst of delighted laughter. They laughed as well, all of them- except for their leader. She only continued to watch him as he was passed about from one to the other like a new baby. When the swans were finished, they sat him down on the water and took up their positions once more, he found himself between them and the lead swan. Uncertain, but dizzy with joy and belonging, he took a step toward her, still marveling at how the water was not water but the most polished marble beneath his feet, the feathers on the swans were not feathers but fur and cashmere and silk and satin, threaded together, hand-sewn to their disciplined bodies that were designed only for adornment. And HIS swan now- that was how he thought of her, and would forever, naming her, claiming her, forgetting already that it hadn't been his privilege to do the choosing- held out her hand, and he took it, as trustingly as a child. 
 Mischievously as an imp. 
 Then the swans closed ranks about him. 
 And has home." 
 I think the author's insights into Truman's psyche, the type of person he was deep down, before and after his meteoric thrust into fame and fortune was probably spot on. I think she may have nailed it perfectly. She also did a great job of making the privileged life of a socialite seem shallow, hollow, and empty, tearing down the illusion of glamour and excitement to expose the dark and more depressing aspects of the lifestyle. 
 These women were dying for excitement when Truman stormed into their lives and penetrated the darkest corners of their existence. He even forged a close friendship with Babe's philandering husband, William, who was initially put off by Truman, not quite knowing what to make of him at first. 
 This set up, based on true events, made for some very interesting characterizations, and frankly, none of the people examined here are all that likeable. They seemed morally bankrupt, living without any real directions, admired solely for their beauty, trapped by the rules and laws of society. This atmosphere fit Truman to a tee, I must say. 
 But, in the end, fast fame, coupled with a nasty and cutting side to Truman's personality, that existed all along, brewing just beneath the surface, caused the house of cards to collapse spectacularly, and when it did, it took Truman by surprise, having grossly underestimated his swans, and gave me a look at Babe Paley, more than any other character, that left me feeling bereft on her behalf, as her immense sorrow and loneliness was palpable, making me furious at Truman and heartbroken for them both, at the same time. In the end, I came away feeling sorry for Babe on many levels, because her life never seemed to be her own. She was always under pressure to be perfect, was never more than an extension of her powerful husband, and her friends had no depth, thinking nothing about indulging in affairs, and resorting to catty gossip. But, when she met Truman, Babe came to life for the first time, and then faced the ultimate of betrayals. 
 One of the most interesting events that truly highlighted Truman's acerbic nature was in regards to the former socialite, Ann Woodward, who was suspected of murdering her husband. Truman often referred to her as "Miss Bang, Bang", even to her face. But, of course, as you shall see, his cruelty extended much further than mere name calling, which shocking results. 
 I also came away with a wistful sense of nostalgia for the glamour of New York in the fifties and sixties. Long gone are the days of 'dressing for lunch' and fabulous and newsworthy parties. Casual dress, pantsuits, jeans and T-shirts were allowed in the most exclusive clubs and restaurants, effectively ending this age once and for all. 
 Overall, I thought the author pinpointed the era, the atmosphere, the personalities, and events perfectly. No, the people are not easy to feel strong emotions for most of the time, except perhaps intense anger at the way Truman gave himself over to his insecurities, his perceived power, and his belief he was better somehow, that the hearts of his friends were something he could play with and use for his own gain. 'The Swans' did show some mettle in the end, closing ranks around each other, effectively. 
 This book is like a portrait, frozen in time, a rare glimpse into high society behind closed doors, a true life cautionary tale, filled with bitter poignancy. I was fascinated, outraged, mystified, and saddened, but came away with a firm respect for some of the players, and for a world that no longer exist, for better or worse. It's seductive, alluring, and absorbing, well written, and reads like a Shakespearean tragedy, an epic love story, that ends badly, but which left an indelible imprint on many, for a long time to come. 
 Most of these events are long forgotten now, so, many modern readers may not fully grasp the reality of this life, but it was all true, and remarkable in its own way. As I finished this novel, I was left with a grudgingly admitted respect for Babe Paley, who held her head high through scandal, heartbreak, and most impressively as she faced her own mortality, whilst the person she loved most in the world, stuck a knife in her back, cruelly twisting it for the entire world to see. 
 I highly recommend this book for those who love historical fiction, and would also suggest taking the time to read the books the author suggested, for more insight. 
 4.5 stars

Note: I received this book from the author/publisher in exchange for an honest review. 
 This is one of those books where I feel like I'm missing something. I see all the reviews saying how engrossing and fascinating and...I didn't feel that. The book started off very interesting and I spent a lot of time googling characters in the book to match names to faces- the plus to a historical fiction novel based on real people. I really enjoy the era- was mostly raised on movies and TV of the late '50s and into the '60s- so it was fun to get a semi-behind-the-scenes look at life during such a famous time period for fashion, media, and the stars. But after awhile the fun wore off and I got bored with the gossiping and the drama and the socialite lifestyle. I can only imagine how these women felt- it seemed like they did the same thing day after day, forever lunching, shopping, pleasing their men. If the point of the story was to show how dull their lives were- mission accomplished, I was terribly bored from about the halfway point on. This could have been a much shorter book since most of the important parts took up a small portion of the overall text. But the story was stretched out and dragged on, leaving me feeling quite underwhelmed. 
 Interestingly enough, I had planned on reading In Cold Blood early this year (like, next book after I finished catching up on 2015 books I said I would read...so the next book after this book) and was interested to see that Capote's book sparked drama and mishaps. I look forward to actually giving it a read to get the full effect of the mood from Swans.

There's a fair amount of grumbling about this book: how shallow! How vapid! These people had more money than sense! Truman Capote was a terrible person! 
 Guess what? I loved every page of this story. It's inspired me to reread Clarke's _Capote_ and all my favorite Capote books again. It's gossip at its finest and best. If you're a Capote fan like me, and you're always a little wistful for the glamour of a New York that predates you by a few decades, read this one!

Do yourself a favor. Read the biographies of all the main players in this book, especially Capote's. Then read Capote's "La Cote Basque". Congratulations! You've just read the true version of this weak fictionalization, only played out in real-life, with footnotes, and vastly more well-written.

2.5 What sad, superficial people these were. Their stories are cautionary tales about the constant pursuit of money, status and access. Benjamin's writing is at times interesting but it is often tiresome and repetitive.

The Swans of Fifth Avenue had all the makings for being a really great book, but the story was so scattered. The story was very indulgent. A lite gossipy read that I wanted more from. Melanie Benjamin tried to accomplish too much, different perspectives and various lesser story lines, that the main point gets lost in the end (the friendship between Truman Capote and Babe Paley). The cohesion in the novel was better in the beginning but the break down of the friendship wasn't explored enough. Maybe more historical references would have been helpful to note the changing times and the effects on the characters. In the end the story was ok and made me want to read unanswered prayers the short story Capote wrote that lost him his society swans.
Historical fiction about Truman Capote and his society muses.

I've always liked Melanie Benjamin, but now I see that she can be saccharine 
 And has been before. This story of Truman Capote's and Babe Paley's friendship has so little substance that the faults of writing and tone stood out. This whole sixties moment of high society in New York was never that interesting and is certainly not worth revisiting. Benjamin adds nothing to the scene.
"The poor soul wouldn't know a wild oat if it were wrapped in a Louis Vuitton handbag." Good grief, these people...

DNF 1.5. There are way too many books out there to read for me to read this one until the end. I can't stand the characters and it's honestly boring as all get out. Aviator's wife and Mrs. Tom Thumb were way better. Her writing is not bad though, so I'll give her the half star and round up.
