This was an advanced reader's edition. I had been anticipating Miss Benjamin's next book for quite some time! I was not disappointed! This story takes you into the lives of these special women and their interaction with Truman. There is love, hate, turmoil, anguish and Truman! To be honest, I despise the man! To know why, you must read this novel!!

Clearly the author is taken with the glam and beautiful people of NYC during the 60's and 70's. I found the book as superficial as the people. I felt for the protagonist but did not really get into the book. Sorry.

Writer Truman Capote beguiles a group of socialites into telling him gossipy stories of life among the New York elite, then betrays them by publishing their tales in this fictionalized version of a 1965 literary scandal. It's an interesting story that made for a fairly quick read, though it's a little heavy-handed at times, and I'm not sure the last chapter is necessary (though I'm not going to tell you why...)

4 1/2 stars 
 See my review and others here: http://onceuponatime-bookblog.blogspo... 
 In this wonderful novel, Melanie Benjamin portrays the story (and ultimate betrayal) between Truman Capote and his "swans" - famous New York socialites of the 1960s. These women were basically well-known because of their marriage to rich and successful men. There jobs were basically to look gorgeous, socialize with the right people, and spend lots and lots of their husband's money. The favorite of Capote's swans was Babe Paley, wife of CBS founder Bill Paley and the story centers around her, but intertwines the story of the other women as well. 
 I did not know much about these people (or this time period) before reading this book, but Benjamin brought it to life with such energy and showed not only the glamour, but the ambition and loneness and betrayal as well. These women's lives were so far from my comprehension, but I found them extremely intriguing. I thought that the novel was not only beautiful written and well-research, but entertaining and addicting as well. I read it in only a few days (which is rare for me at this point in my life) and cannot wait to go back and read the author's previous novels.

Most of the books I've read this year lacked depth in the lead characters. This book fulfilled what I'd been missing, strong character studies of the two lead characters, plus depth and background in the entire entourage. Ms. Benjamin painted a vivid picture of life and culture in the late 60s and early 70s, and I was fascinated by the lifestyles of these remarkable, yet flawed, women. While I'd also enjoyed another of her books, The Aviator's Wife, I found The Swans of Fifth Avenue to be an even better read. Bravo!

Wow, I was not expecting this book to be what it is. I learned a lot about Truman Capote, which I had read a little about in "The Mockingbird Next Door". Next I need to watch the movie "Capote" I think. "Trueheart" was quite the little conniving liar it seems.

This was a heartbreaking depiction of the sacrifice and betrayal of the swans of "high society". It is difficult to understand the motivations that govern the women of the upper class. Their lives appear to be completely defined by a fashionable image of distorted elegance. Too thin, too rich, bone crushingly lonely, they gravitate to a sycophantic betrayer in Truman Capote, who feeds off their desperation with a glee that is difficult to understand or observe. All the women depicted in this novel die young, in their 50's and 60's. You have to feel that this uniform early death indicates the stress of their misdirected lives. May God have mercy on them.

Gorgeously written, with great characterization. I'm not quite sure how I feel about the little twist near the end. In a way it works, but in another way it feels a bit much. On the whole, though, this was an enjoyable read.
Ho, Hum. boring.

I wasn't a fan of this. I didn't see the point of their story and didn't feel sympathy or interest in these characters. I understand the time period and appreciate the fact that these stories are told but it wasn't my cup of tea. I was just waiting for it to be over -- I felt like it should have ended a lot sooner than it did.

This was the audiobook edition borrowed from library. I had been waiting for this for quite awhile. Couldn't get past the first CD. Just did not hold any interest to me. May try a print read in the future. I really do not like not finishing what I start, but bent my own rules in this case.

I don't know that I've ever read a book and felt the tone landed on "breathless," but here we are. As with her previous books, Melanie Benjamin takes real people and what is known of them and fleshes out a narrative. In Swans, we're keeping up with the top socialites of the first half of the 20th century, concentrating specifically on Babe Paley and her friendship with Truman Capote. It's a story of quiet desperation and a bond of friendship that can't be trusted. It's not cynical, simply honest about the world these women ran in and how the expectations were exhausting. 
 Also, Truman Capote is an asshole, but we all knew that, I think.

Audiobook. Couldn't stop listening, I have always been intrigued by Truman Capote. This book is a fictionalized account of his relationships with his socialite friends in NYC and how it all came crashing to an end.

I read Breakfast at Tiffany's a couple years ago, and the movie is one I watch at least every year. So I had to read this book obviously. Historical fiction about a writer? Give me all the books like this and I will be forever happy. 
 The Swans of Fifth Avenue did not end up being exactly as I thought it would be. For one it's told by multiple POV's, from our two main characters Truman and Babe to the Swans and even Babe's husband. You all know that this is usually something that bothers me, strangely it didn't in this book. I thought the different narrators were actually done well, though it gave the book a feel of being a collection of connected short stories rather than a novel. For another it's not a normal love story. Truman is gay and Babe is married, and they love each other not really as lovers. The whole situation is kinda messed up, after what ends up happening with Truman's rise to fame. 
 If you want to read a book where you like and empathize deeply with the characters, this book is probably not for you. While you feel sorry for Babe and Truman, both characters almost feel like aliens. In fact all of the characters feel that way. All so rich and different and above the rest of the world, it's like they aren't part of it. Now I found this interesting and enjoyed it actually, but it's not for everyone. 
 I gave the book 3 stars on Goodreads. It was entertaining, and I would probably read it again in a couple years.

It pains me to write this, but I DNF this book. The list of books I Did Not Finish is low and I hate adding to that list. Really.But I just couldn't get myself to get into this one. When I went a week without picking it up, I knew that - for right now - it was a lost cause. 
 The Swans of Fifth Avenue was the second historical fiction book that I picked up in one month. Which is two more than I have probably read in my lifetime. Needless to say, it is not my favorite genre, but it's also not my style to give up on a book. I found myself skimming past a lot of names and then getting stuck on a scene wondering for too long if this part was fiction or the author's artistic license to describe the setting, etc. 
 Not all attempts are successful and I unfortunately have to take this DNF.
An interesting fictionalized look at Truman Capote and his 'swan's who were high-society leaders in the 60s and 70s.
The characters were not likable and their problems were all tied up in their obsession with being rich. Not for me.

book_b.title: Crenshaw
book_b.user_review: I'm probably not the best judge of this book, because one of the 5th-graders told me it was really good, and it's definitely a story for that age group. Jackson's imaginary friend is a cat named Crenshaw, who appears to help him when he's under stress. His parents have a hard time supporting their family, and they live on-and-off in their van. Not a whole heck of a lot happens, and I finished it so quickly not because it was a compelling story, but because the chapters were so short.

sample_reviews.review_text:
** spoiler alert ** 
 I had really high hopes for this book. I think it may have been over-hyped by bloggers and the publishing industry. There are aspects of this book that I loved - REALLY loved. The ability for the narrator to be unflinchingly honest about hunger, homelessness, and the struggle of the working poor in America WAS outstanding. This book is definitely important in that regard and I am thrilled to have purchased it for my library and will be sharing it with many students. Here is what I didn't like about it - the character didn't resonate with me emotionally, and he felt very flat. I wanted more about his relationship with Crenshaw to be explored, and I even wanted more from that relationship. Even when his dad has MS, it is just mentioned as a blip, and I felt that it needed for be addressed a bit deeper too. I can understand how things didn't end up in a near package - that IS life, even if we want something different. The hopefulness is there, and even though things are still rocky, there is a resolution about being more honest between the family members about what is going on in their lives.

Stories about families in financial crisis need to be told more often. I am grateful to Applegate for taking on the task. This book is a fast read and Jackson, along with the people he loves, is an endaering and authentic character. Great read-aloud for upper elementary.

I wished I have my own Crenshaw. Yep, it's a cool name for a cat. I don't think I've ever had an imaginary friend. 
 This book reveal a social issue that is seldom being talked about. The issue about homelessness. On the outside Jackson's family looked fine, but they struggled to make ends meet after several setbacks like his father's sickness and the lost of jobs. His parents had to hold several part-time jobs and every month they were in danger of eviction from their rental apartment. They are hardworking, but life just threw them some curveballs that hit them hard. Readers can feel how humiliating it was to be homeless. The uncertainty, the shame, and the fear. 
 Jackson's family became homeless for a few months when he was in first grade. It seemed that it will happen again. And then, Crenshaw appears.
A simple and heartwarming story about friends and family.

This was an amazing book, so relevant to so many of our kids today. This is this years Bluebonnet book that hits you on a deep meaningful level, one that sticks with you long after you finish reading it!

Well it is closer to release date so here it goes 
 Crenshaw by Katherine Applegate 
 Age Range: 8 - 12 years 
 Hardcover: 256 pages 
 Publisher: Feiwel & Friends (September 22, 2015) 
 EGalley provided by Feiwel and Netgalley free in return for an honest review. 
 So this story showed up in my inbox at Netgalley and it is by an award winning author so I said Ok and went for it. I finished the story in under two hours and then sat on a review for two weeks. This is a tale of an unusual friendship between a boy and a large cat creature named Crenshaw. Fans of Japanese animation will find many similarities between Crenshaw and Studio Ghibli stories and characters (Totoro, fantastic mr fox etc) And while I did think Ms. Applegate' earlier acclaimed novel about a gorilla named Ivan told a story that fostered good dialogue, this novel seems to be trying to force an issue into it rather than letting the tale tell itself. 
 Jackson knows something is wrong in his family. His Dad can't get work since getting ill, and his Mom works two jobs and there never seems to be enough food to eat. Then there is this latest yard sale where absolutely everything they own is being sold to make some money leaving Jackson and his sister with just what they can out in a trash bag. Along comes Crenshaw, Jackson' imaginary friend to help him out and get him through this hard time. 
 I am not a huge fan of a stories written -with an agenda- however, a great novel dealing with relatable kids going through becoming homeless is relevant. My problem is less with the subject and more with the execution. I could never tell if this was supposed to be a serious story, or a flight of fantasy. And the ending was a little too fairytale for this subject as well. Despite the seriousness of the subject matter, the story is actually pretty light on well, a story. It felt like a junior novella not a complete novel. If the cover and Crenshaw were more relevant to the story and a little less cartoony then possibly I would rate this higher. I also might be suffering from a bit of expectation letdown. I expected a fantasy, but got a completely different story. 
 All that said though, it is a story that brings up something worth talking about, and that is homelessness, and its effects on families. So, be prepared to have an honest discussion with your children about what we tell them and why as parents we feel the need to shelter our kids from hard truths.

My 5 year old son and I listened to this on audiobook. He was delighted by the cat and laughed out loud on numerous occasions. This book may have been written for an older audience (8 and up), but younger audiences can enjoy it as well.
Excellent for upper elementary! I loved when Crenshaw compared the waiting room for invisible friends with a teacher's lounge!

I really don't get why this book is getting such high ratings. Maybe kids like this book more than I do? But to me this book just fell flat. I was expecting something magical, instead I got an imaginary friend who didn't do much of anything or alleviate the problems that Jackson was having in any way whatsoever. There was pretty much no point to him being there. Then there was Jackson and his family, who had issues with poverty and impending homelessness (and past homelessness), but I didn't feel that there plight was written well enough to actually feel much empathy to or for it. All I could think of, from a teacher's perspective, was that this would be a good book to show that not all homeless people live on the street. That...lack of resonance does not bode well for my liking a book, because I SHOULD feel more, and if I was reading this book to my students I'd want THEM to feel more (like the feelings I get when I read the far superior and shorter book "Fly Away Home" by Eve Bunting). 
 One personal connection I did draw between myself and Jackson, however, was him wanting his parents to keep him in the loop of what was going on / be honest. When I was 11 lots of shit went down in my family, and suffice to say I was really agitated to be kept in the dark, but yet at the same time I was expected to cook meals for my siblings and watch over them. It makes no sense to keep your kids in the dark about serious issues in order to "protect" them, when they are already heaped with more responsibility than many their age. If they know that something is going on and they have the maturity level to process it and understand, not telling them just stresses them out more. So yeah I totally understood Jackson's point of view in that respect, but overall this book was not my cup of tea, coffee or juice.

As I read this book, I wondered about Applegate's intentions in writing it. I found it to be a gentle way to introduce some students to the idea of homelessness, and to also show some understanding to those who might have experienced it. I found the somewhat-sudden ending a little jarring. I liked the fact that Applegate wrote about a family with two parents and that even they can strugggle, included helpful librarians and teachers, and some humor. However, I would have liked to know a little more about Crenshaw. The imaginary friend idea could lead to some interesting conversations with students. Ironically, I read this book just a few hours after Mac Barnett's Leo: A Ghost Story. In both cases, who does or doesn't see the ghost/imaginary friend, and what physical presence could they actually have? (None in reality, questionable in the books.)

Katherine Applegate is too good for this. 
 Applegate has been among my favorite authors since I was a kid. I love Animorphs, I like Remnants, and I like The One and Only Ivan. Applegate understands what kids want out of a book and why kids read better than almost any other MG author I know of. She writes books about complex topics that are accessible for kids, and that still speaks to older readers. There aren't many MG authors I read just for fun, but even as I get older, I still enjoy Applegate's books the way I did when I was younger. That's why I'm so disappointed in this book. This book, for the most part, just doesn't feel like an Applegate book. It feels like a less smart, less insightful imitation of her. This isn't a terrible book, but it does lack most of what makes most Applegate books so effective for me. 
 I think the biggest problem is in the structure of the novel. There are (sort of) two stories here, one told in flashback about when Jackson and his family were homeless, and one set in the present about their family trying not to be homeless. And I'm a little confused about which story was supposed to be the primary one. Both of them feel like they should be in service of the other - neither of them feels like they're supposed to be the main story. You can tell a story in flashback, but it didn't feel like Applegate was trying to do that. The flashback sections are equal parts narrative summary and action, creating a disconnect from them that makes them feel secondary. That's why it's sort of confusing that they take up so much of the book. Applegate can't seem to decide if they're meant to be a setup or a main plot. As for the sections set in the present, there's just not much to say about them. There's very little story in them, no real conflict that Jackson has to overcome. It's honestly more of his parents' conflict than his. The book is called Crenshaw, but Crenshaw isn't actually in it that much - Jackson's parents are shown to be supporting figures a lot more than Crenshaw is. If this had been an adult book about trying to support your kids while being poor, I could picture it working. But as a kids book, this story just doesn't work. 
 The effect of all this is that Jackson's character arc feels very didactic and rushed. I understand, this is a kids book, you can't be too subtle or else kids won't get it. But there's nothing in the story that really warrants an arc for Jackson - the flashbacks happen so far before the main story that they don't really affect things very much, and there's so little main story that Jackson can't really grow from it. So at the end of the novel, Applegate sort of just tells us that Jackson went through all these changes, and we have to take her word for it. It's a shame that this is how things happened, because Jackson was actually a pretty well-developed character. Applegate's characterization techniques feel a little simple to me, now that I'm not a kid anymore, but she does flesh him out pretty well, and a compelling story could've been told about him. But I find it difficult to tell what Applegate was even going for, structure-wise. At different points in the novel, I thought maybe Jackson's arc could've worked better if Applegate had given us more bits with Crenshaw, or if she had only told the flashback story, or if she had cut the flashback story entirely, or if she had just thrown everything out except his characterization and started from scratch. Who knows what would've made it work? The book is too muddled for any clear vision to shine through. 
 Just like I don't understand what Applegate was going for structure-wise, I'm confused about her intentions on a larger level. Specifically, I'm not sure why she decided to write this book. Or maybe I do understand why, and I just don't want to accept it. See, the thing is, this book kind of feels like Applegate wrote it because she was appealing to award committees, kind of the literary equivalent of Oscar Bait. She's writing about poverty and homelessness, the kind of topic that wins awards, and I see no other reason to include Crenshaw, who seems to be a cross between Hobbes and The Cat in the Hat. But I really, really don't want to believe that one of my favorite authors wrote something just because she wanted another Newbury. And, to be entirely fair, I do see sincerity in how she writes about poverty and homelessness. I really do think she might have something to say about these topics, something that could help homeless kids through this sort of situation. After all, she was quite poor herself before Animorphs was a success, and her husband was homeless himself in his twenties. And that does come through in the story. The most riveting parts of the story tend to be parts when Jackson overhears his parents discussing their poverty and impending homelessness, and flashback sections when Jackson's parents try to entertain him and make things okay through their bad situation. And that's why that lack of focus, both in structure and intent, are so frustrating to me. Somewhere, beneath all of this laziness and pandering, there is a good story. But then I read sections like Jackson's interactions with Crenshaw, and Applegate's horribly cheesy attempts to flesh out Jackson's social life, and I lose that feeling. 
 Given all that, a three-star rating may seem a little generous. But there are good sections to this book. It's not an actively painful book to read, and apart from some of the narrative summary in the flashbacks, there's nothing actively wrong with most individual scenes. As I said, Jackson is a very well-rendered character, and Applegate's writing is smooth and efficient as ever. But the whole of this book is less than the sum of its parts. And okay, maybe I'm being a little generous because I love Applegate so much. But I wouldn't recommend this book. The One and Only Ivan wasn't a perfect book, but there, Applegate had something defined she wanted to say, and a clear vision of how she wanted to say it. I don't sense that here. I hope Applegate doesn't continue down this path of pandering and muddling her intent, because I really do love her old writing, and I don't want to read any more like this.

Thursday night I was standing in the brightly colored children's section of the bookstore, I held three books in my hand and knew I could barely afford one. I put back the intriguing The Secret of Dreadwillow Carse and a new book by the beloved Karen Cushman, Greyling's Song. I did that thing that I'd always imagined doing but never dared. I took home Crenshaw and returned it the following Monday. 
 That which piqued my interest was that it was by the same author as The One and Only Ivan, a book I was sure I was going to love and wasn't sure I didn't already own digitally. It also had a boy and a cat on the cover, and was somehow about this cat being able to talk, so therefore slightly magical. I rarely watch movie trailers this day, so I didn't even read the book flap, trusting enough in these previous criteria that the book was worth full retail price. 
 I didn't return the book only because I read it, but also because I didn't really want to own it. 
 Crenshaw was a short and interesting novel about poverty and homelessness from the perspective of a child, Jackson, but also about the line between needing an 'adult' honesty from your parents, sharing in the family problems and being honest not just about problems but about your needs. 
 Crenshaw is the name of an imaginary cat who is at least five feet tall, likes bubble baths and walking on two feet. He was the star-by-proxy and was so enjoyable to read. I could easily see this book being turned into a charming movie, with Cary Elwes voicing him. But I'm biased because of his performance as The Baron in two Ghibli movies. 
 This book isn't very complicated, and yet it is. The main character is ten, and the novel sets out to accomplish a single, complex point: deal with the possibility of being homeless. I will spoil for you the fact that this is done with some fine-feeling and a happy ending, but I won't hash out the details. Whatever you do, do read this, to your child, at the beach, while taking the train to Grand Central. 
 Do it for Jackson or do it for Crenshaw.

** spoiler alert ** 
 I received an e-galley of Crenshaw from NetGalley. 
 I really liked this book, and I think the young patrons at my library will, too. Crenshaw is a wonderful novel that is mostly realistic but with a hint of magic. I was, admittedly, skeptical when I heard Applegate's newest book was about homelessness, but it's handled in a way that makes the issue not very traumatic, and the aspect of Crenshaw being an imaginary friend helps lighten the mood at any intense parts. However, I can see the argument that the novel may handle the issue of homelessness (which in this case, mostly manifests itself in the family not always having enough to eat and generally doing without extras, as well as a stint of living out of their minivan in the past) a little too lightly. Overall, though, I think it's a good way to introduce the issue to young children, especially those who have never had to worry about their family's stability. 
 Much of the novel is a flashback, and as such, there's not a great deal of action. I think the emphasis on flashbacks may deter some readers. I found myself getting near the end and wondering when something big would actually happen and how it would wrap up so quickly. However, there are a few very suspenseful pages towards the end. Also, I thought I knew exactly what would become of Crenshaw at the end, but I surprised, pleasantly so, and it's a twist that I think kids will especially love. Overall, a quick (less than 90 minutes!) read about some serious issues handled with respect and humor, if not complete realism.

This book was okay but nothing really stood out to me after reading it. This story's lead character basically deals with facts vs imaginary things, since he aspires to be a scientist while his imaginary friend keeps popping in out of nowhere. His imaginary friend from when he was young revisits him only in times of trouble, when he really needs him, sort of how we retreat back to our innocent selves when unsure or frightened. I don't think this book handled the concept well. There was hardly any plot, or anything significant that happened, just a passage of events describing Jackson's life. There was so much more room to elaborate on Crenshaw, Jackson's journey growing up, and the other imaginary friends from his friend and dad that were suddenly introduced near the end of the story. This book has the potential to be so much more intriguing and haunting, and to resonate better with readers.

Full Review: http://pattisbooknook.blogspot.com/20... 
 Jackson is a fifth-grader whose family has fallen on hard times. The plausible reasons for this are revealed throughout the story, which is done in a well-paced way that allows the reader to connect with the family's hardships. I thought her depiction of his parent's glass half-full positivity inspiring. I hope young readers will be grateful for what they have and think carefully about how they can help those who don't. There are many good takeaways from the book 
 I appreciate the way Applegate tackles tough issues that kids face and does it in a heartfelt, easily understandable, and appropriate manner. As a parent, I would love nothing more than to shelter my kids from the harsh threats of the world. Unfortunately, since this isn't reality, it is wonderful to have stories that tackle difficult subjects well. 
 I was a bit surprised that Crenshaw was more of a background character than I originally thought he would be. However, his representation of comfort through a tumultuous time was the crucial point, no matter what animal form that took. I'm sure Applegate carefully considered an animal that matched the traits needed. Also, imaginary friends bring joy and help fill any voids, and I love the idea that they will always be around when needed the most. I wish books like this had been given to me as a child, I'm so impressed with the great literary choices our children have today.

** spoiler alert ** 
 Hmm.. I bought this book for a 9 year old. Her mom read it to her and then she told me to read it so we could discuss. After I finished, my first thought was to apologize. I said, "wow. I'm sorry I accidentally bought your daughter this terribly depressing book." 
 She said she thought it was important for kids to read these kinds of things, to appreciate what they have. 
 But the discussion she wanted to have was over how frustrating books like this can be. It's one thing for kids to understand their parents are human and make mistakes but this seemed... different. 
 -*** SPOILERS ***- 
 I wanted Jackson to go live with Marisol. He would've been happier there, but, at the ripe old age of 11 he felt obligated to stay and look after his little sister. It felt wrong. I wasn't happy at the ending, either. Maybe it wasn't supposed to, but it didn't feel hopeful at all. It was very depressing.

In her first novel since The One and Only Ivan , winner of the Newbery Medal, Katherine Applegate delivers an unforgettable and magical story about family, friendship, and resilience. 
 Jackson and his family have fallen on hard times. There's no more money for rent. And not much for food, either. His parents, his little sister, and their dog may have to live in their minivan. Again. 
 Crenshaw is a cat. He's large, he's outspoken, and he's imaginary. He has come back into Jackson's life to help him. But is an imaginary friend enough to save this family from losing everything? 
 Beloved author Katherine Applegate proves in unexpected ways that friends matter, whether real or imaginary.

Jackson, a fifth grader, knows all the signs because his family's faced financial struggles in the past. At one point, they even lived in their van for several weeks. As he makes note of his parents' whispering, arguments, hardly any food, and visits from the landlord, he knows what's coming. They're going to end up homeless again. Jackson has a trustworthy friend, Marisol, to whom he eventually tells the truth about their plight, and an imaginary friend, a large cat named Crenshaw who has helped him cope in the past and urges him to tell the truth about how he feels to his parents who seem determined to shield Jackson and his little sister Robin from the truth. And yet, with all that secrecy, the father refuses to accept help from social services. This beautifully written book provides insight into the feelings of a boy who's doing his best to keep a stiff upper lip and maintain a positive outlook on tough times. Young readers' hearts will break as they read Jackson's ruminations on homelessness: "I guess becoming homeless doesn't happen all at once" (p 89) and his and Robin's hard choices about what to keep and what to donate to the family's desperate yard sale in an attempt to raise money for the rent the family owes. Can you imagine what parts of your history you'd be willing to sell in order to keep a roof over your loved ones' heads? I'm glad to see such an important issue as homelessness and poverty tackled in such a respectful way. After all, it isn't as though these parents aren't trying to pay their bills and get out of debt. Reading and discussing this book will allow youngsters to raise many questions and challenge the assumptions that many of us make about those who are homeless.

This was a really well done book that I enjoyed it a lot. The story is mostly about a kid going into 5th grade whose parents are struggling with money problems. The kid's childhood imaginary friend comes back to help him out. 
 I listened to this on audiobook and the audiobook was well done. The narrator does a great job with emotion and different voices. 
 There's a lot about family and friendship in here. As well as some magical realism. While the story can be a bit of a tear-jerker (at least for me as a parent) it's done in a somewhat humorous tone so it ends up being a fun read. 
 My ten year old son is reading it right now and has really been enjoying some of the humor and the imaginary cat :-) He was also discussing with me how lucky he feels to have never been in the situation the main character ends up in; so I think it was good for him to read about that. 
 Overall this is a quick little book that I would definitely recommend. It packs a lot of story for its short length and is great for all ages.

I'M NOT CRYING. YOU'RE CRYING. Okay, I definitely was crying. I had to go get a hug and a glass of water before I sat down to write the review for it. 
 If you are considering reading this to your child as a bedtime story, I really encourage you to pick a different book. This book may sound a bit whimsical, but it's really kind of rough in terms of the material. 
 Crenshaw is an imaginary friend, but he's also more symbolic than necessary as an imaginary friend. Jackson, the main character, is part of a financially challenged family. With his mother, father, sister, and their dog, Jackson and his family have been struggling for a long time. The first review on the Goodreads site is a 1-star review, and it claims that the parents are irresponsible ones. Obviously, said person is very obviously privileged and has never had a family member suffer from a terminal or even serious illness like this family is. I'm not here to rag on other users at all - I just want to point out that treatment for terminal illnesses are expensive and doctor's visits are even more so. While Jackson doesn't understand what it means, his father has already been diagnosed with Multiple Sclerosis at the start of the book. As an adult reading the book, that absolutely broke my heart. I feel that children reading this book wouldn't fully understand the gravity of what having MS means. 
 To those who wish to criticize the parents in this situation, the only ground you have to stand on is that they didn't want to grovel at the mercy of friends and family. It's more out of pride and worry that even if they asked for help, they couldn't get any help from them due to their friends and family's own financial situation. Other than that, the parents try to keep the kids in the dark about how awful life is. As a parent, you want your children to be happy. You don't want them to dwell on how hard their life is and why they have to beg for money so they can eat or why they're scrambling to make rent payments. That's not a burden you want to place on the shoulders of your fifth grade child. 
 Jackson's imaginary friend, Crenshaw, is more of a symbolic way of Jackson telling himself that it's okay not to be okay with what's happening. He's so worried about crying about the situation or not asking his parents questions about what's really going on. Sure, they try to deflect the questions in a fun or positive way, but if Jackson had persisted, I feel like a lot of his emotional turmoil would have been avoided. But that's what kids do sometimes. When they know life is tough, they bottle it up and bottle it up. Crenshaw was his way of telling himself that bottling it up wasn't okay anymore. 
 Even at the end, the foundation of their family's stability is still a little shaky. Their dad got a job working and an apartment as a result of that job that they can stay at for at least a month. While a kid might not know it, MS doesn't get better. Even at the end of the book, with hope there in front of you, you know there's a pitfall up ahead on the path that Jackson's family has to travel. You know his dad is only going to deteriorate further. That, more than anything, made me said. Life isn't fair, and in a way this book teaches you that. However, it also teaches kids reading it to keep going when life is hard, that it's okay to ask questions or ask for help when things are rough. It's a good lesson for kids.

Beautifully subtle story about a young boy facing the realities of possible homelessness and s struggling family - there are no easy answers, and the ending is one of optimism without Disney-fication.

To me this book was horribly depressing. This has been a more and more frequent scenario in the United States, and this is a reflection on the state of the economy. 
 It was somewhat heartening that this child was able to cope as well as he did.
3.5 stars

I was disappointed in aspects of this story. I really don't understand why the Invisible cat friend was necessary in this story (although books featuring invisible friends seem to be popping up everywhere at the moment). The story depicting homelessness and helplessness from a child's perspective made for empathy inducing reading and most of my readers in Y5-6 that like this genre would enjoy the story very much - but Crenshaw - somehow adding the unsubtle invisible friend was too much in my opinion and makes for a 'harder sell' to my student community.
Such a good book for kids in that tough transition time and having a rough patch. Really well done!

Jackson is in the 5th grade and something weird has happened. His imaginary friend, a large human-sized cat named Crenshaw has reappeared. Crenshaw showed himself when Jackson was in 1st grade when his family became homeless and they had to live in the family minivan for several months, and disappeared after they found a new home. Jackson is trying to get Crenshaw to vanish, but Crenshaw says he doesn't make the rules and that Jackson needs to tell the truth to the person that matters the most. As if Jackson doesn't have enough to worry about it looks like his family might end up homeless again. A quick excellent read and a must recommend to late elementary school readers.
I didn't love this book right away, and as a matter of fact, I almost abandoned it. I'm glad I didn't.

This book was tricky to rate because of the subject matter. It's definitely well written, but homelessness isn't a subject I'd choose for entertainment. Even as an adult, I found the book to be depressing, lending a sense of anxiety. I recommend that parents read with their children and explain anything they don't understand. The story deals with telling children the truth about every situation, which the book exemplifies, but I would have to disagree that trying to protect one's child is always bad. It's what parents do, and each situation is different as well as the child's ability to comprehend. I did like the author's use of the imaginary friend to help the protagonist with his issues and the fact that the ending wasn't predictable or too Pollyanna in it's conclusion.

A sad story about poverty from a child's perspective and his imaginary friend, Crenshaw, who is a cat. The story of the parents struggling along was hard to read but the imaginary friend part didn't really add much to the story for me.
Wonderful.

Jam-packed with real life, Crenshaw delivered! It's very difficult to engage kids in conversation about those less fortunate, the concept is sometimes just too foreign. This book does a beautiful job of bringing hard times and homelessness to life in an approachable and appropriate manner; making for really meaningful conversations.

Staff Pick 
 Jackson and his family are struggling. They don't have money for rent, even after selling a lot of what they own, and there's not a lot of food in the house. Suddenly, Jackson's old imaginary friend Crenshaw has returned, and nothing will be the same. 
 Keep the tissues handy for this one.

4.5 stars. 
 I listened to the audio book for this because it was under 4 hours and I had time to kill. This book had me feeling so many emotions. This book however, is less about the imaginary cat on the cover and more about how perceptive children are/can be, and that skirting around the truth can have adverse effects on them. 
 In this story we have a boy named Jackson who while on the beach one day he sees a giant cat surfing on a great wave and holding an umbrella (not really a spoiler its on the first page). Crenshaw honestly could have been left out and I think the story would have only lost a little bit of its charm. Don't get me wrong, I loved the giant furball. I'm just saying he doesn't add that much to the overall story. He does do what imaginary friends are supposed to do and that's help Jackson with his problems. 
 The book tackles some a pretty heavy issue and I feel like it was handled really well. It did give me anxiety while listening to parts of the overall issue going on with this book, but my gosh it was just so good. 
 This book has one of the BEST set of parents I think I've ever read. I really liked how they would sacrifice their own happiness for their kids. I liked that even when the main character has his meltdown moment, they stay calm. I liked that they tried to keep their problems as much to themselves as they could so that their kids could remain innocent. There were drawbacks to them keeping secrets of course, mainly because the main character is a bright kid who is wildly observant, while his sister is pretty much the opposite with how much of a dreamer she is. I really loved the family. I loved their friends. This story was just spectacular. Everyone should read this one, even if you don't have kids. Just go read it.
This was not at all what I expected! It didn't move me as much as The One and Only Ivan did bit it was a sad story as well.

Every once in awhile you read a book that you know is going to be a classic. That is how I feel about Katherine Applegate's newest book CRENSHAW. She touches on one of today's biggest problems for our children-poverty. Food insecurity, homelessness, helplessness are constant stresses for Jackson and his family. Just when he thinks he can't take much more, his imaginary friend from 1st grade comes back into his life. Jackson begins to wonder if he is crazy and wants his friend to leave him alone. "Look," Crenshaw said as he extracted his claws from my quilt, "I can't go until I help you. I don't make the rules." Thus old friends are reunited and Jackson doesn't feel so alone. 
 As Crenshaw says, "Imaginary friends are like books. We're created, we're enjoyed, we're dog-eared and creased, and then we are tucked away until we are needed again."

This book made me feel anxious the entire time I was reading it. I didn't feel like there was comic relief or anything interesting and complicated in the plot to distract from the anxiety about homelessness and give the book an added layer of depth. I didn't think it was a very insightful or engaging treatment of the topic.

This book was neither here nor there for me. I wanted more of the poverty-through-a-child's-eyes angle and more of the fantasy-imaginary-friend angle. Or at least more of a focus on one of those pieces. Actually, I think what I wanted was a book that was going to really teach an empathy lesson for my students, a reminder that kids at our school may also be hungry and having to sell their few possessions to have a place to live, that someone they know might have lived in their car, or goes without regular meals when they aren't at school, etc. This one didn't quite have the emotional punch of The One and Only Ivan, and it took me a ridiculously long time to finish these 245 pages.

First line: I noticed several weird things about the surfboarding cat. 
 I loved The One and Only Ivan I cared deeply about the characters, so I assumed that these new characters, Jackson a boy who is dealing with his parents' money problems and Crenshaw an imaginary cat, I would also love. But, I didn't. 
 I did enjoy the book, and my heart ached for Jackson and children like him, but I didn't love him as much as I did Ivan, Ruby, or Stella. And Crenshaw was a character whom I just did not like. I think he was suppose to come across as a "real" cat would, aloof and arrogant, but I didn't like it. I wanted him to be more caring towards Jackson and his situation. 
 If you have a student or kiddo who liked How to Steal a Dog or Hope is a Ferris wheel then they'll probably like this one. If you have an older student or kiddo who's dealing with a difficult issue and struggles with addressing the issue honestly like Jackson then I'd recommend When a Monster Calls. 
 Check out the great book trailer and resources about hunger at: 
 http://www.mackidsbooks.com/crenshaw/...
A very touching story about a boy and his imaginary friend.

I picked this book up at work (school library) at 5:40PM this evening, and I just finished it. I only put it down to drive home, cook, and eat my dinner. 
 I laughed and cried with this book, and I'm a bit thankful I read it fully before I start reading it to my 5th grade classes...hopefully I won't cry in front of them!

Jackson's family is having a difficult time. Even though mom and dad both work several jobs, they can't seem to stay ahead financially. Dad has multiple sclerosis, which doesn't help either. Both mom and dad are musicians, but don't work in that field. They have been homeless before when Jackson was younger and he is afraid they are going to be homeless again and have to live in the family van. When Jackson was younger he had an imaginary friend named Crenshaw, who helped him during the first bout of homelessness. Now that things are getting dire again, Crenshaw has reappeared. Jackson isn't sure what to make of his imaginary friend coming back, but he knows he doesn't like where things are headed with his family. 
 I had been put off by the imaginary friend aspect of the story and by the giant cat on the cover of the book, but I decided to give this book a try. The story is a wonderful, timely story about a situation many kids face. I still think the imaginary friend aspect of it throws of the realism, but I would still like to get this book in kids' hands. It deals with homelessness and financial problems in a way kids can understand. Not everyone "gets" how people who have jobs can be homeless or not have enough to feed their kids. This book does a good job of showing a family trying and failing to get by. It was a wonderfully touching story.

Katherine Applegate has an amazing talent for taking a deep, serious subject and presenting it in a way that it can touch the hearts of readers from young elementary students all the way to adults. The book made me laugh out loud at one point and brought me to tears at others. She writes beautifully yet simply enough for us to share her story with young readers. 
 There weren't quite as many scenes with the actual character Crenshaw as I expected, but I think his presence helped to send a message to readers about friendship and being there for one another.

Pretty much straight realistic fiction with a slight element of magical realism in the potential that Crenshaw (the protagonist's imaginary friend) actually exists -- with other imaginary friends -- rather than simply being a stress reaction to the family's homelessness and economic insecurity (the final determination is left up to the reader).

CRENSHAW is a heart-breaking but hopeful story told by fourth grader Jackson about his family and his imaginary cat. Jackson's family has hit some hard times. His dad has MS and his mom has lost her job as a music teacher. There isn't enough to eat and they are getting close to losing their home. 
 When Jackson was in first grade the family lost their home and lived in their mini-van for fourteen weeks until they found their current apartment. While they were living in the van, Jackson met a black and white skateboarding cat that he named Crenshaw. Crenshaw kept him company and was his friend during that difficult time. 
 Now, Crenshaw is back. Seeing Crenshaw is difficult for fact-loving Jackson. He's sure that he is too old for an imaginary friend. But Crenshaw helps him deal with the yard sale they have to sell all of their things but a few keepsakes. 
 While times are hard for Jackson, his sister Robin and his parents, the one thing that isn't missing is the love that they all have for each other. I liked the hopeful ending of the story.
No es el mejor libro del mundo, pero estuvo bien. Muy duro y realista.

This is a children's book covering a very serious topic, but somehow Ms. Applegate keeps it from overwhelming the reader. Jackson and his family have seen hard times when both parents lost their jobs and the family, including their dog, were forced to live in a van for several months. But they kept their spirits up and things got better. 
 Jackson can read the signs when everything starts to spiral out of control again. The first real sign is the reappearance of his imaginary friend Crenshaw, a human-size talking cat. He helped Jackson through when the family was homeless before and has returned to support him again. 
 The author gently builds the tension Jackson is feeling while watching his parents attempt to appear unconcerned when they're late on rent (again), when there isn't enough money for food, when they start selling all their possessions to make ends meet. We see a family so intent on putting forth a united front that they don't see how terrifying the situation is for Jackson and his younger sister. 
 The book gives a gentle nod to Harvey, the classic movie where Jimmy Stewart is befriended by a pookah in the form of a giant, invisible rabbit. Crenshaw teaches Jackson how to be honest with himself and face his feelings. 
 Homelessness is a scary topic, for children and adults alike. I recommend this book to anyone who has faced or witnessed someone else sliding off the grid of work, home, and a secure family life.

3.5 Stars 
 Oh Katherine Applegate, won't you ever stop writing such emotional stories?! :'/ 
 But however, it dint quite create much of a deep impact in me unlike your other book 'The one and only Ivan' which made me wet my shirt :'P

Mi error fue crear expectativas, pensar que el libro estaria a la altura de The one and only Ivan. La historia es un poco floja, el tema del amigo imaginario no esta muy bien explotado. En fin, definitivamente no es, ni sera de mis historias favoritas.

"And right then I knew, the way you know that it's going to rain long before the first drop splatters on your nose, that something was about to change." 
 Applegate does a great job of helping children understand the tough subject of becoming homeless.

maybe 3.5. i don't know how to review kids books because i am not a kid and don't have any.. but this was cute and adorable. it dealt with a lot of big issues - probably too many smooshed into one book - and Crenshaw isn't as big a part of the book as i expected. it was a cute book.

reference_books.title: The Brief Wondrous Life of Oscar Wao
reference_books.review_text:
I picked this up months ago to read. I have this thing about wildly popular/award winning books: I feel that I should read them. However, it has sat on my pile of books since then, I just couldn't get up the energy to read it. I shouldn't have waited. 
 I found this book totally riveting. I loved the footnotes to explain the history (including the narrator's history) and the fact that you had no damn idea who the narrator was for the first half or so of the book. It frutsrated the hell out of me, but kept me interested too. The pacing was interesting, the characters were captivating and authentic, and I kept wanting to know how Oscar met his demise. 
 But the true gems of this book are twofold: the voice of the author and the wonderful nerdy references. I imagine reading this book without understanding any Spanish is probably frustrating. However, I think that Diaz's writing allows for a reader with no Spanish to follow along. I didn't always understand the slang he was using, but he always got his point across. That being said, I was glad that I do know some Spanish while reading this. I LOVE LOVE LOVE that the book flitted back and forth between Spanish and English, it makes the language that much more real and lends itself nicely to the author's voice coming through loud and clear. Also, the language is like you are sitting there hearing Yunior tell you the story rather than read it. It is immensely personal and intimate and I find that is seriously lacking in most books I read with a narrator. I know that there is more than one narrator in the book, but as Yunior is the main narrator, I choose to focus on him. However, Diaz does a good job even when the narrator isn't Yunior, but Yunior is so easy to listen to you long for him to be narrating again. What is also wonderful about the voice in this book is that the characters aren't upper or middle class and it reads like they aren't without dumbing down the language. I have no idea how Diaz achieved that, but it is undoubtedly one of the most charming parts of the narrative. 
 That Diaz was able to weave in sci-fi, fantasy, horror and graphic novels seamlessly into this novel amazes me. He assumes that the reader is as familiar with these genres as he is, and luckily for me, I followed most of the references. I thought the book-long comparison of the DR to Mordor was wonderful and evocative. I was especially charmed with the reference to the Ritual of Chud (from Stephen King's IT), and that made me wonder how many other obscure references there were in the book that I didn't pick up on. I'm guessing a lot. I felt like I could have read a million books and watched a million movies and even then I might still have missed a wonderful comparison or reference in this book. But at the same time Diaz makes this accessible, he uses the references as a nod to those who know without making those who don't feel like they are missing out on his story. 
 Only a wonderfully gifted writer can reference a million other works and write in what is basically Spanglish and keep the interest and imagination of those who don't always understand the language or the references. I can hardly wait to read another novel by Diaz.

reference_books.title: Cruel Beauty (Cruel Beauty Universe, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
I have read this book a thousand times, and so have you. In fact, for the first 100 pages or so, I was really wracking my brain trying to figure out if I had read this exact book before. No, I have not, but, then, yes I have. I have because this is Beauty and the Beast. And its every romance ever written. And it's like ALL of the teen angst ever. 
 If you are someone who thinks its possible to spoil a story that everyone in the western world knows, by all means, feel free to avoid the following "spoilers". 
 Nyx is a likeable heroine? protagonist? teenage girl. She was raised to essentially be the human version of a beef cow and is as fucking angry about it as you'd be. She hides it, but poorly, and blames herself for being bitter. Her father has made a faustian deal and she pays the price. Off she goes to marry a demon and finds that she falls in what-might-be-love with his servant, only to then actually fall for the demon. You know, Beauty and the Beast. 
 I for one, think that the ONE thing this book did well was explain what I would typically label Stockholm Syndrome. She falls for her beast because he sees everything that is bad about her and likes her for it. Do you know how powerful that is? No? I pity you. There is NOTHING so intoxicating as having someone know how awful you are and still wanting you, nothing so able to make you forgive anything as being wanted for the parts of you that you've been taught to hate. Its worth Everything. Seriously, everything. I know this sounds like either 1- teenage hyperbole or 2- sarcasm, but as someone who had this and made and entire world of bad choices because of it, I assure you its neither. 
 This is what made me give this book 3 stars, what made me love Nyx and what made me forgive the GOD AWFUL plot insanity. Read this, but for the love of all that is holy, do not try to understand the world or the magic. It's impossible and you will drive yourself crazy trying.

reference_books.title: Love in the Time of Cholera
reference_books.review_text:
GGM is an amazing writer, his prose is fluid and draws you in. I wish my Spanish was still good enough to read this in the original, rather than the translation. 
 Unlike many of the people that disliked the book, I had no problems with Florentino sleeping around. His promiscuity was no issue for me, I mean, people do this all the time. I struck me as an honest dipction of how some people live. And I even get that he could never really kill his love for Fermina. My personal opinion is that everyone you love you love with a different part of your heart and love in a different way. What I couldn't like was his inability to incorperate his past into his present, to live in the present, to embrace life and enjoy those who cared about him. (Yes, I get that this was intentional.) I felt bad for him, but in the same way I feel bad for addicts...they live in a hell of their own actions. Which, when you think about it, is the case for much of humanity. 
 I never really got the sense of love from either Florentino or Fermina. I got obsession pure and simple. I do remember being head over heels for someone when I was a teenager and I get that obsessive is the best way to characterize those feelings. But to classify it as love, and a love that is worth dwelling on for 50 years, I never got that in all of the beautiful writing in the book. I felt like I could identify much more with the kind of comfortable, familiar love that is clearly expressed between Fermina and Juvenal. The two "loves" are very different, and the problem is that the marriage and their relationship is so much better illuminated than whatever existed between Fermina and Florentino. Admittedly, the relationship between Florentino and Fermina became much more understandable and relatable when they reconnected during their twilight years. 
 The only time that I really disliked Florentino's character was in the incident with America. I can overlook the pedophilia, but I can't overlook that he took advantage of someone he was supposed to care about. I can't overlook his abuse of power and I can't overlook his lack of empathy for her. What really "got my goat" was his total lack of remorse when his own horrible actions caused her death. 
 All in all, I thought this was a beautifully written book with a horribly boring plot. Its worth reading just for the prose, but if I were going to recommend a GGM book it wouldn't be this one, it would be 100 Years of Solitude.

reference_books.title: Pride and Prejudice and Zombies (Pride and Prejudice and Zombies, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
I have read Pride and Prejudice probably a dozen times. I enjoy it because I love Elizabeth Bennett (and because I've been required to on several occasions). However, I've never liked Mr. Darcy. Hate as much as you want, I just don't. 
 I'm not sure if I like the characters more or less in the zombie infested version. I think they might have become more ridiculous by incorporating a warrior code, this doesn't mean it wasn't fun to read. 
 It was fun, it was entertaining and it was poorly written. Not the plot, that's basically the same with zombies. The actual writing is a bit painful. If you can deal with that and are looking for something light and fluffy you might enjoy this.

reference_books.title: The Vegetarian
reference_books.review_text:
I struggled deeply with this book. I'm pretty sure that was completely cultural. Scratch that. I know it was completely cultural. 
 I found everything about this book that South Koreans would have found normal completely off-putting. Women's role in society, the family, a marriage. All made my skin crawl. I should be more understanding, but I'm not. Sue me. The family dynamics were squicky. I'm sure all of this was pretty typical/traditional for the Korean readers, but for me, it was difficult to look past the culture and focus on the story. 
 So I'll unpack my own bias here. I find patriarchal societies repressive and they make me feel like I can't breathe. I know that more collectivist societies have benefits that individualistic ones don't. I know that they have support networks and care for the vulnerable. (I admit I struggled with even putting into words ANY benefits) But I find them completely suffocating. The idea that you can't eat what you want because it's "not normal" is completely foreign to me. I can't even imagine a family beating someone because they decided to stop eating meat. Or stop eating carbs. Or gluten. Or dairy. I'm aware that we have our own expectations here and that every family is different. But it was just so outside of my realm of reality that it seemed over the top . 
 Worse for me was the marital interactions. The expectation that a woman is completely subservient to a man makes all of my skin try to crawl right off my body. I know its a common and very traditional way of thinking. It also pisses me off right down to my core. But that's a rant for another day. 
 I wasn't expecting the sexuality in this book. It came out of left field for where I thought we were going. It was weirdly enjoyable (the painting part, not the rape part) and frankly, the tone was a 180 from the rest of the book. It was an odd part and I'm still not entirely sure what the point was. But the visuals were fanfuckingtastic. 
 The study on mental illness was fascinating. Not only was there a cultural component but the examination of mental illness from both the patient's perspective and the family's perspective was something I rarely see done. The idea that we are all holding on by a string and could as easily let go as hold on is one I often agree with. It was beautiful and haunting and awful. All at once. It's the only reason to read this book.

book_a.title: Atlas Shrugged
book_a.user_review:
As an allegorical philosophical story, I think this is really well written. As a philosophy that I can get behind, I think its total crap. I had a really hard time reading reading the book, and it took me several months to muddle through all the passages that ramble on about her theory. I'm glad that someone else saw through the the problems with her theory and the depths of unhappiness her philosophy could lead us to. I admit that she makes some valid points about government and people who are essentially living off the taxes of others, but to say that everyone who receives social assistance doesn't deserve it and doesn't want more is a huge blanket statement to make and inherently elitist. 
 I did enjoy the story part of this book, but there was too little story and too much preaching to really make it an enjoyable read for me. Although, I am glad that I read this, if only to make me think about what really is important to me and to solidify my own beliefs.

sample_reviews.review_text:
As easy as it would be to throw on one star and spend the entire review mocking Atlas Shrugged and Ayn Rand, I'm not going to. There's already plenty written about the glacial pace, the painful dialogue, the unbelievable characters, and the book's myriad other flaws, and to a great extent I agree with all of that. However, because that's all been said, I'm going to talk about why I think it deserves two stars instead of one. 
 It's much more of an allegory, like The Pilgrim's Progress or The Faerie Queene, than a novel as such. Like those two, most of the characters that appear in the book aren't fully-realized characters, but instead archetypes--either the Glorious Titan of Industry, the Vile Socialist Looter, or the Undecided Masses. Dagny Taggart and Hank Rearden are much more fully realized, and there are other characters that get some depth (Francisco d'Anconia, Cheryl Taggart, Eddie Willers, etc.), but mostly the names and behavior are interchangeable. If Midas Mulligan ran an oil company and Elias Wyatt ran a bank, the story and themes of Atlas Shrugged would only have to be changed in one place: the story of why Midas Mulligan is named "Midas." 
 That's another thing. You can usually tell which archetype a character is simply by their names. The Glorious Titans of Industry have names like Midas Mulligan and Judge Narragansett (well, that's a title, but you never learn his first name) and John Galt and Elias Wyatt and Ragnar Danneskjold, whereas the Vile Socialist Looters have names like Tinky Holloway and Balph Eubank and Kip Chalmers and Cuffy Meigs and Wesley Mouch (the most blatant example). 
 And speaking of interchangeability, the other countries in the world are all interchangeable. Literally every other country is repeatedly referred to as "The People's State of [x]," though in a couple cases the transformation into a Vile Socialist Looter country occurs during the course of the plot. Any People's State produces nothing of value and exists only to sponge supplies and money from America, the only country in the world which still counts Glorious Titans of Industry among its populace. 
 With this kind of cartoonish background, I think it's unfair to hold Atlas Shrugged to either the standards of a philosophical treatise or a novel, because it's not often trying to be those and where it does, it does it badly. As a philosophical treatise, the work is amateurish, relying on philosophical arguments that have already been effectively answered by people who wrote before Ayn Rand did (just one example--Objectivism smashes hard on the rocks of Hume's Is-Ought Problem). As a novel, it's long-winded, with stilted dialogue (example: I don't think there's a single instance where anyone says, "I know." They all say, "I know it." Every time), terrible pacing, and minimal character growth. As an allegory about the possible dangers of collectivism, which Rand was well aware of from her childhood in Russia, it actually isn't bad when it isn't being sabotaged by the aforementioned flaws. 
 And that's why I have to give it two stars. When judged under that standard, it doesn't do as badly as I had expected, and I finished the whole book and was pretty curious about what happened next at points, even if at other points my eyes were glazing over and I had to fight to keep going (*cough*TheSpeech*cough*). On the other hand, it still does pretty badly, because while the actions of the characters make perfect sense in the context of the world that Rand sets up, that world has so little resemblance to our own world that it's not actually useful as a guide to determine what to do or how to live your life. 
 Would I recommend this to anyone? Emphatically no. If you want to learn about Objectivism, just read Anthem, which is a fraction of the length and doesn't have to cram in a plot, and if you want a gripping business/economy-oriented novel, there are thousands of better choices. 
 And finally, I end with this Bob the Angry Flower Comic:
This book is simply the worst sort of dishonesty.
