[Dear Reader: Have 20 minutes to kill? Excellent. Please enjoy my magical journey through the pages of Ayn Rand.] 
 *December 2012. 
 I am doing this. I slogged through The Fountainhead some years ago just to see what the fuss was about. But now, after so many patrons have come to the library in a wild-eyed search for the new Atlas Shrugged movie, and after hearing the expression 'going galt,' and then seeing some guy on the road with "John Galt" painted on his back windshield, it is clear to me that I tortured myself for nothing and read the wrong Ayn Rand. So here we go. 
 My copy is 1168 pages and seems to weigh about 60 pounds. It has been checked out a total of 162 times, but is in surprisingly good shape, which may indicate that no one has actually finished it. Still, I hope that there are penciled notes in the margins. From a library standpoint that would be bad, but it would increase my entertainment value. 
 *UPDATE, 1/6/13. I'm on page 100 or so, which is like being on page 5 of a normal book. I've decided that if I were going to be stranded on a deserted island, I would bring this title with me -- not for enjoyment or for spiritual consolation, but because editing it down would keep me amused for years on end. I suspect there's a weird but readable 400 page novel in here somewhere, but you'd have to pick it out line by line. And then, of course, you could start to argue with her philosophy and world view, which is good for another few years of entertainment. 
 *UPDATE, 1/11/13 
 Some characteristics of Ayn Rand heroes: 
 -- They are not good party guests. 
 "Darling, you take everything too seriously. One is not supposed to be intellectual at a ball. One is simply supposed to be gay." 
 "How? By being stupid?" 
 -- They like it rough. 
 "He took her wrist and threw her inside his room, making the gesture tell her that he needed no sign of consent or resistance." 
 "He seized her arm, threw her down on her knees, twisting her body against his legs, and bent down to kiss her mouth." 
 (So, the next morning, keep an eye out for injuries.) 
 "She saw a bruise above her elbow, with dark beads that had been blood." 
 -- They get real worked up about antitrust law. 
 "Excuse me for interrupting, Mr. Rearden...I thought I must tell you that the Legislature has just passed the Equalization of Opportunity Bill." 
 It was the stolid Mr. Ward who screamed, "Oh God, no! Oh, no!"--staring at Rearden. 
 Rearden had leaped to his feet. He stood unnaturally bent, one shoulder drooping forward. 
 Also, anytime these characters get remotely flirty, there's a noticeable amount of creepy silent laughter and "mocking." We get "mocking" gazes, "mocking laughter" (again, usually silent), "mockery" in people's eyes, & etc. Either Rand is a big proponent of angry sex (likely, see above) or, to misquote Inigo Montoya, that word doesn't mean what she thinks it means. 
 *Update 1/23/13 
 On page 488 and I am already exhausted. Rand spends fully half this book describing, at great length, what something is not, before finally naming what it is. At least another third of each page is devoted to rhetorical questions. So I am tired. But I will persevere, because I am increasingly convinced that when I finish I will join the ranks of a select few who have actually read this damn thing cover to cover. I can't believe that half of the people who say they live by this book have read more than a few key pages. (Which might be fine, actually. Rand is changing my mind about the merits of abridged literature.) 
 Anyway, as I read I am developing a multiple choice test to ferret out those Atlas Shrugged fakers, the Cliffs Notes skimmers, the people who listened on audiobook in the car but had the volume down while they were on the phone and then forgot to turn the sound back up. Here's my quiz so far. 
 When driving down a country road and gazing at the scenery, you say: 
 a) Isn't this gorgeous? 
 b) Look, a red-tailed hawk! 
 c) "What I'd like to see is a billboard." 
 If someone gives you a gift that they think you will enjoy, you: 
 a) Thank them -- how very thoughtful. 
 c) Give them a gift in return. 
 b) "Throw it in their face" for convoluted philosophical reasons. 
 Someone is wearing an orange shirt. How should you describe this shirt? 
 a) The shirt is orange. 
 b) The shirt is the color of a tangerine/marigold/something else that is usually orange. 
 c) The shirt was not white or black, nor brown nor any of the greys, dark or light, and was without any hint of blue, green, or other cool spectrum colors. Nor was the shirt yellow or red; it was something in between those two hues, an orange color, of a shade favored by people who do not like to pay taxes. 
 *Update 1/29/13 
 Last night I had a dream that one of the characters, Hank Rearden, had started to build some kind of steel structure. And in my dream I took this to be a good sign, and felt relieved, because it meant the tides had turned in a positive way. I cannot begin to describe how f***ed up it is that this book and its childlike, hero-worship philosophy have invaded my subconscious, and that my subconscious is apparently completely fine with that. 
 But I have turned some kind of corner. I'm on page 648 and totally into it. I cannot put this book down, even though it is heavy, and my arms are literally getting tired when I read for too long. I've also started skimming all the many political speeches so I can hurry along to the next plot twist, which defeats my original purpose for picking up the book. But forearm toning has been an unexpected benefit, so maybe I'm breaking even. 
 Btw, there is actually a scene in here where an honest-to-god pirate approaches that Rearden character on a deserted country road and tries to give him an honest-to-god bar of gold, because said pirate has long been an admirer of Rearden and thinks it is unjust that Rearden has had to pay so much income tax. This must be a vivid fantasy for about half of America. 
 *Update 2/4/13 
 On page 760. She has taken her perfectly good love triangle and distended it into a grotesque love quadrilateral. (I could call it a square, but I'm too irritated for that.) In other news, we have reunited with most of her characters and discovered that for the past several hundred pages they have been hiding out in the Shire -- except for instead of singing and ale, Rand's Shire is characterized by sanctimoniousness and lecture series. 
 Obviously, I have some frustrations. I've decided to seek my revenge by (heavily) abridging the last 100 pages I read and then translating them into lolcat. I believe this is an appropriate response to the text and you will just have to trust me on that. 
 [Scene - Our intrepid industrialist heroine, Dagny Taggart, crash lands in a strange valley.] 
 John Galt: Hai. 
 Dagny: Oh, hai. 
 Midas Mulligan, Ken Danagger, Ellis Wyatt, Richard Halley, Quentin Daniels, and ten other characters: Oh, hai. 
 Dagny: Wer iz I? 
 John Galt: U r in mah treehaus 
 Dagny: I can haz gold coins? 
 Tax Pirate: Yez. 
 Dagny: John Galt, I can haz sekz wif u? 
 John Galt: No, because even though I just told you that I have been creepily stalking you for 10 years, you must swear allegiance to the tenets of my cult before we consummate our love. Also, I am too busy being weird and inscrutable to take my clothes off. 
 Dagny: I haz a sad. 
 To be continued. 
 *Update 2/16/13 
 JR: What is this?...Get that tome off of here, I could hurt myself on that. 
 Me: Many people have... 
 On page 951. I certainly get the point by now, and since the book's central purpose is to make that point, it's hard not to feel like this show ended hours ago and I'm still in my seat. I suspect even Rand is beginning to fray. Having run out of vague-but-scary words to explain the outcome of anticapitalist philosophies, she recently had one character describe our dystopian future as "the end of the world, not fire and brimstone, but goo." I would have been less surprised by 'slime.' 'Goo' reads like Rand was writing at 4 am, perhaps drunk or high on pixie sticks. That same character later runs screaming at the sight of a social worker ("No! No! Not your kind of world!") and jumps off a bridge and dies. I'm wasting an opportunity for a joke here; choose your own adventure. 
 At the marked risk of summing up too early, my personal journey with this book has so far gone something like this. 
 1. Mockery (to use one of Rand's favorite words) 
 2. Fascination and mockery. 
 3. COMPLETE AND TOTAL FASCINATION. 
 4. Disappointment. 
 5. Fatigue and mockery. 
 Did you ever hear that Peggy Lee song, 'Is That All There Is?' That's kind of where I'm at, ever since we met Rand's imaginary friend, John Galt. The whole force of the narrative hinges on your approval of him, or at least your admiration -- without that, it's just a bizarre farce. But as a tent pole, he's not tall enough to lift the fabric of these 1200 pages. Or maybe I'm just bitter because I was on Team Rearden. 
 Anyway, I will finish, and when I do I may want to come back and surreptitiously delete these words, who knows. See you on the other side. 
 *Update 2/20/13 
 Surely, I must be done with the book by now, right? I was nearing the end. And then I arrived at John Galt's speech and I can't stop falling asleep. It is like trying to read Dianetics. 
 Here's the thing: I'm pretty sure Galt's speech is supposed to be the climax of the story. The Man of Mystery is revealed, and the appropriate people look suitably surprised about it, and when he finishes talking (if he ever finishes talking) I suspect we will begin our roll toward the finish line. But why did Rand spend all that time illustrating her philosophical argument with a cast of characters and a high stakes plot, only to punctuate that plot with a 69-page lecture? She was much better off with the novelization method. Her points are not more meaningful now that they are boring. 
 Galt mentions halfway through his speech that he's already been talking for two hours, and it's the biggest element of fantasy in this fantastical novel -- that anyone would be listening that long. I hear that people claim to have read, if not the novel, at least this speech, but I think they must also be fakers. No human could endure it. My quiz is in development. 
 This update is dedicated to Shek, who refuses to join my Objectivist Discussion Group. 
 *Update 3/3/13 
 I finally finished. I'm on the other side now. The weather is nice over here, I like it. 
 While I ruminate, on what, if anything, I have to say about this book now that it's no longer happening to me in an active way...let's do a literature review, shall we? The following are articles I would be pleased to read if someone would write them. Calling all academics: these titles have semi-colons colons [DUDE, SORRY], and one of them uses 'towards.' How can you resist? 
 Revenge of the Strawmen: How Rand's imaginary friends and make-believe enemies make her arguments irrelevant. 
 If Rand hates a 'Zero' so much, why does she write like one? Towards a better understanding of description through process of elimination. 
 Neutering Robin: the powerless sidekicks of Atlas Shrugged. 
 20 Questions: Or, why Rand's characters take two pages to order a sandwich. 
 Believe me that this urge is an exception to my rule, but the next time I see a teenager with this book in their hands, I'll beg them to put it down and go smoke some weed instead. Rand's writing style (perhaps I should say rhetorical style?) is particularly effective on youngish minds (those with long attention spans, anyway), and in addition to her infantile economic principles, she has some interesting ideas about what justifies murder, what level of consent is necessary for sex, & etc. The book is like a 1168-page a**hole pill. So please excuse me while I go visit all my neighborhood school libraries (damn, any of those left?) and mis-shelve it. The 800s should be a pretty safe spot. 
 *Final update OMG. 
 A couple of lovely people have congratulated me on finishing my Atlas Shrugged saga. Perhaps there was a little bit of relief in your tone. But I'm not quite done! Sorry. I have one more left in me. 
 I've had difficulty deciding where to stand regarding this book. My indecision, according to John Galt, is a sure indicator of moral turpitude. Quoth Galt: "There are two sides to every issue: one side is right and the other is wrong, but the middle is always evil." [Page 1054]. 
 I started reading because I assumed Atlas Shrugged's longevity and its apparent influence were due to something special about the book itself. I have to admit that I still think there's something particularly effective about the novel, whether in spite of or because of its flaws. I read that E.B. White once told James Thurber that if he actually knew how to draw, his cartoons wouldn't be any good, and Rand benefits from the same kind of raw, unembarrassed force in her fiction. What I'm saying, in essence, is that some parts did not suck. The scenes describing the first run of the John Galt line are rather fine. It's certainly a page turner at points, with a strong, if confusing, romance element. It is brave and bold in its scope, an early zombie novel, perhaps -- where the zombies are you and me, in case you were wondering. 
 But when I complained that few people have actually read this book, I meant it. So we have a contradiction, something Rand tells us, SIX MILLION TIMES, is not possible: 
 "Contradictions do not exist. Whenever you think that you are facing a contradiction, check your premises. You will find that one of them is wrong." [Page everypage.] 
 So let's try and play by her rules. 
 Premise A: This book is influential and widely read. 
 Premise B: Few people have actually read this damn book. 
 Which one is false? Premise A? Is Atlas Shrugged really influential, or do people just namecheck it, like they do Ronald Reagan? What if none of the Randites ever read it? What if Alan Greenspan never even read it, and just sweetly nodded and smiled along with the rest of her boy toys? Wasn't Paul Ryan embarrassed recently, after he claimed to live by Atlas Shrugged principles, but forgot that one of those tenets was unapologetic marital infidelity? Which is like, a third of the book? It's hard to forget all that rough extramarital luvin' if you've actually read this thing. 
 Or, maybe I'm wrong on Premise B, and people have do read this it. Could be. There are elements in here that would carry a modern reader along. Frankly, the whole thing is like some kind of economic episode of Super Friends, where the superhero hideout is Galt's Gulch, and everyone's superpower is making money. It also reminds me of that bit in Tom Sawyer where he crashes his own funeral. You'll be sorry when I'm gone is woven through every page of this book. In fact, it's the whole book. What Twain tossed off as a quick satire of self-absorbed adolescence, Rand made a career and a following out of. In that light, it does seem unfair that she's the one more frequently voted to the top of influential books lists. But at any rate, she has harnessed a kind of basic storytelling momentum here, and it might carry more than one reader across the finish line. 
 I must pick a premise to discard, or John Galt will call me evil. And, in the interests of my future business enterprise, the Atlas Shrugged merch store (Look for us in SkyMall!) I will trash Premise B, and conclude that people have actually read the book. Although how anyone gets through it without being able to vent on Goodreads, I can't imagine. Thank you for reading, or politely ignoring, as the case may be. I've obviously enjoyed myself. And I will now return this 10 pound instrument of torture to the library, where it is currently 90 cents worth of overdue.

If you must read Ayn Rand, start with Anthem. It's awful, but it's wicked short and it'll give you an idea about what Rand's like. (She is awful.) Move on (if you still must) to The Fountainhead, which is her least bad book, and just look this up on Wikipedia. It's way too long. There's a famous 70-page speech by John Galt near the end that's famous because literally no one has ever read it. You know who writes 70-page political screeds? The Unabomber and Ayn Rand and that's it. 
 Rand's political views are one thing, and that one thing is inane, but she's also a mostly dreadful writer - boring at best, wincingly amateur at worst - and her characters, particularly the women, are sock puppets. Rand has very little going for her as an author of books. 
 Here's the problem with Rand's philosophy. Let's take John Galt's utopia, a group of high achievers taking care of themselves. Sounds fun! What happens when two of us have a kid who turns out not so bright, or lazy? That seems inevitable, and what do we do? Kick him out? That won't happen; it's not how parents work. We will have to take care of that good-for-nothing kid. And over time, we'll have them at a regular clip, because that's how humans work, and eventually we'll end up with a society just like ours, where there are some high achievers and some low achievers and we must make decisions about how the fortunate among us take care of the less fortunate. 
 What I'm getting at here is that any decent philosophy must envelop all humans, the awesome ones and the not-so-awesome ones. Libertarianism doesn't deal with that, which is why it's naive and stupid. 
 And of course we haven't even touched on racism - there are only white people in Rand's books - or other social injustice. Real societies must also deal with the fact that many humans - even high-functioning ones! - have bad judgment. 
 When you take these things into account, I don't know about you but I end up with a messy, imperfect society where few people are perfectly happy: we have to take more than is comfortable from the fortunate, and we have to give less than is comfortable to the less fortunate, and it's all kindof a pain in the ass. But that's how humans work, and to imagine less is a failure of imagination.

Well, I've been thinking about writing a review for this book since I first got on goodreads. I've been saving it because I thought that maybe I can write it better a little later on, but I'm not getting any younger, and I hate this book only more. You know how sometimes when you're trying to get to sleep at night and you've previously had an altercation with someone, and you didn't get a chance to really speak your mind? Say it's with a teacher, or a parent, or a boss or something-someone in authority. That's what Ayn Rand is to me, but the really beautiful part is that Ayn Rand in a sense would approve of this review: namely the idea of better ideas putting lesser ideas to waste. 
 On the initially topic of waste Rand's magnum opus is a waste of paper-a lot of paper. In this book the world is not so evenly divided between those ubermenschen: Dagny Taggert (a clear stand-in for Rand herself), Hank Reardon, Francisco D'Ancona, and John Galt are all perfect-especially John Galt. John Galt is indeed so perfect he has a phrase named after him: "Who is John Galt?" that reappears throughout the text. These perfect individuals must now navigate and destroy a world not at all perfect and actually quite hideous and inept because of your everyday slack-jawed simpletons, and your high rise simpletons in positions of political power who have sacrificed every other country in the world to the lamentable fall of having "People's State" as their prefix, and now are poised to do the same to The Land of the Free itself, that is until Galt leads the whole lot of brilliant minds into his invisible Galt's Gulch where they will wait out the inevitable "Great Simpleton Die-off" to emerge at the end of the novel to finally recreate the world. There's a whole bunch of Dagny rape-but this is good rape mind you-and just terrible dialogue. Plus, as I alluded to earlier, there is a whole lot of nothing going on. The book sets itself up as a mystery: "Who is John Galt?" It then drifts off into railroad speak, bureaucratic ridiculousness, and continental meanderings that while seeking to show how the country is collapsing, only show some really terribly drawn foils for the main characters to gloat over how stupid they are. This is really more akin to a fictional treatment of a journey to an orphanage where the main characters just ridicule the orphans for not having parents, a private school education, or their own Ferrari. Ultimately though since none of the main characters have any development whatsoever the novel is more picturesque, although it's an impressively inaccurate view of the world and so doesn't even qualify for that label. But, again the point is that the only thing that actually happens in these pages is that the main characters are removed from this society which collapses only because of the stupidity of everyone else, but then the main characters are brought back in to no doubt make the world in their image. It's length implies complexity, but only succeeds in casting out the message that if one has a lot of money, one is inherently better, and better people ought to rule the world. Indeed, better people ought to rule the world. Unfortunately for Rand the people she says should rule the world already do. And they are really bad at it. 
 Back when the right wing urged everyone to read this book because "it was coming true." they were correct in that we are living after the events of the book; it just wasn't how Rand said things would work out. As it actually happens when you have the wealthy in charge, behaving selfishly, and then urging everyone else to follow their example you don't wind up with utopia, you wind up with 2014 and counting. You wind up with a sociopathic government that can justify cutting education to beef up the army to secure oil rights and property rights for a select few, you wind up with sociopathic business owners like Steve Jobs who can be applauded for the meaningless excess that iPods and Macs represent, a sociopathic media that proclaims "body image uber alles," and a socipathic economic system that champions growth over everything else. What's worse you produce a readership eager to behave without remorse for anything. The time has not come for Atlas Shrugged, the time has past for Atlas Shrugged, and it is a complete and total failure as work of fiction, and work of philosophy.

I wanted to like this book. It is filled with important ideas (ok, maybe just one important idea) and it did challenge some of my own values and assumptions. You would think that this qualifies it as a good book, no? Well, my problem with it lies not in the ideas it contains, but rather how they are expressed. 
 It is boring. I found it a chore to read. The characters are one-dimensional, and all the hero industrialists speak like the same person having a conversation with themselves. There is no depth in any of the characters introduced: either they're a brilliant beautiful hero who creates wonderful things and whose farts smell like cherry blossoms, or your a scumbag mooch who looks like a sloth and acts like one too. The only person that deviates from this two-part formula is Eddie Willers, and he's just an average joe who looks up to the industrialists in awe. Boring. 
 Railroads are an important symbol in Atlas Shrugged. I wouldn't say the book was a train wreck; rather, it reads like a train ride. Slow, long, boring, and you know exactly where it's headed the moment the train leaves the station. 
 Another problem I have is that the antagonist is a society who advocates, and indeed forces sacrifices of those with wealth/ability for those in need. All the advocates for this society are idiots who can't form a critical thought and just repeat unconvincing platitudes. There is not a single rational argument in the Anti-capitalist camp. Every time a hero explodes into a pro-capitalist monologue in the midst of a sea of moochers, they all just sit there attentively and look dumbfounded. I sat there, reading these speeches, and thinking, "ok, I don't even disagree with you, but nobody in the whole crowd can defend their position intelligently?" It's easy to look smart when everyone who disagrees with you would sooner accumulate a puddle of drool than interject with a thoughtful counter-point. The whole book was a straw man assault on the "progressive agenda" 
 All in all, interesting ideas, terrible storytelling. If you're looking to learn about Ayn Rand's philosophy, save yourself the punishment of Atlas Shrugged and try one of her shorter novels.

The book is great reading and you cannot help but strengthen your commitment to personal responsibility as you absorb it. It focuses on a seldom seen but greatly feared hero named John Galt. The government cannot do anything competently in Rand's opinion. It cannot make the trains run on time, but Galt and a band of society's brightest and most creative geniuses can. 
 Galt leads this band, who refuse to do anything because society takes too much from them in taxes. Without their brainpower and creativity, ystopia ensues. Only when the leaches of the world are overthrown and presumably left to starve as they so richly deserve for the high crime of being born less intelligent than Ms. Rand and her followers does Galt assert himself to launch a new order where ambition, drive and greed are the only rewarded values. 
 Ayn Rand's writings articulate a value system and philosophy now know as Objectivism. The problem I see with it is that Objectivism leads to unbridled greed. It leads to plutocracy where the accumulation vast wealth is put above people, the environment, the future of our species and all else. It is incredibly destructive. Her focus on personal responsibility is fine, but responsibility extends to our fellow man, to the environment, and to building a better future for our children and grandchildren. It is irresponsible in the extreme to focus only on enriching ourselves, at the expense of all our other responsibilities. 
 The truth is that no John Galt, no matter how smart, can single-handedly make the trains run on time. That takes lots of people, including ones willing to do inelegant jobs like laying and repairing track, emptying chemical toilets, and cleaning the sleeper cars; things the best and brightest of us are not anxious to do -- but things we should be bright enough to realize we need someone to handle.

The quantities of cheesy novels produced by Christian authors have become almost infamous and, to many of us, embarrassing. We cringe when we face the psychologically unreal characters, overly didactic messages, and the deux ex machina conversions with which many Christian novels are filled. But at least we have the Divine Comedy, Paradise Lost, and Pilgrim's Progress to comfort us. 
 Now recall the preachiest, most head-thumping book (whether Christian or not) you can remember reading. Maybe it was a call to prohibition era "temperance," maybe it was on saving the earth's resources, or perhaps it was on why eating meat is a sin. 
 And then think of a book two or three times that size, with a proportionate increase of force against your poor head. You would be thinking of Ayn Rand's magnum opus Atlas Shrugged, pounding you with the Virtue of Greed. 
 Utterly apart from all philosophical and religious objections to Objectivism, it may be added that Objectivists has been singularly unfortunate in their front-running novelist. Rand's characters are unrealistic and her plot contrived. Prepare to find almost every character with whom Rand personally disagrees a contemptible cheat, and the supposed "good guys" towering pillars of brain and hardened steel. (If the Cross means more to you than the dollar, prepare to take your place with the moochers of society--because that's where Ayn Rand is going to put you.) 
 May I mention the book's complete lack of humor? Did Ayn Rand have philosophical objections to allowing a "hero" to slip in a muddy puddle? Or to having a manufacturing giant sit down on an egg? This is no mere quibble; it represents a major flaw in the book's philosophy. Human relations cannot be built off respect for a fellow human being's value as a producer and achiever alone; often we must reach out to one another through a shared identity as undignified clowns. If Hank Rearden cannot survive being made a fool of, and Dagny Taggart cannot take a joke, then I say that they are not my heroes. I'll take the man down the street--the one who has built no bridges and made little money--but who has accepted that the joys and tragedies of life sometimes come with ridiculous trappings.

So setting aside the moral philosophy for a second --which is hard to do with this book, as it's essentially just a vehicle for Rand's philosophy-- I'll talk about what I liked and didn't like about the writing itself. Interestingly it feels weird to critique this book as Rand seems to go out of her way to trash nearly every occupation that might say something critical about it (anyone left wing, students, the general public, government leaders, etc...)-- it seems oddly defensive, though I guess it makes sense given how much outrage it can evoke. 
 Pros: 
 -It's really remarkable from a story telling perspective that you can make your main characters sympathetic merely by having them struggle against a faceless incompetent bureaucracy. While I would describe most of the main characters as unsympathetic, it really is a testament to how much people love fighting the good fight, and how much they dislike ridiculous government regulations and red tape. 
 -It's quite a novel perspective to read a about unashamedly rich and selfish people who are supposed to be the good guys. 
 -For the most part I liked the style of writing for maybe the first half or so (exceptions outlined below). 
 Cons: 
 -The characters are incredibly caricatureized-- the "good" industrialists are all shinning Grecian gods with perfect posture, beautiful faces, and brilliant fashion sense. Conversely the "bad" politicians/hangers on/general public/ and everyone else are all hideous monsters, who hate truth and beauty and only want to make the world ugly and despoiled. While it's an effective storytelling technique in that you immediately identify the "good" character, and on some subconscious level it makes you like them more (truth is beauty and beauty is truth and all that) it grows very tired after the first few hundred pages, and comes off as a child's idea of morality. 
 -There were many passages where characters were forced to abruptly end their conversations so as not to give away key plot points. Eddy never asks his friend in the cafeteria what his name is; Dr. Stadler doesn't bother telling Dagny that he taught Galt, Fransisco and Ragnar; Fransisco isn't able to finish convincing Rearden to leave; etc... it was all just a little too much in terms of convenient interruptions which prevented key information from being shared, which would have cleared up key plot points a lot sooner. 
 -Rand can be painfully repetitive at points- and tends to repeat things we've already heard, symbols, or little points of comparison to death. 
 -The philosophy of the book can make it a chore to read. 
 -It's too long-- the book as a whole starts to drag a lot after the first half or three quarters, and at one point her main character gives 3 hour speech over the radio-- that's 3 hours of just reading his speech where he's essentially just chewing out the world for not thinking, or being thankful for the industrialists enough. 
 -The book is weirdly racist in parts, particularly against people from India and 'the orient'. 
 Now coming back to the philosophy: 
 -I really don't understand why conservatives glom onto this book so much-- Rand is extremely critical of the Washington types who come up with bail-outs for companies or are beholden to lobbyists of any kind. 
 -At one point Ragnar (a pirate) presents Rearden (an industrialist) with a block of gold worth the amount in income taxes that he has paid over the last 12 years, as a way of "paying him back for the money that the government has stolen from him". All the industrialists describe themselves as traders in this book, so I guess Rearden just didn't feel it was necessary to pay for his share of the roads, utilities, hospitals, defense, police, firemen, and education systems that allowed him and his factory full of workers to be in the position where they are today-- which in my opinion makes him a pretty shitty trader. 
 -The philosophy of the book essentially boils down to "I don't owe anyone in this world any help unless they are willing to give me something in return". This is the philosophy of a psychopath, and the characters clearly exhibit psychopathic tenancies-- Dagny closes a rail line and watches emotionlessly from her private car as the people in the towns along the line try to buy tickets to get on her train but there are none to be had, could she delay it a day, or let them use her private car to hold the extra passengers? Probably. But she does nothing instead. Later she murders a guard who can't decide if he should get out of her way, or stop her; Rearden spends a long time telling Dagny she's a whore for sleeping with him; Galt goes about the systematic destruction of a government which will result in millions of deaths, because he doesn't want to pay taxes. If you don't see anything wrong with being a psychopath then maybe this philosophy is good for you. 
 -If you stand by the statement that trades made at the end of a gun aren't valid then it's a little hard to swallow when you describe what the native Americans did with the colonists as 'trading', which means you don't have any rights to any of the lands that you're currently occupying. 
 -There's a lot of weird sub dom sex stuff dressed up as a testament to a celebration of being. Kind of strange. 
 -The main thing that the industrialists want in this book is a country where the only money you pay goes to supporting the military (to protect you from other countries), the police (to protect you from other people), and judges (to adjudicate disagreements). They emphatically insist that the government should not have the right to institute any rule which would negatively impact business. If you honestly believe that companies should be entrusted to regulate themselves in terms of the treatment of their workers, the harvesting of natural resources and environmental regulations then I hope you want to live in a world that's a smoking crater devoid of life where you work in a sweat shop because that is the logical outcome of that system. 
 -This book makes a lot more sense if you think of Rand growing up in communist Russia and seeing her father's store seized as state property. Applying it to your basic left of center person who just believes that it's wrong to let poor people die in the gutter, and that businesses should experience some level of government oversight is insane. I've read this book and I understand Rand's philosophy, but throughout it she makes it clear that she doesn't understand the other side. 
 Miscellaneous: 
 -This book would be a lot less controversial if the first part was a prologue about evil mind controlling aliens coming to earth and sapping people's will to live / decision making ability .

I have to admit to not finishing this one. I also tried "The Fountainhead," but failed with it as well. (I figure that it's okay to count one of them on Goodreads. I am aware that this wouldn't work with scalps.) 
 The problem is apparently not an unusual one, as I've found out from looking at other reviews. It's not so much that Rand is ideological; everybody knows that. It's not even so much that I entirely disagree with her ideology; there are aspects of it that speak to anyone who has ever gone against a crowd or tried to fight a bureaucracy, public or private. The problem is with her "straw man" approach. Or maybe I should say "straw Ubermensch." 
 Except that it's straw all the way down, too. 
 It's not to say that she wasn't creative. There is a case to be made that Rand perfected a new genre: the melocartoon. Her characterizations invariably link physical characteristics to moral ones; the characters are either good or bad. I can easily imagine the first edition of either of these two books being in the "Classics Illustrated" comic book format. She would've gotten a good four-decade jump on the recent elevation of the fiction comic to the "graphic novel." 
 It's a shame in a way. The most telling comment I can think of relating to Rand's status as a visionary is that she published a book about heroic individuals building a transcontinental railway in 1957, a year after a decidedly unheroic government established the Eisenhower Interstate Highway system. 
 Her vision, her John Galt objectivist platform, is no more than a gripe elevated to a philosophy of hubristic atomism. But atoms bond. Rand's ubervolk don't.

 No one can doubt the writing abilities of Ayn Rand. An immigrant American who lived the all Big American Dream. And, how! 
 I idealized her, even when disagreeing with her philosophy of 'The Virtue of Selfishness'. I may not agree with her life style, where she tried living an extremely selfish life, taking all at a whim with scant regard to who she was hurting or betraying. Her own needs far exceeded any other human emotion. But, more about it when I write a review of her biography written by her best friend! 
 It was later in life that I learned about the real threat to Capitalism from Communism and how Ayn Rand's writings/ tours and talks fitted in popularizing capitalism! By romanticizing capitalism, she made it aspirational to the youth. In turn the capitalists footed the bill for her tours and supported her in her various endeavours. 
 But, nothing takes away the beauty of her books. Atlas Shrugged is a must read for everyone remotely interested in reading good fiction. Its a study in what all is right in a book. The nerve wrecking plot, crisp dialogues, philosophy eloquently woven into the fabric of the book, handling extreme fantasy with conviction, it takes a superior mind and great writing skills to do so. Its a 1000 odd pages tome (what I recall). But a book one has to read day and night to reach to the very end! Ayn Rand has romance, betrayal, fortitude, science, undreamed of success, abject failure, imagination, pathos, hope, fantasy, reality; all under tight control. Like the keys of a fine tuned Piano, she knows which chord to strike with ease. 
 I have read some great books in my time, but this one has stayed with me. Always...

 This book was the only possible ending to this trilogy that didn't fuck up everything Collins did in the first two novels. Why, you ask? Because the series is dark. Its dystopian. And it sends a lot of really important messages to the intended audience: teens. 
 1. No one is good at everything. People have skill sets. Some people excel in one setting, some another. Not one person is excellent at everything and does well in every setting. Heroes are no exception. Heroes are NOT PERFECT. They have flaws (real ones. Not clumsiness). And this is perfectly fucking ok. Perfect characters are boring . 
 Message: We don't expect you to be perfect. Its ok that you have a hard time adjusting to what is going on around you. You don't have to be flawless to be good and do good things. If you aren't amazing at everything, no one will think less of you. Hell, if you are amazing at ONE thing thank your stars, because not everyone is. 
 2. Katniss is a teenager who has an amazing will to live. She has survival skills up the wazoo. What she doesn't have are people skills. That's to be expected. Look at how she grew up: rural, poor, unexposed to politics. Look at her personality: independent, untrusting, guarded. Of course she didn't do well in the political arena. Hell, she was thrown into a situation that she didn't even know existed. She didn't understand the impact and double meaning of what she did or said. How could she? And no one let her onto this until she had already screwed up. 
 Message: The adult world is nuanced and subtle. What you see on the surface isn't always indicative of what's underneath. As you jump into this world, you'll make mistakes. Its ok. Adults have a hard time predicting what messages people will receive from their statements. Hopefully, you'll have mentors who will guide you to see what else is going on. People who want you to learn without getting hurt. People who can help you learn the language of tact and hidden meanings. Don't expect to know all the moves when you're still learning the game and the players. These are skills that take time to build and not everyone learns equally well. 
 3. Soldiers experience trauma and have a difficult time adjusting to non-combat situations. People who have been focused on physical survival have every part of their being tuned to those needs and its damn hard to turn those down. IT IS COMPLETELY NORMAL TO HAVE PROBLEMS ADJUSTING TO NONCOMBAT LIFE. Hell, the VA should make this mandatory reading. You've been focused on surviving. You've seen horrible things. You've done horrible things. People you cared deeply about have died. Maybe someone sacrificed themselves to save you. You have been living on increased adrenaline and decreased sleep and food. You have nightmares. Trouble sleeping. You feel alone, like no one could love you after what you've done. Maybe you think you don't deserve it. Maybe "real world" problems seem petty to you. You've changed. Maybe you have PTSD, or adjustment disorder. You still deserve to have a life, a happy one. Its going to take time to learn how to live in a setting that doesn't require you to focus on physical survival every second; its going to take time to learn how to connect with your loved ones. You aren't going to be the person you were before the trauma/combat/survival experience. Its ok, and you don't have to be. 
 Message: See above? No, the message is all of that but its simple, too. It is ok and encouraged to see medical treatment for what you are going through. This includes mental health treatment. You should be actively engaged in your treatment and be prepared for this to take longer than people want it to. 
 4. Don't lose yourself to please other people. Everyone has unique skills, personality and gifts. Don't feel that you have to fit into someone else's mold. Just because you are working for the same cause or ideal doesn't mean that everyone is going to agree on everything. People should be in positions to work from their strengths; everyone should be in a position to succeed. See First, Break All the Rules: What the World's Greatest Managers Do Differently for a manual on how to make that happen in the real world. Or feel free to peruse it for character modeling for your fiction. Whateves. Don't let someone who is on your team push you into being someone you aren't. Authenticity matters, particularly for public figures (in case you're ever in that situation...). 
 Message: Be authentic. If someone is asking you to do something that you aren't able to do, be honest. Work with your allies, but don't blindly trust them to always have your best interests at heart. And remember: its hard to stand up to your enemies, harder still to stand up to your friends Thanks J.K. Rowling .

The last book in the Hunger Games trilogy and it doesn't disappoint. 
 Katniss, her mother, sister, Gale and a few others from District 12 are in District 13 where everything is regimented, down to when to eat, when to exercise and when to sleep. 
 A revolution is happening and the leaders of the rebels need Katniss to become 'The Mockingjay'. However she doesn't feel up to being the spokeswoman for the revolution, until she sees Peeta alive and being paraded by President Snow on TV. 
 A rescue attempt is made and an assault on the Capitol is planned. 
 The ending seemed to be a little rushed to me, but I didn't want this story to end. 
 Warning: There are a lot more deaths in this book, each more vivid than the other.

My theory that the third book in a trilogy can never be as good as the first two is in full effect in this series. 
 Without the adventure/anxiety/thrill of the games, the book was completely separated from anything resembling the first two novels. Instead, Mockingjay became a long-winded story of preparing for war, only to FINALLY reach the battle and be completely underwhelmed. 
 The entire time spent in district 13 was a complete bore and Peeta being brainwashed seemed so far fetched and a desperate attempt on Collins' part to make this book exciting. It was so cheesy and something out of a bad 80s Sci-fi movie. 
 I finished the book because I simply can't start a series and not know how it ends, but the ending went far from reaching my expectations. I've just had it with "corrupt government" plots. Thats all there ever seems to be in these dystopian novels! 
 That said, overall I enjoyed the series and the first two books were good enough for me to forgive the misfortunes of this one.

Where to start... I devoured this book as quickly as possible. I had to know what happened after the cliffhanger ending in Catching Fire. However, I was mildly disappointed. When the actual Hunger Games ended, there seemed to be something lacking from the plot. I had a hard time getting into the complicated political overthrow plot. This book also had some new characters that seemed a little out of place. Maybe out of place isn't the right term. They were there, but I couldn't figure out what purpose they served. It was hard to connect to any of them because there wasn't much depth. It was as if they were there for the purpose of the plot's subterfuge only. I really felt like there was no attempt to grow the new characters at all, except for maybe Boggs. 
 ** Spoiler alert** 
 Then there is the problem with Katniss herself. In the other books I thought she was so strong and defiant. Now, she seems so weak. In the aftermath of the events in Catching Fire, it makes sense. Her mental breakdowns and nightmares are acceptable and one hundred percent justifiable. What annoys me, however, is her constant pity party. Everyone knows that bad crap happens (that was obvious in the first two books), but to keep harping on it drove me nuts. It's as if we needed a constant reminder of how crappy life could be for her. Complete over kill. 
 I hate to say it, but this time around my favorite character was Finnick. He had the most depths out of all of the characters in this book. Oh, the secrets he has to share! Holy smokes. That was a dark turn I didn't expect. But then he gets killed off. That irritated me. I really wanted him to survive. It's not the fact that he died, either, that bothers me so much. It's the manner in which he died. What a waste. That entire scene seemed so rushed and out of place. I didn't even realize so many people died until two or three pages later. One of the major deaths in the book didn't even stand out to me. I knew she died because of the massive bombing that occurred, but what was the purpose? 
 I will say that there was one surprise that caught me off guard. Peeta. Wow. I didn't see that one coming. Poor, sweet Peeta. 
 No review would be complete if I didn't talk about the ending. WTH?! I am so unhappy with how things ended. I'm all for Peeta, don't get me wrong, but the way things were left with Gale seemed so wrong. No closure. I know there is supposed to be some great message about war and the roles we play--whether knowingly or not--but still... I felt so invested him that love triangle. I wanted a better solution. I don't care so much who Katniss ended up with, it's just the why that bothers me. It's like she didn't have a choice in the matter at all. She gets sent back to District 12 alone under the impression that no one will come for her. But then someone does... Only, it seems like he's there because he has nowhere else to be. Did anyone else get that feeling? Obviously Peeta wouldn't stay in the Capitol after what happened, so it only seemed natural that he would return to his home. With Katniss being there, of course they would end up together eventually. They are the only ones who can fully understand what it's like to be a survivor of The Hunger Games. But does that mean he wants to be there with her or she with him? Not necessarily. It felt like they were both going with the hand life dealt them because they didn't know what else to do. 
 ** End spoiler alert ** 
 I guess there was some sense of closure after the epilogue, but I still don't know how satisfied I am with it. The pieces do fit together and there is plenty to think about afterwards, that's for sure. Leaving the series with this book unread would be wrong. Be forewarned, though, it's a rollercoaster ride of emotions, and how you feel at the end really depends on whose side you're on.

But all in all it was a brilliant new concept although I wont be reading it again.
