Finished with the series, rapidly turning page after page. I have to admit Collins knows her stuff about plotting. Even more than in 'The Hunger Games' and 'Catching Fire,' this one delivers chapter after chapter that end in cliffhangers. At some point, you're bound to go beyond the time and space you've allotted reading installments of 'Mockingjay.' 
 Despite my irritation with the relentless seriousness of Katniss Everdeen's narration, I get her appeal, and understand that she is less a real person and more of an icon, a brand--an extremely popular brand. 
 Katie Roiphe got it perfectly in her NY Times review (http://www.nytimes.com/2010/09/12/boo... Katniss is 'the small, difficult teenage girl who manifests enormous physical and moral strength. She is both murderer and victim, somehow representing female strength and female vulnerability all mingled and entwined, dangerously, ambiguously, into one. She is Pippi Longstocking. She is the girl with the dragon tattoo.' And a perfect marketing ploy in what Roiphe calls 'the perfect teenage story with its exquisitely refined rage against the cruel and arbitrary power of the adult world.' 
 So I realize that my reservations will matter more to me and less to zillions of other readers, including Roiphe. And those reservations are only in the context of me avidly plowing through this trilogy, and feeling a part of the excited buzz surrounding that experience. 
 The reservations center around Katniss herself, and the heaping doses of inventive torture and violence Collins serves up. 
 Katniss's two suitors make a kind of peace in 'Mockingjay' and decide to just wait her out because at some point 'she will pick whoever she thinks can't survive without.' Katniss is outraged when she overhears this, but there's no doubt in her mind, or the reader's, that it's true. She is good at clinically cataloging characters' value (to herself), but not at developing characters (or having a good laugh). What she excels at is action, as in getting mutilated and wreaking havoc. 
 I feel a little odd making anything near a complaint about violence. One of my favorite movie scenes is the pre-gubernatorial Arnold Schwarzenegger using an innocent bystander as a human shield against a barrage of bullets in 'Total Recall.' I'm the kind of guy who laughs with delight while viewing that. 
 But there I know that Paul Verhoeven is playing to the beast in me, without trying to impart any moral lessons. Suzanne Collins wants it both ways--lots of gore, but it's all in the service of a heartfelt antiwar message. I'm not going to object to titillation, unless you call it something else. The 'Hunger Games' trilogy has a sleazy sanctimoniousness to it that soured my enjoyment of one unexpected shock after another. For that reason, the 'Kumbaya' epilogue seemed flat to me, and left me a little disappointed. 
 Entertaining, but 'The Hunger Games' was not nearly as earthshaking for me as for many, many others.
Slow and boring compared to the first one.
It was sooo tragic! :( But i loved the funny parts

This was the weakest book of the trilogy. The focus was more on the war than the characters. I wasn't thrilled with how the characters were portrayed. Don't want to spoil for anyone. Just know that you might not be as engaged in this one.

** spoiler alert ** 
 Outstanding conclusion to a great trilogy. I know I'll re-read the entire thing at least once someday, and I don't usually pick up the same book twice. I'm a little pissed that the ending follows a too-common YA/Female Lead trend:--"Having children is the only way your future will have meaning, girls!"--but the rest of the book outdid itself and earned that fifth star I considered knocking off. This is a fucking war novel, with graphic (but not gratuitous) gore and negative emotions aplenty, and it's about freaking time we get a beautiful young heroine who doesn't shave her legs, who makes decisions for herself (decisions that have real consequences for people other than herself), a heroine who ends up disfigured, broken, and hopeful instead of resplendent, whole, and blushing. Katniss spends every other chapter recovering from a new injury or psychological breakdown, but it never feels repetitive because we never see what's coming. Well-loved characters die (Finnick!); and foundation characters undergo striking change, not only in themselves, but in the eyes of Katniss (Gale!). And finally, finally, Katniss is able to make a choice that hasn't been handed to her in front of a camera, a choice with real and positive effects on Panem's citizens, by assassinating Coin. The best part is, the author keeps you guessing about whether or not Katniss will pull through (and if she does, what her future will look like) until the very last paragraph.

I was really hoping to see Katniss kick Pres. Snow's butt in this story, but she never got that chance due to the fire. As a reader, I was disappointed by that, but as a writer, I can see how the fire went along with the themes in the stories - she really did end up being 'the girl on fire.' Plus it forms doubt in Katniss's mind about Gale (were the fire bombs his idea? And if so, how could she continue a relationship with someone who could think that way?)Some have argued that she didn't choose Peeta, but I'd argue that she did. She could have just ignored him even though he was around, (something she was practiced at) but she chose him because she needed the hope he provided. 
 I liked that the series ended with her having children since that's the one thing she swore she would never do in the beginning. She might not be the best parent since she's so messed up, but it was a good note with which to end the series. 
 And those white lizard mutt things - that was inspired! And yucky. Can't wait to see those in the movie version. 
 Yes, the story is hard and depressing, but it shows the power of the actions of the individual. I didn't enjoy this one as much as the others as a reader, but it gave me more to think about as a writer than the others. Plus, you can really tell the author was involved in television writing in her career. Some of the scenes she creates could be done so only with the knowledge of a TV insider.

This finale I read first, out of order, in the painful tragic vividly violent alternate-future trilogy. I mourn so many unnecessary deaths. I guessed the moral "War is Hell", confirmed by DVD extras http://annetoronto1.blogspot.ca/2013/... pending. 
 Katniss is a soldier, and others want her to lead as the bird of the title, so we must watch those around her scream and die in blood. Dangers are high-tech weapons and DNA-warped monsters. 
 Previously, rebels based in regimented restrictive underground District 13 rescued District 12 young heroine Katniss and allies from the gladiator-style competitions televised by the extravagant Rome-like "Bread and Circuses" Capitol. Her relaxed rural home area is in ashes. Her lover is captured, tortured, and damaged into a weapon against her. 
 We persist with Kat through her physical and mental pain, wandering hiding avoidance, morphling (morphine) nightmares, ghosts and guilty regrets, because she fights, supported by family and friends we also care about, loyal and honest amid deception and manipulation. We cheer the surprise finale, when her arrow flies for honor and truth.

As an author, I hate the idea of giving only 2 stars, but in this case, I think I'm being generous. I loved the The Hunger Games. LOVED IT!! And I liked Catching Fire. But Mockingjay was a huge disappointment. 
 The first three quarters was achingly slow, and I only stuck with it because a few of my friends urged me to, telling me it would get better. The last quarter seemed to try to make up for the boring start by throwing in everything the author could possibly think of to shock the reader. It was imaginative in its extreme violence and the horrific ways in which people died. But the style was so clipped, so short on description, I could never really get an adequate picture in my head of the devices used to cause such devastating destruction and death. And just when the story was being most impactful, however abhorrent, the action stopped. The protagonist goes into a hazy, drug-induced recovery mode where she doesn't know what was what. And neither did I. It was like a rollercoaster that had just made it to the top of its first big hill, only to fall backwards to the start line. 
 Though I love first-person POV, I'm not a big fan of present-tense, though I've seen it done well elsewhere. And while the first two books didn't bother me too much, this last one felt like I was at the end of a chain of people, each one telling the one next to them what was happening, and by the time it got to me, it was so filtered and spotted, it made no impact; it had no depth. And the characters bothered me, too. I loved Finnick in his infinite sadness, and I found Peeta to be tragic and compelling. But Gale and Katniss were infuriatingly bitter, combative, and disappointingly affected. 
 I would never, in a million years, suggest this book to a teenager, especially a girl. Though its theme was the impact of war, the violence felt gratuitous and exaggerated simply for impact's sake. I was actually angry when I was done reading this book, though not because it ended, but because I was so patient with it and it disappointed me so thoroughly. But this is a subjective business, and I seem to be in the minority. That alone makes me sad, because it shows how desensitized to violence we've become. 
 I really wanted to love this book. I was looking forward to reading. I only wish now that I had put it aside when I was first tempted.

Wow. Just wow. Just when I thought that this series couldn't get any better- it did. I, personally was counting down for this book with some of my friends. We knew exactly how many days there was until Mockingjay came out. And I got it the first day. And I read it slowly (as in it took me a week) as I knew it was going to be the last Hunger Games book and I wanted to make the most of it. 
 As with the two preceding books it follows the same mockingjay pin theme except on the cover of Mockingjay, the mockingjay has taken up most of the cover as to show the importance of The Mockingjay in this final book. So my personal break down of the cover is this: I believe that the reason that the mockingjay has taken up the majority of the cover is because of how huge a role the mockingjay plays in this particular book. Another thing that I noticed about this cover is that the standard Hunger Games design in the background, that reminds me of circuitry, has been broken on this cover. I find that it probably means to interpret that there is a rebellion happening and people are breaking out of the Capitol's control after many years of being under it. The other element to the cover that I find important to the book is how the mockingjay has full color now that it's not just a pin anymore. I think it was trying to show that the mockingjay was more than just the pin anymore, it was the icon of the rebellion; it was to, ultimately, represent Katniss as the spark and leader of the rebellion in Panem. 
 Over this whole series, I just can't believe the growth that occurred in these characters. Katniss started out as the provider of her family who would jump the fence to hunt a bit and talk with Gale while out. She was always brave with everything from getting extra rations by entering her name multiple times for the reaping, going past the fence even though it was illegal just to provide food and then going to sell her extra portions to The Hob for profit. That was in the beginning though when her life was simpler, then she saved her sister by volunteering to take Prim's place in the Hunger Games where she survived twice and lied to an entire nation. And in the end, she became a national icon by leading a revolution in an impossible dictatorship and she came out alive. That's a big jump from going past the fence for food to leading a successful revolution to overturn a terrible dictatorship. And then there's Peeta. When the first book started, we didn't know anything of Peeta or who he really was. Then he pulled many game changing moves in both the Hunger Games and in their tours after. But it wasn't until Mockingjay that I really fell in love with him. From his bravery to his love for Katniss, he was the perfect character for this book and an even perfecter (new word!) love interest for Katniss. 
 Though Mockingjay took a while to get into, once you did you were strapped in for the rest of the book. There was just as much action as the first two, even without the Hunger Games to help the story along. Along the way we also meet some beautifully introduced characters that can only be the handiwork of Suzanne Collins. The writing and story in this book were truly something to be in awe of. After getting into the book, there were few dull moments and even fewer times that the writing didn't make you feel something. The story was just as great as the writing. But I really just loved the darkness of the story that it didn't try and sugar coat what was happening in the book. She was out right with everything and she didn't tip-toe around death. And the ending. It will make anyone one cry. ANYONE. It just killed me what happened and it just crushed me into tears and extreme sadness. I was thinking about that ending for days and how devastated I was (in the best way possible). 
 In my oh-so-humble opinion, this was one of the best series I have ever read and this, by far, is also one of the best conclusions to a series that I have ever read. There is something for everyone in this series and I believe that everyone needs to read this book if not for the story, for the message behind it. That's why this book gets/ deserves a 5/5. In fact it deserves a 100000000000/5, but that's unfortunately not possible.

reference_books.title: Of Fire and Stars
reference_books.review_text:
"I wanted Mare. I was promised to her brother. I was in deep trouble." 
 It pains me to only give this book three stars. I had such high hopes and great anticipation and it just didn't live up to it at the end of the day. 
 Of Fire and Stars was a decent read that really started picking up near the end. The world building and explanation of the magic system in Of Fire and Starswere weak. I have my doubts that the world building will get much stronger but I have faith that the magic system being explained better will happen in the next book. I found the names of the characters frustrating. Most were hard to pronounce and what was worse is a couple of them had names that were fairly similar so I started mixing up a couple of the side characters. 
 The main protagonists, Denna and Mare, were interesting enough. They were really the only solid part of this book for me, but they didn't save the novel sadly. The idea of a princess falling for another princess is awesome and something I haven't seen at all in YA fantasy before. I did think the romance between them was nice and the sex scene was very well-done I thought. It wasn't smutty but it definitely got fairly steamy. I wouldn't call it graphic though. I did think the women had a really nice chemistry and I could see me shipping these two if I could get a little more invested in the story itself. 
 The side-characters were not developed at all. Anytime one started to get interesting, it never went anywhere. One of the major players in this book is Mare's brother Thandi. It was like the author couldn't decide what personality to settle on for him. One moment he was strict and tradional and the next he was causal and didn't seem to care one way or another. His role was very important to the plot, it just ended up falling flat though. 
 I gave this three instead of two stars because I thought the romance between the women was well done - a bit cliche but nice enough. Also, near the end it really picked up the pace. It left off with a cliffhanger and that has interested me enough to pick up the second book in the series when it comes out. 
 Overall, I just feel middle-of-the-road on this one. I was really excited to get it and I'm glad I read it but I wouldn't recommend this book for anyone going through a book slump. It is not a fast moving book at all.

reference_books.title: Fables, Volume 2: Animal Farm (Fables, #2)
reference_books.review_text: This one was still cool but it wasn't my favorite storyline ever. I'm still pumped about reading this series though.

reference_books.title: A Child Called "It" (Dave Pelzer #1)
reference_books.review_text: I feel weird saying that I "liked" this book as really, what's to like about it? It's about a child being horribly abused by his mother while his father does nothing to stop or help him. It was fairly well-written, not the best ever but the story itself was strong enough to overlook any writing issues. I have also read the book by his brother, which brought to light even more of this horror story.

reference_books.title: A Court of Mist and Fury (A Court of Thorns and Roses, #2)
reference_books.review_text:
"To the stars who listen-- and the dreams that are answered." 
 The following review will have major spoilers - if you haven't read the book yet, I would suggest not reading any further. 
 I am a completely and utter emotional wreck and I'm sending you my therapy bill, Maas!!! 
 A Court of Mist and Fury took me on an emotional roller coaster ride to say the very least. I am officially on the hype-train for Maas and I'm not getting off anytime soon. All of these characters are just so well-written. I laughed, screamed and cried with them all. Maas might not be offering a lot in terms of inventiveness to the fantasy genre but the woman can write one hell of a romance and interesting/refreshing characters. I could've read another 600 pages and would've been content, even if it was filler. I just wanted to be in this world as long as possible. 
 It won't be shocking to hear that I'm complete trash for Rhys. I really liked him in the first book because I was drawn to his charisma and mystery factor. In this one, Rhys still has that going for him but you seen how fiercely he loves the people he cares for and it's just so endearing. His relationship with Feyre is probably one of the best relationships I've had the pleasure to read about. I adored the banter between them and watching them slowly fall in love. The scene where they danced all night at the Starfall had all the makings of something really terribly cheesy. Somehow, Maas managed to pull off that scene as being one of the sweetest and swoon-worthy scenes in the book. I was smiling the entire time. Also, when Feyre and Rhys had that very risque scene at The Court of Nightmares - it was the most fun thing I've read in a long time. The chemistry between these two is as hot as it gets. 
 We were also introduced to Rhys's crew and some of the greatest side characters. Cass, Az, Armen and Mor - I loved each and every one of them for different and wonderful reasons. They all brought something completely different to the table. We haven't learned too much about Az and Armen yet but I was still very intrigued by them and want to know more - NOW! 
 I have to say that I almost fell over in happiness when the Suriel told Feyre that Rhys was her mate. For some reason I hadn't given the idea much thought so I didn't see it coming at all. I read that scene several times in a row, because I was so excited. I realized then that I had basically reverted to my 12 year old fangirl self and wanted to have posters all of my wall of this book haha 
 Of course, I have to talk about the infamous chapters 54 and 55 because what would a review be without them? I know most people loved 55 because it gets very steamy and I loved the chapter as well but for me chapter 54 has to be my favorite. When he tells her the entire story and when he tells her the moment he truly realized they were mates and everything just clicked into place, I just sat there in awe of it all. I had been frustrated at Rhys in the first book for certain actions and each and every one of them were all addressed. Rhys good reasons for them, without having to put plotholes in to make them work. I want to go back and read the first one just to see the various reactions/actions now because I think it would be an entirely different book with that knowledge. Of course, 55 was amazing as well and yes the rumors are true - the sexual content in this book is quite graphic. It verges on smutty. That isn't a bad thing in my book - I loved their love scenes but I know it's been a problem for some. This is a New Adult book but like many it's been placed in the YA section, so just a heads-up about the material. 
 Everyone warned me that I would need a few tissues to get through this book. I was nearing the last chapters and I had no idea what people were going on about - then I hit the last few chapters. First, Cass has his wings shredded - hadn't lost it yet but am starting to become upset. Then that fateful sentence that Feyre says to the king - "break the bond." I seriously fell to pieces. I was full out, ugly crying hysteria. I was ready to toss the book out the window and possibly myself with it! Later, when I found out that the bond was not broken there was some relief but when Rhys said she was The High Lady of the Night Court - again I was a mess. I cried from happiness and sadness all at once. See, why I need therapy now? 
 I've been putting off this part because I honestly really hate to even say Tamlin's name. I hate this guy as much as I hate Umbridge I think - yep, I went there! I mean you might think I'd hate the King or Durian more but I don't - they owe Feyre nothing and they are just fun villains. We all knew these characters were likely going to be pretty ruthless. However, I feel the betrayal with Tamlin - I once liked this character, I knew he was flawed but I liked him. I even liked him and Feyre together for a bit. I don't feel sorry for this character and I don't understand how anyone could still be #teamTamlin at this point. It's mind blowing to me. I'm actually dreading reading more about him in the next book because he's not a fun villain - he's one that makes you want to throw things at walls, often. 
 Oh, and Lucien's mate being Elaine! Interesting. 
 Bottom line is that this book must be read. It's so much better than the first book I can't even compare the two in terms of how much I love this book. Five stars all day long. Easiest rating I've ever had to give!

reference_books.title: Alice in Zombieland (White Rabbit Chronicles, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
I should start by saying that I did NOT finish this book. I probably shouldn't have bought it to begin with. I've never read a really great retelling of anything Wonderland yet. I am a little surprised at how the rating is for this book, maybe people knew something going in that I did not. 
 First I think it's pretty fair for me to have assumed that this book was based (even if loosely) on Alice in Wonderland. I mean it's got a girl with blonde hair and the Alice traditional colored outfit on the cover, not to mention it's referred to as The White Rabbit Chronicles. That is about where the similarities to the original story stop though. 
 No, I did not read it all but I just wasn't feeling it at all. The only real mention of Wonderlandish (it's a word, sh) stuff mentioned is that the main character is named Alice, but prefers to be called "Ali" and she sometimes sees white rabbit shaped clouds... Really? That is the connection? I haven't felt this frustrated at a book for a very long time, I just can't stress enough how much the title misleads it's audience. That alone would get a low rating from me. 
 I normally start my reviews with a quote but I couldn't find anything that felt quotable. This book just really is not for me and I probably wouldn't read anything by this author again unfortunately. 
 I will say the covers are very pretty, I have the first two in hardcover (not my best purchase) and I happen to collect all things Alice in Wonderland so I will just keep them for display.

book_a.title: Broken Prince (The Royals, #2)
book_a.user_review:
"I'll go, if that's what you want ... But we're not done, Ella. Not by a long shot." 
 You can find this review and all of my other reviews at Novel Descent Thanks for the support! 
 THIS REVIEW WILL CONTAIN SPOILERS! 
 Another fast pace installment in the Royals series. Not as good as the first but still good trashy fun. 
 Broken Prince picks back up where it left off. Reed is looking for Ella after she ran because she found him in bed with Brooke. Oh the scandal! Brooke is blackmailing Reed to get him to put in a good word to his father so that Brooke can weasel her way back into the house and into Reed's father's bank account. 
 This book was fun, I don't think it couldn't be. Like the first it's just an easy soap opera type of book that won't change your life but is a great way to kill a couple of hours. I did get a bit bored at parts in this one though. Reed spent a lot of the time looking for where Ella had run off too and then spent another 100 pages trying to win her back when she returned home. I didn't find the push and pull that engaging and I just wanted to see something new thrown at them. I already saw the cat and mouse shit in the first book - give me a new storyline damnit! Easton is messed up as per usual and it doesn't really fix itself at all, not sure if it will. 
 Of course, the second Reed and Ella finally get back together then more shit hits the fan. Reed gets stabbed by the guy who tried to rape Ella in the first book. There was somewhat of a build up to this moment, you knew the guy was going to retaliate because Reed and Ella had humiliated him several times. I don't know if that storyline is particularly strong though - it doesn't feel fleshed out enough. Reed gets stabbed but it's not like the end of the world - they don't even seem THAT concerned. It's over as soon as it begins. Just another day at the Royal house I suppose. 
 Of course, in true Royal fashion the book left off with a massive cliffhanger - the author is excellent at making sure you will have no choice but to pick up that next book. It ends with Brooke murdered and even crazier than that Steve shows up. Yep, Ella's dead dad is standing in the room at the very last page. Say whaaaaaaaaat? I will be finishing up the series soon.

sample_reviews.review_text: I loved that this book had Reeds POV along with Ella's POV. This was so sad at first, I hated that Ella was hurting so much. Then Reed is on a mission but Ella does not change her mind quickly or easily. Then more drama with certain people, a big surprise, then a huge mistake. Once again this book ended in quite the cliffhanger, can't wait to read the next book.
Wtf man???? The first one was unrealistic as hell but it was damn entertaining for sure. This one though.. ugh kill me now

I had issues with the entire first half and then some. Until basically the very end, I was getting bored with the characters' actions... I thought that Reed was over possessive of Ella and that the relationship was incredibly unhealthy for most of the two books until the last half of the second one. I'm probably the only one who thinks this though :/

WTF WAS THAT ENDING!?! I can't cope with what just happened I need the next book right now. I ordered Twisted Palace as soon as I finished Paper Princess because I knew I would want to read it after finishing this but its not arrived yet and damn the postman for making me wait for it! I don't know what to do now. 
 4.5 Stars

Okay, Reed didn't cheat of Ella. Do I care? Nope, because if you've read my review of Paper Princess, you would know I never got invested in the romance. 
 Broken Prince was boring, a filler book. Reed's POV made me yawn and the story only picks up toward the end with another bomb being dropped just make everyone one-click Twisted Palace (which I did btw). 
 The Royal series is like that bad soap opera you can't stop watching. It has way too many eye-rolling inducing moments and unbelievable situations. 
 I'm not sure I will buy any new work from the Erin Watt duo.

Book two is all sorts of bad too, just like the first book--outrageous characters, and plot line that is laughable, there is far too much boozing-sex-fighting-teenage arrogance-stupidity and still, I read the entire thing. A train wreck! 
 But my oh my, it entertained me through all the horribleness. 
 The thing is, this plot line and the characters had great potential to be a good story; it did not need to be an in your face GI Joe manly teen and a female teen with a smartass, tough-persona chip on her shoulder. The boys are spoiled permissive rich brats with no consequences, and with an idiotic but yet likable Father, and the girl -while not rich- is pretty much the same as the boys. 
 I doubt I'll read the third book, but maybe so because yeah....I'm liking this train wreck--its full of unbelievable nonsense that is greatly entertaining me. 
 So yep, there are moments in my life when I am entertained by a storyline that is cheesy, ridiculous and horrible with characters that are outrageous. For one recent weekend, it worked.

4.45 
 AMAZEBALLS!!!

The Royals are an addiction! Honestly they're too hard to resist. I am, however, slowly finding their antics to be getting way too dramatic. What has me glued to the pages and unable to stop is how entertaining the storyline is. Someone needs to adapt this series into a movie/tv show asap. 
 The dual POV this time was helpful in learning how much Reed was struggling to make things right with Ella and his family. Though I can't say I cared much. I was annoyed with his smug attitude regardless of how accurate his words were. Also, the constant "babe" and "baby" were a bit much, no? I only liked that he legit realizes his mistakes and put effort into trying and making it up to the people he wronged. 
 At the end of Paper Princess Ella was too quick to judge but under those circumstances I didn't really blame her. Still, I found her hard to warm up to in Broken Prince. I thought she was strong and would firmly hold onto her standpoint but she wavered quite easily in my opinion. I wanted to see her put up more of a fight! At least she's standing by her choice and choosing to believe in those she has come to love. 
 Callum Royal is not a fool. His involvement in his sons' and ward's well-being made him the shiny star in this installment. In contrast, Gideon, Easton and the twins took another dark turn. They were kind of nasty. The spotlight was especially on Gideon as we come to learn his big secret. All the expletives cannot convey how I feel for what he went through and is still going through. No wonder he has such a sad tense presence in the story. I can only pray justice will be served. Harshly I hope. 
 Erin Watt sure knows how to write cliffhangers because we're left with yet another at the end of Broken Prince. And this one features two shockers. Can't say I feel sorry for what happened to Brooke because she's despicable but not for one second do I believe Reed did it. But we shall see... Steve's appearance (I called it) will also for sure stir up quite the crazy. I'm just rubbing my hands in glee for more drama ;) 
 This story is cheesy but highly amusing. I definitely will keep reading because I need to know what the end game is. Whether the bad guys will burn in fiery hell and our beloved Royals will smile in blissful heaven we will find out soon enough in Twisted Palace.
3,5. !?Por que demonios son tan adictivos estos libros?!
Mehhhh... lackluster angst.

I got completely sucked into Paper Princess and stayed up late into the night to finish it in one sitting, because I couldn't put it down. So I was extremely excited for the sequel. That excitement faded after I started reading it, and I actually set it aside to read another book. I've continued to read Broken Prince in short increments since then, because it's not as compelling as the first book. 
 I loved the angst and the sexual tension in the first book, and there is none of that in Broken Prince. The problem here is that we get Reed's POV, and that takes away all the uncertainty and intrigue about his intentions. I couldn't connect with Ella's doubt in this one, because I already knew the truth straight from Reed's thoughts. He was also more interesting when he was ambiguous. Knowing all his thoughts ruined that. It also took away all the tension and anticipation. It made the story too predictable. 
 I enjoyed Ella's showdowns in the first book, but they were ridiculous and overdone in this one. All the drama here quickly became tiresome. It dragged on and on, and there was no fun. The first book had fun scenes to enjoy, but I can't remember any in this book. Even Easton was depressed during the entire book. I love angst, but this tipped over into melodrama. The only unexpected thing that happened was Gideon's secret. That piqued my interest, but it was only a brief part of the plot. 
 The worst part of this book was the ending. The cliffhanger in the first one promised all kinds of antagonism and fireworks that this book didn't deliver. The cliffhanger in this one was just plain stupid. It made Reed look stupid, because there was no reason for him to go anywhere near the mess his dad was already taking care of. book_b.user_review:
"A villain is just a victim whose story hasn't been told." 
 This one breaks my heart, I was sure this would be a higher rating. 
 The Wishing Spelltook me forever to finish, I really pushed on it. I probably should have given up after awhile but I was trying so hard to convince myself that I liked this book. Why would I do that? Mostly because this book should have won me over so easily. It had all my favorite elements: middle-grade adventure, fairytale-retelling and lots of fun recognizable characters. This book was such a disappointment for me. I did get excited to see the crazy amount of fairy tale and nursery rhyme (loved that they were included as well) characters that were in the story. I did find the Red-Riding Hood plot pretty entertaining but the rest of the book fell pretty flat. Oh, and Mr. Frog was a hoot. 
 I wasn't big on Chris Colfer's writing style (I am a fan of his acting though). It was very simplistic and quite clunky. The sentences were short and not that descriptive. At first I was going to give this book some slack because it's for a younger audience (6-12 probably) but I really couldn't do that because middle-grade should be held up to the same standard as anything else. Middle-grade gave us masterpieces like Harry Potter and The Chronicles of Narnia. Middle-grade can mean some very quality writing that all ages can enjoy. 
 Another big issue with this book is that there was NO sense of danger for me at all. I mean they would get into dangerous situations but nothing seemed very urgent to them and everything moved too fast so things were over before they began. I think he put too many characters into one book and so we really couldn't get to know most of them that well. 
 I know a lot of people really like this series and this would probably be a fun read for younger children. It just didn't work for me. I'm sad that I won't be continuing the series because I know later on in the series characters like The Queen of Hearts and Merlin show up. 
 I can't say it's not worth a read because it might work for you. I would definitely suggest this book to read with your children as small as five or six.

Encouraged by a student (okay, it was more like begged and then demanded) to read the first book in this series after commenting to her class that the current title received a couple of literary nods, I postponed the inevitable until last night. Much like the main characters Alex and Connor, I fell into the book and didn't finish it until the wee hours of the morning. The book does begin a little slowly because it is the first in a series. Pleasantly surprised, I can see why this fractured fairy tale captivates my student readers. Part humorous and part suspenseful, Chris Colfer (of "Glee" fame no less...), manages to weave a clever quest to retrieve items from fairy tales so that our twins might return to the land in which they came. Although predictable in some parts for this adult reader, I am always a fan of stories that encourage our kids to (re)turn to classic fairy tales. Sadly, many children grow up now without a strong working knowledge of them; they are a strong foundation to all future reading and a missing link if not read early. Though I flagged several pages for its sage words, here are a few of my favorite lines: 
 "I've learned that the more people embrace their disadvantages, the less disadvantaged they become!" 
 "I'd rather die trying than live the rest of life wondering if I could have done it." 
 "I'm so glad Dad and Grandma read to us so much growing up!" Connor said. "Who ever would have thought it would be this useful?" 
 "A flame may love a snowflake, but they can never be together without each harming the other." 
 "Every driven person comes from a mountain of pain they wish to keep hidden." 
 "It's easier to hate, blame and fear than it is to understand. No one wants the truth; they want entertainment." 
 Highly recommended with a note that there are a few (ahem) "colorful" words sprinkled throughout and a few more adult jokes hidden within.

I think Chris Colfer is a pretty cool person, but definitely needs to get a better editor. It's pretty apparent that his fame and not his raw talent for writing was the cause for this book being published. I really love fairy tales and how much they've changed over the years from the dark and gruesome originals to the lighter stories that are told now. This isn't one of the better retellings. 
 The modern day portion is sort of grating in that none of the characters have any depth at all. Connor is a slacker, Alex is a brainiac. Their mom is struggling over the loss of their dad and has nothing but love for everyone and everything. They don't really grow or show any amount of depth beyond those surfaces. 
 (some spoilers) 
 The fairy tale world was more interesting but he could have done a lot more with it. The goblins and trolls are, of course, evil. All the princesses were kind. Goldilocks and Red Riding Hood and Jack of the Beanstalk have some weird love triangle going on that took up more of the story than it needed to. I liked the spin Colfer put on Snow White and her stepmother. That was really interesting and I would have liked much more of that than anything else. Goldilocks and Red were mildly interesting but the back story and romance in that was very forced and it was pretty unfortunate that a man had to be the source of most of that plot. 
 The class assignment of finding the correct meaning of fairy tales was a really lame part of the story. The great thing about stories is that anyone can interpret something different from each of them, so it felt like Colfer was encouraging only one right answer instead of being open to different ways of thinking about things. 
 Overall, this read like it was the very first rough draft for something that could have been much better.

Colfer has jumped on the bandwagon of new takes on fairy tales and the result is a cute story that appeals to children. The writing is awkward and stilted at times and includes some cringe-worthy moments like his use of the term "Siamese twins" and the pointing out of one black character that really draws attention to the fact that everyone else is white. I won't be reading the rest of the series or adding these to my classroom library.

I kept cringing at the writing or rolling my eyes at how easily things came to them. It seemed like an attempt to cram the book with all the popular fairy tale characters you know. Characters were one dimensional and the thread of the story did not make any sense either. 
 Everything that happened to them was just too neat which is a sign of lazy storytelling. They get kidnapped by trolls and goblins and their fellow inmates despair and tell them it's useless but within minutes of being locked in they are saved by a stupid she troll. There was never any moment where I got carried away with the story because as a challenge befell them I knew they would get out of it in the next paragraph! At one stage in the book, Alex was asking the Little Mermaid why she was helping them and she said it was just because she's good. All the main fairy tale characters who meet them instinctively trust them and help straight away even though the kids are essentially stealing from them. There are so many other wonderful children fantasy stories out there and it seems a waste that something like this was published. Had the author not been famous I doubt it would have happened.

I persevered because the students LOVED it. Me? Not so much. I think they may have loved that the author was a face and name that they could relate to (although even for this rather easy going parent Glee is not really suitable for the age this book is written for - but that is a whole other rant). To sum up - well, I can't. It's every fairy tale ever after but not sure that was a necessary literary addition that was required.

The Wishing Spell is the first book in The Land of Stories series written (and read) by Chris Colfer. This children's fantasy novel offers a new look at some favorite fairy tales. Twins Alex and Conner Bailey have lost their father and are just trying to get through each day. On their birthday their grandmother gives them a treasured fairy tale book, they have no idea they're about to enter a land beyond all imagining: the Land of Stories, where fairy tales are real. They come face-to-face with the fairy tale characters they grew up reading about. As their search for the ingredients for The Wishing Spell, possibly their only way home. They encounter princesses, a frog man, witches, wolves, goblins, trolls and much more. Getting home is going to be even harder than they thought. 
 The Wishing Spell started off giving readers a look at just who Alex and Conner are. Their father died, their mother works too much, and their grandmother travels. Alex is a book worm with no friends but plenty of smarts. Conner is a good kid, but has trouble staying awake in class and has a bit of a smart mouth. When their grandmother passes down her treasured storybook strange things begin to happen, resulting in the twins falling through the book into the 'Land of Stories'. I really liked the twists on some of the stories, and I especially liked that even the evil queen is given a back story to help readers understand just how everyone came to be who they are. Goldilocks is not what you would expect, neither is Red Ridinghood, but some of the princesses are just as sweet and simple as you might expect from the tales you already know. I think Goldilocks, Jack, and the Evil Queen were my favorite characters through out, simply because they were fresh and new here. They had new stories and new motivations. 
 There were a few things that bothered me as I was listening to the audiobook. I was less thrilled with Alex's seeming willingness to give up completely on her home (i.e. mother and grandmother) in lieu of staying in the stories, even though it was temporary. My other sticking point was Conner's personality- he seemed like the entitled kid that I always dislike running into in public. He felt free to criticize everyone (including royalty) and put other people down. He made rash assumptions and stuck with them regardless of their validity. My other complaint is that sometimes the solutions just seemed to easy. No wonder Conner acted like an entitled brat, everything seemed to work out for him (except the loss of his dad prior to the beginning of the story). They slipped away from wolves, tricked a witch, convinced otherwise intelligent adults to hand over what ever he wanted, and pretty much skated through things. There were some suspenseful moments, and those were done well, but the effect was kind of ruined by the precedent of things just working out for no good reason. 
 That might make it sound like I did not enjoy the book, but I did. This was the debut book from a young author with plenty of other things on his plate,and I think The Wishing Spell demonstrates that he has talent and great potential for growth. I would recommend The Wishing Spell to readers that enjoy fairy tale reimaginations, fantasy quest stories, stories about growing up, and fun adventure. The second book in the series is The Enchantress Returns.

I just wanted to love this and did not. However I really liked Connor and some of the fairy tale reselling aspects were interesting. I can see why a middle grades reader would enjoy it but I have read more complex and moving fantasy books for children.
A good book. Sometimes couldn't tell exactly who the audience was supposed to be because some of the language was a bit beyond the target audience. My daughter will like to read this book!

While I liked the ideas for the plot lines in this book, the execution was poor. I don't know a lot about the publishing industry but it seems to me this book could have benefitted from a thorough editing and a refresher lesson on using words other than "said" when writing conversation.

This book was very disapointing. I don't at all like Colfer's style of writing. It was very juvenile, and simple and he wrote like an elementary school language arts student. His writing was repetetive and boring. Everytime the characters got in trouble, he would stick in the solution on the same page! Like he was thinking "Hummm... I need some conflict. There we go, so now we resolve it!" I love the story idea, just not the way it was presented. I probably will try the next one. I am so unsatisfied that I might take the time to write an additional review about everything I specifically disliked, in more detail.

Maybe it was really meant to be a rough draft for a TV pitch? Anyway, there are so many better books out there. Your time is too valuable for this. I think that the love of fairytales and the new takes on them is definitely here. You can tell that author Chris Colfer was not only deeply impacted by the beloved stories, but wanted to share them in a new light. The plot is a typical adventurous quest, but the personality of what-happened-to-the fairytale characters is what makes it so intriguing. After having recently listened to Colfer's audio book reading of his first book, taking on the various characters' voices and demonstrating his vocal chops of what the male and female characters sounded like, are making the future books of this series so enjoyable to read. Colfer has a very nice wit in his writing, with some sarcasm, enough humor, heart, and action to make this an enjoyable read.

I may love Chris Colfer in his acting career, but I will say again that just because you have the money and/or fame to get a work published does NOT mean that you deserve that honor. The Wishing Spell is unoriginal and unsuitable even for a very basic level of YA audience. Give your fantasy-loving friends something like Jasper Fforde's Thursday Next series (adult audience) or Gail Carson Levine's absolute classic Ella Enchanted (YA and adult appropriate) if they are looking for a plot that plays successfully with the conventions of fairy tale narrative. Skip this novel -- one that, if anything, is carried entirely on Colfer's Glee fame . . . you deserve better.

I guess I misunderstood the age group this was written for, but regardless, nothing can change the fact that it's too simplistic and entirely lacking in charm for a book based on fairy tales. Colfer's grandmother should have written this book. Her quote in the dedication was very charming.

This book wasn't bad. It definitely drew me in and had a fast pace. 
 A few things I didn't like: 
 1. The choppy writing. 
 2. The flat, one-dimensional characters.

 4. Alex and Conner get into trouble! Oh no! Good thing that the fairytale characters are all so kind and willing to help. 
 I did like the fairytale setting, but I wanted a bit more depth to Alex and Conner. Yes, I know it's middle-grade, but still...

I rarely find a book I just can't make myself finish, but this was one. I read to about page 150 or so and just couldn't finish...flipped to the end, read the last couple of pages, and decided it was going back to the library. 
 I picked it up originally because of the cover. It looked fun and creative and after reading the synopsis, I thought it might be a good story (I didn't know the author was an actor until I read the author bio on the back cover). Unfortunately, though there may be nuggets of a good story buried here, it really needed a good editor to make a ton of major changes. (Things like: short, boring sentences with virtually no description, terrible similes, and never showing anything, always telling...so much use of "was"!) Because of the many editing needs and writing style (very, very juvenile), I don't think any kid above the ages of 9-10 would enjoy this. And yet, I can't in good conscience hand it to any children those ages because it has some language I don't want kids reading (swearing, almost-swearing, religious profanity) and other more grown-up things that younger kids wouldn't get, like discussions of political correctness.

And I felt like, in the lessons of fiction writing where they tell you to not just tell but also show, I just felt like there was a lot of telling and not enough showing. 
 All in all, this is a highly imaginative fairytale book with lots of action and I think someday I may read it to my own kids if I have any in the future!

First picking up this book I reminded myself to keep my expectations low because of the two simple facts that this is Chris' first novel, and that I had only pictured hims as an actor and didn't think he would make it as a very successful author, but I was pleasantly surprised by the end of this first installment. 
 One of the things that surprised me the most is Chris' simplistic yet descriptive styles of writing which was very enjoyable and easy to follow, but never dull. 
 Alex and Conner where enjoyable and entertaining characters. 
 Even though their personalities where polar opposites it was clear that they both shared a tight bond, and that they would not leave each other behind which made for some character development. 
 Another character duo that I very much shipped throughout the entire novel were Goldilocks and Jack. 
 The twist on both of their stories, including Red Riding hood's, where very entertaining and ADORABLE I just simply wanted them to be together since I first read about them. 
 Another thing that I would like to appreciate about Chris' styles of writing is that he was able to sneak in some important lessons here and there through the course of the book which made it really relatable in some ways, and will hopefully teach all of the children who read this a thing or two. 
 Even though some minor things where predictable and ordinary there where quite a number of enjoyable twists and turns that kept the story going making up for the others.

If I had only one word for this book it would be "boring." There are problems with this book at every level. I bought it because I like Chris Colfer and was interested to see what he wrote like. He sings way better than he writes. 
 However, all the problems I have with this book are age-related. He writes like a teenager. His diction is painful, problems are CONSTANTLY being solved through happy coincidences, the tension is poorly handled (basically non-existent), there are italics and ellipses everywhere, and cliches coming out of every hole. The characters are only just there, all of them are very flat. There is a very childish representation of all emotions, but especially grief and love. There is also a very convenient morality present: it ends in a very preachy manner, and yet it's okay to lie if you "know your audience." Similarly, a fall that the evil character has no chance of surviving is cheerfully limped away from by a good character. There is also a problem of time, which Colfer tried to conveniently fix at the end, but forgot about the parents: it took the dad a long time in fairy-time to get back, so their mother would have been old by the time he made it. There are no shortage of similar sloppy holes present in the narrative. 
 The thing that annoyed me the most is Colfer's claims about fairy tales at the beginning. He throws around terms like "correct interpretation" and "the original Grimm story" both of which are oxymoronic statements. Both Alex and the teacher act like fairy tale experts, but they run into walls at every turn as they chase down the "correct morals" that need to be brought out of a text. I just want to buy Colfer a book of Frye and Propp. ANY research on his part would have prevented him from making these kinds of mistakes. For all his condemnation of modern fairy tales, his fairies could have walked right out of the new Disney Tinker Bell movies. His whole understanding of fairy tales reeks of modernity, and yet he slams the kids at the beginning of the book for that very fault. 
 Having said all that, Colfer has time to improve. He's young, he has the drive, and I do believe he loves stories. He needs a strong editor in the worst way, or maybe just some writer's training. If he keeps reading and keeps writing he could very well come up with something worth reading. At best, this book is "cute." It had a decent plot arc and if he had waited and put some proper editing into it it could have been very good. So while I wouldn't waste my time on this one, I'm interested to see how his writing evolves (and hopefully it does).

reference_books.title: Frigid (Frigid, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
4 Stars 
 Sydney has been in love with her best friend, Kyler, since she was little. And she doesn't just love him as a friend. The problem is, Kyler doesn't know about her feelings and he is a HUGE manwhore. He sleeps with any girl he can, unknowingly hurting Sydney every time. When they get stranded at his winter cabin during winter break, the truth comes out. Only Kyler doesn't think he deserves Sydney's love, especially after being with every girl but her for years. 
 "What else do I deserve?" 
 "Everything, baby, you deserve everything." 
 I recommend reading this book on a cold winter night, snuggled up next to the fire with a glass of wine or hot cocoa. It's just that kind of satisfying, delicious read. 
 I thought it was a sweet romance. I wanted to think that Kyler was an a-hole, but he's actually a sweetie. This book is told from his point-of-view as well as Sydney's, so we get to know what he's thinking. It's clear that he respects and cares a great deal for her. She shocks him with her declaration because he always thought she was out of his reach in that way, and he has to sort out his own emotions about this new possibility. 
 Kyler: 
 In reality, even though I'd been with everyone else, I'd always been Syd's. 
 He has insecurities about whether he can give her what she deserves, and she has insecurities about whether she can measure up to the hundreds of beautiful and experienced girls he's been with through the years. As emotions (and other things) get heated, they try to figure out if they can be more than friends... 
 "Look around the room, Syd. There's something you're missing." 
 Scanning the room, it took me a couple of moments to catch on. "My clothes? Where are my clothes?" 
 His answering grin was pure sin. "You're not going to need any clothes today, baby." 
 Combine the sizzle with a little bit of mystery and suspense, and this book was one of those you could read in one sitting. And it's a stand-alone with an actual ending. Thank you for that.

reference_books.title: More Than This (More Than, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
5 Stars 
 I enjoyed this sweet, refreshing love story! Mikayla and Jake were absolutely adorable. 
 In one night, Mikayla's life gets tragically turned upside down and she loses everything that matters to her. It also happens to be the night she meets Jake Andrews. Left alone and broken, she turns to Jake and he's there for her. Their relationship is hard to identify because from their first meeting, they are MORE than any label. But Mikayla is terrified to let Jake be what he wants to be. And she has every reason to be after what she's been through! But he knows what he wants and he's patient and loving and caring. 
 There is plenty of drama and jealousy and heartbreak (but not TOO much). The focus stays on the development of Mikayla and Jake's relationship as it beautifully unfolds and becomes MORE. It's dual POV so we know what both characters are thinking and feeling. 
 I love the parts when they don't call each other boyfriend or girlfriend or friend. Instead they just refer to each other as 
 theirs 
 . 
 "This is, um...this is for my girlfr- um, I mean my Kayla. Just my Kayla. Just um, mine." 
 -Jake 
 So cute! And Mikayla was definitely not willing to share him, even though she wasn't ready to be his girlfriend. 
 I was pleasantly surprised by this little gem! I LOVED the title, the cover, the dialogue. I liked how it was a standalone and the sequels will focus on other characters. I will definitely read the next book about Logan. 
 .

book_a.title: Sempre (Sempre, #1)
book_a.user_review:
There were many things I loved about this book. It was a satisfying combination of high school forbidden love, bad boy/good girl love, captive/slave love, and straight out romance with a touch of mystery/thriller thrown in. One aspect of it that I adored the most was that it was a full-length novel that actually had an ending! In the age of cliffhangers and numbered books, it was refreshing (although I do feel that there were plenty of loose ends that could become a #2 - just not unfinished cliffhanger loose ends like in multitudes of other books out now. 
 I didn't give it a 5 because of the many unanswered questions I had throughout the book and at the end of the book. I was confused about some of the key plot lines. As I read on expecting all to be clarified, I was a little disappointed when that didn't happen to the point of rereading parts to see if I had missed something along the way, only to find that I hadn't missed anything. These secrets were kept from the readers as well as the characters in the book continuously. On purpose? Maybe. I also found myself wishing for more description instead of relying on my own imagination regarding what the characters looked like. With the exception of Carmine, the characters changed in my head according to the tiny clues we would be given from time to time about their looks. I also needed more information about the supporting characters. They had so much potential. And Nicholas just started getting interesting. Even Tessa and Dom seemed to have more to them than was revealed. I just kept wanting more of...something...all the way through. 
 So whenever I found myself doing the "wanting more of something" thing, the author would focus on the most important plot line of the book, which was the romance between Carmine and Haven. It started out slow and steadily morphed into a strong, rare love. It was forbidden, unlikely, tragic, but somehow the author made me believe in it. Haven had every reason not to trust him, not to love him, not to believe in him. But she saw a side of him no one else knew existed. Yes, he was a manwhore who treated girls like crap (and wouldn't even kiss the girls he f***** on the mouth)! But with her he was different. He simply became a boy with a crush on a beautiful girl. 
 She giggled, and he had the sudden urge to tell her she was beautiful. The words almost came out, but before they could, she turned away from him. He sighed and remained quiet, annoyed he wasted the opportunity. 
 Although the "thunderbolt" hit fairly early on in the book, it wasn't insta-love. There were enough pages for the feelings to build and grow. the scenes between the two of them were so sweet and emotional and perfectly angsty. Oh, the poetry! Oh, the proclamations of love (in ITALIAN)!!! Yet Carmine stayed Carmine - a foul-mouthed, hot-headed, emotionally immature, damaged boy. And Haven slowly came into her own with the support and love of her "beautifully flawed boy." 
 To Carmine, she wasn't a possession. She wasn't a title. She was just a girl. 
 Haven's transformation from a meek and fearful "possession" to a confident and capable woman worthy of love was a beautiful thing to read. Carmine's love did that for her. And in return, her love healed him. 
 "And I love you,"he said, his voice a whisper. But Haven felt it powerfully, deep down in her soul. "Ti amo, mia bella ragazza. Per sempre." "Sempre?" she asked. Cracking a smile, he brushed his pointer finger softly across her lips. "Always and forever." 
 Overall, I was pleasantly surprised by Sempre.

Okay, to be honest, the only reason I started reading this book was because of the reviews and high ratings. And to say that I am extremely disappointed will be an understatement. 
 Firstly, the writing style sucked bad. Darhower was aiming to make this book as sophisticatedly (is that even a word?) written as possible but she failed. Miserably. I couldn't keep track of what was going on in some chapters because of the multiple POVs. I had nothing against multiple POVs until this book planted seeds of doubt that I cannot stop from growing. I think the fruit's already ripened. 
 Next, the characters were fucking stupid. The girl ran from every thing, I swear to God. It was so frustrating. She'd run to her room and lock herself there because of a single conservation or an encounter with someone. She was like, a coward. And there is no space in my heart for cowards. The boy wasn't any better. He was nothing but a compound of mainstream and unorthodox characteristics. Possessive, tattooed, womanizer, bad-tempered- you name it. Then there was the cheesy stuff. How he changed his lifestyle for her. Seriously, cut the bullshit. Can no author come up with something original anymore? 
 The only good part about this book were the conversations (some of them) and Nicholas' jokes. Either way, I am definitely not going to read the sequel.

I am attempting to be fair in this review. This book came so highly recommended, maybe the pedestal I placed it upon was too high. 
 PROS: It's easy reading; doesn't require deep thoughts or anything above minimal intellect to understand. (I said I would try to be fair) 
 CONS: 
 Plot: Teenage mafia prince and all around bad boy/stud muffin meets slave girl who has mafia roots of her own when his father "buys" her. Star-crossed lovers, yada yada yada, discovers she is grand-daughter of mafia boss/Godfather. 
 Herein lies problem #1--Yes, I am well aware human trafficking exists and it is repugnant. However, I find it difficult to believe this child lived 17 years in California without ever having medical attention, attending school, or being discovered by a FedEx/UPS delivery man not matter how remote the location. 
 Problem 2: Was there an editor? The novel was over 500 pages in length, many of which were filled with useless information that did absofreakinglutely nadda to develop the plot, endear the characters, explain their psyches, etc. Seriously, cut this thing in 1/2 and it might stand a chance at being interesting. 
 Problem 3: Self-confessed casanova, Carmine, had NO SKILLS in the bedroom. Yes, I realize he's only 17-18 but someone somewhere along the way should have taught him something of use. At least add a little spice to the dialogue, apparently no one told him that women enjoy sex more when their mind is engaged. Inserting piece A into slot B is about as advanced as this lover boy ever was with poor Haven. Seriously, chicky, in the end he did you both a favor. 
 I'll add more later when I'm no longer seething.

This was a horriblely written story. To be honest, i did try to finish the book but couldn't do it. The grammar was terrible ! As for the story, the slave and master relation was hardly depicted. It was more like a bonded servant story. Haven ran away from her previous master to save her life and help her mother (Oh, and it was hard to believe that a girl slave was not sexually assalted. And she was told to be 17 or 18 ! Girls way younger than that get brutally raped in less vulnerable situations). However, she forgot about her Mom as soon as she was comfortably ensconced. You don't do that to the person who gave berth to you, even if someone threatens you with your life. Atleast fret a little, remember her plight or wonder what she was doing and how she was ! Then, being a slave, Haven is potrayed as a very frightened girl who knew that she could get punished or killed for mistakes that aren't even her fault. But it was a huge contradiction, when she bravely speaks her mind without a fear. She wasn't allowed to leave the house, but the first time Carmine asked her to step outside, she just says, 'Is it okay ?' then it's all smiles for her. Now Carmine - He , his family, is suppose to be very rich but there is not one servant in their house. Who looked after it before Haven ?! Even she was hardly shown working after a time. Carmine's father is no mobster but a man who works for one, unofficially (what's that suppose to mean ?) - though his father (Carmine's grandfather) had been a mob boss once. The hero, Carmine, said to his father near the beginning that he didn't need his money. Why the attittude buddy, if you can't even manage to wash your own underpants ?! He had a big mouth but scarcely anything to show for it. I believe the author wrote with a sort of blinders that had her see just straight ahead not the vast stretches expanding to the left and right.

Wow. Just W.O.W.

And don't even start me with Carmine. That kid drove. me. nuts. OMG, this character is the most annoying, immature, stupidest, and dumbest male character I've ever read. He's a foul mouth motor-boat and swears consistently for no reason. His actions question his age and maturity. Literally. The WORST. So stupid....I have no idea why in God's name would Haven love him. The way the author writes both of these characters, I would have thought that they were different types!! Overall, I wish I never read this book. The plot: nothing I haven't read before, the characters: stupid, annoying, and immature, the writing: meh. 
 Because I have to rate the book: 0.5 stars.

I legit had no idea what I was reading. It felt like it was some backwards third world country or even a fantasy novel until it was revealed to be taking place in South Carolina. Also the added fact that everyone spoke English.

 He scooted closer to her. "La mia bella ragazza." 
 "You know I don't know what that means," she said, blushing from the intensity of his stare. 
 He ran the back of his fingers along her flushed cheek. His touch was soft, and she leaned her head in his direction. "My beautiful girl," he said.

 Before I begin to review this, its important to know that I originally read the fanfiction the book is based off, so my views on the novel are already biased. 
 A fanfiction allows the author an unlimited word count, meaning that they're able to go into a level of detail that is sometimes unnecessary, but I feel for this story it was vital. When trying to fit the same into a book its important to know where to cut...and unfortunately after reading Sempre I'm left feeling...unsatisfied. For me, the cut has been too thorough, and while the story is still nice to read, it is less believable and I felt it hard to connect with any of the characters on the same level I did before. 
 That's not to say that the novel is a complete failure - on the contrary it is a well-rounded text in a regular sense, and I believe I wouldn't be so harsh on it if I didn't know all the potential it had. Carmine and Haven are a cute couple, and the level of devotion to one another is something that holds the story together when all the shit goes to hell. The intricately weaved storyline of who Haven is and what happened to Carmine's mother are brilliantly executed and add a twist which I don't think any reader expects. 
 I kinda miss Carmine having two brothers, but that being said Dom is a perfect combination of the two and I understand the cut. 
 Surprisingly one of my biggest disappointments for this was Dr. DeMarco. In the original piece he came across as a far kinder, gentle man...meaning that when the anniversary came around, his actions were FAR more frightening and his character became scarier than what he was here. 
 Overall, the story is great and I would recommend it to others who love romance novels which are different. Slave and master stories are common, but this is a completely different take which focuses on how people can be imprisoned by the lives they live; literally and figuratively in this case. Beautifully written.

Ramblings. If I'm not mistaken, Sempre is originally a Twilight fanfiction under the title of Emancipation Proclamation. I've come across EP for years already (years where left and right, Twilight fanfics flourished) and fully remembering some of my friends even raving about it. I think I even saved a copy of the fanfic but just haven't got the time into fully reading. Or maybe I did try reading it but just wasn't that enthusiastic and kind of iffy towards it. *Shrugs*, that was years ago already and I'm just a teen being too picky with what she's reading. So when all of a sudden Netgalley places Sempre up for reviewing, I thought of giving this another shot and ended up requesting it. 
 My thoughts. Is it just me or this book is a really long read? Ha ha this book took me forever to finish reading it. Yep, quite lengthy but I can tell you that reading this book will be totally worth it because it's so good and quite a package when it comes to the events that happened in this book. It somewhat perplexed me that all of it just happened in a single book because it's like curveball after curveball being thrown at us readers. 
 Sempre is a story that revolves around Haven Antonelli and Carmine DeMarco. Haven grew up in a terrifying and abusive world, considering that she is a "second-generation slave". All she's ever known in her life is to obey and serve his Master Michael. Then one day, she ends up being bought by Dr. Vincent DeMarco - who's involved in an Italian Mafia. In the DeMarco household she meets Dr. DeMarco's son, Carmine DeMarco, who's a little bit of fucked up. Carmine and all kinds of trouble are like a package, wherever Carmine goes trouble always seem to find him. She falls in love with Carmine ... but remember that this story isn't a love story which involves rainbows and unicorns in it. 
 This story is set in a darker world with SECRETS, LIES, LOSS, LOVE and most especially SACRIFICE involved. We see the extent or how much farther a person can go just for the sake of the safety/life of the ones he or she loves. And oh boy, Carmine will really go to the ends of the Earth just to keep Haven safe. That is how his love for her goes, it runs very deep. He may be an ass towards other people but when it comes to Haven and his love for her ... it means all business to him. 
 This book also deals with the constant battle between good and evil, which will conflict your thoughts and feels. I know mine was. But you will certainly see reason and understand it as you go along with the chapters of the book. OneRepublic's song Counting Stars keep nagging my brain while reading this book, especially these lines "I feel something so right/Doing the wrong thing/I feel something so wrong/Doing the right thing/I could lie, coudn't I, could lie/Everything that kills me makes me feel alive" Ha! 
 I wouldn't consider Sempre as that of a page turner or a book that I couldn't find myself putting it down because there really are chapters wherein the pacing of the story trickles down. BUT what blew me away the most about this book is the amazing character development because with just a number of pages J.M. Darhower managed to give us a 180 or even 360 degrees development with Haven and Carmine's character. 
 I tell you, this is one of those books that I've read with a really great character development and it was very beautiful to read and witness considering the characters we have in the beginning of the story. It was like watching a bud bloom into a flower because that was really how Haven's character transformed. Oh let's not forget Carmine (though his change was mainly directed to Haven ...AT LEAST there was lol), even if there were moments that he slips up to his old self. 
 While developments are happening with our characters, the overall tension of the book is gradual picking up. I think it was when I reached 70-80% of the book when shit hit the fan. From there, I was just literally at the edge of my seat waiting for everything to unfold and was like "WHAT? WHAT? WHY? OMG!". Those last bits of the book were sooooo good and it was quite scary. Wow. 
 All in all, Sempre is a beautiful, touching and thrilling story. I definitely recommend this to you, guys.
