 So these are the problems I had with it: 
 - Although I liked Bree's point of view, I kept wondering Why does she keep acting like this? Why is she not like the other new borns? Meyer said that they're a bit. . . mental, so why is she just magically normal? It doesn't make any sense! 
 - They constantly go on about "BFF Ninjas". Seriously, Bree is supposed to be like, 15, 16? And her "bff" is supposed to be 18. . . so I don't think normal people go on about "bff ninjas" that age. It was just so stupid! 
 - Is this supposed to be a love story? The love story isn't even there! They kiss a few times and. . . that's it. Wow. What a great love story. 
 - I really had no idea what Diego was like. Was he supposed to be mexican? What did he look like? And what did the other characters look like? There could've been so much more descriptions! 
 And there's so so much more, but I thought I should stop this rant now, because frankly, I don't even want to think about this book anymore.

I enjoyed twilight long ago when I read all the books, and so I thought that justified reading this book. I have to say though, I am incredibly disappointed. Perhaps I have just grown out of the storyline and my tastes have changed, but I found this book incredibly childish. I also wish that this had been more original. It seems typical of Stephanie Meyer to just write the same ole story, just from another persons point-of-view. It would have possibly been better if Bree showed at least an inkling of rabid newborn vampire ferocity. She was just...a lame little child! She didn't show us any vampire tendencies that were not typical of the ones we (as in those of us who have read the previous books) have already encountered. 
 Action...that is what this book desperately needed. Why pick a character who really has no significance to retell the story? Is it to punish everyone for the leaking of Midnight Sun? I gave this two stars for at least being readable, but I do feel as if I was undergoing an unusual form of punishment. Kissy noises...really? Are we in Elementary? I thought this was targeted for a Young Adult audience?!?

This book was awesome. It helped you to understand the struggles that some of the characters must have went through when they first changed in to vampires. 
 What an awesome addition to the series!

This is exactly what Stephenie Meyer says it is -- a novella, or short novel. I liked that it told the story behind the story -- this gives the reader an insight into what went on when Victoria was building up her army. There are some characters I would like to have read more about -- Fred and his quirky power and Diego.
An all-round awesome plot that made me want even more twilight books and want to watch eclipse again.

I enjoyed this more than I thought I would. This is definitely only something that big Twilight fans will enjoy. All it is, and all it claims to be, is a character study. But the additional perspective is interesting.

I absolutely LOVED the Twilight series, but this book was a HUGE disappointment. The writing style is completely different from Meyer's other Twilight books. I actually found it quite difficult to read because the style reminded me of that used by a middle schooler. It was painful at times. Meyer should have taken the time to complete Midnight Sun instead - THAT I would have enjoyed. My advice is to leave this one on the shelf. Not worth the read.
after 10 pages I gave up.

book_b.title: The Dragon Reborn (Wheel of Time, #3)
book_b.user_review: Moving on in my audio re-read of The Wheel of Time. I'm amazed by how much seems totally new to me. Embarrassing, really. But there at least I'm consistent in the characters I don't like.

sample_reviews.review_text:
Well...I guess this is as far as I will go with the series...And it is almost sad, because of all that I had heard, I was expecting to have 14 new good fantasy books to read!But I can't seem to be able to finish this.The plot feels like it drags, and I'm really tired with the charactes now...I expected them to grow a bit from what they were in the first book, but we find them almost at the same exact spot. Noone seems to have accepted what is going on, and I got tired of reading again, about Perrin not wanting to connect with wolves or about Nynaeve wanting to become Aes Sedai to punish Moiraine, especially after two books, in which Moiraine proved that she wanted to help. Moving on. 
 *Edit* Also I did some reading out of curiosity, to see what will happen in the next books...Well, thankfully I stopped early!Because I read that later on BIG SPOILER Rand bonds to, not one, not two, but THREE women, Min, Elayne and Aviedha, because HE IS IN LOVE WITH ALL OF THEM....and the best part is that the women have absolutely NO PROBLEM with this...I mean I knew that characters were bad, and the relationships between men and women were unrealistic, but this...thankfully I never bought the books! I'm out of here

DNF @ 30% 
 Dear Wheel of time I am breaking up with you. 
 This wasn't easy decision as I don't like to leave things unfinished.My friends keep on telling me how great you are and that I should give you another chance but I think that this relationship has already taken too much of my time and I just can't look past your snail pace and many obnoxious characters.We definitively had our good moments but every time we are together I keep thinking about other series and keep glancing on other books on my shelf and that is not how relationship between reader and book should be.Call me old fashioned but I believe book should hold the reader tight and make him forget about other books until the last page is done. 
 I am sure you will find devoted reader who will adore you and maybe our paths well cross again and we continue from where we left but I just can't see it happening anytime soon.

Pretty solid writing, some interesting characters, decent plot and subplots. The universe seems derivative without virtue of being derived from solid myth or history. The teenage protagonists act like teenagers, mostly, and almost all the characters are paranoid and uncooperative. I keep telling myself this is realistic, but I don't want to believe it. All the females tend to act like David Eddings' female characters on particularly bad days, but since most of the male characters are stupid and fractious, I suppose it makes sense. I am impatient to get the next book from the library, so I suppose I am enjoying the series.

I really, truly want to like this series but I am struggling. This installment was particularly difficult because so little happened plot-wise for a large majority of the book. It could have easily been shortened to a fraction of the size without losing any integrity. So much of it felt wasteful and slow. 
 Don't get me wrong, there is a lot of good going on with the series so far but this book was a lot to get through for such little progress. And for me, the hardest part was wading through the rigid, unnatural dialogue on virtually every single page. 
 Probably my biggest hang ups: 
 1. Metaphoric phrases (e.g. "Why, that's like being told to go up in the hills to find lions, only you do not know whether there are any lions, but if there are, they may be hunting you, and they may be disguised as bushes. Oh, and if you find any lions, try not to let them eat you before you can tell where they are." -Elayne) Yeah it was like that every other paragraph of dialogue. Even from random, no account characters. 
 2. Repetitive soft cursing (blood and bloody ashes; burn me; Light!) ...super annoying after the 20th time a piece. 
 3. Braid tugging (who even does that?!) 
 Again, the dialogue and mannerisms are so unnatural it really ruins things for me. I hear this is a problem throughout the entire series. 
 Yet through it all there is some good. I like the world building, it is very thorough. The cultures are cool and the language (meaning the archaic names etc. Not the dialogue!) is comprehensive and believable, albeit a little overdone. And the story itself is a fine, well conceived tale. 
 I'll probably wait a little while to start book four but I'll bloody well finish this series, the light burn me! *proceeds to tug braids until neck snaps and head rolls off shoulders*

Still enjoying the series, but I would think by book three we would end with the I wish that other farmboy was here because he knows how to talk to the ladies. 
 Also, maybe the point of this book is that teenagers are stupid, but after going through the first two books you would think they would learn to keep their mouths shut. Even though Perrin is given the description as slow to speak in the first two books, he takes on blurting out duty here since he's the only teenager present.

What amazes me to this day about the Wheel of Time series is the masterful way Robert Jordan works me into a frenzy. When The Great Hunt (book 2) ended, I was whipped into a hurricane of conflicting emotions. I wanted to cry because it was over. I also wanted to cry because I was so excited. I felt like shivering from spent emotion and energy. I wanted to run to my book shelf and pick up book 3. I also wanted to wait because I'm participating in a Wheel of Time read along and I didn't want to get ahead. I settled with walking very sedately to the couch and watching reruns of "Say Yes to the Dress" until I was completely calmed down. Well, I still ended up yelling at some of the brides, but at least I wasn't worked up about the Wheel of Time anymore, right? 
 Well, The Great Hunt is over. Let's continue on this journey and see what other amazing things are in store for us. Only, the emotions are brought down, not just to a simmer, but to a complete and cold darkness. We read about our characters sitting in camp. Riding across plains. Complaining about prophecies. None of this is exciting, but of course we're completely entwined with their stories now and curious as to what is going to happen. Robert Jordan-isms sprinkle the pages, but we're slowly making sense of the world he's describing to us. He had so much planned from the very beginning I am now in awe at his patience. I always want to get it all out on the page as quickly as possible but he's ok making us wait, for literally thousands of pages if need be. 
 Slowly...oh so slowly you don't even hardly realize it, things start coming to a head. The net gets drawn closer, and closer, until there I am sitting on that same couch and reading so fast I'm probably missing important details and I turn to the last chapter... 
 And my boyfriend walks in the room and turns on the TV. I balk, my mouth open, and snatch the remote back from him. "You don't understand," I say, "I'm literally at the climax of the book." 
 "Can't it wait? I want to fold my laundry. I need to watch some Deep Space Nine while I do it." 
 "Too bad! Fold it somewhere else!" My indignation should have him backing away with his hands up defensively. 
 "Well I don't mind, read it aloud to me." He says with a shrug, like I do this all the time. 
 I start out with another sassy comment but then I think, Why not? He knows enough of the story to know what the phrase the Dragon Reborn means, who Rand, Mat, and Perrin are. So there we are, the climatic battle that occurs at the end of every Wheel of Time book, and I'm reading it out loud. I know my voice caught in my throat a few times because I got all excited and teary (I cry at literally every emotion) but when my last "The Dragon Reborn!" faded away, we both just sat there, stunned. We started out in a camp in the middle of back ass nowhere and we ended here. 
 "Wow," he says. "That was actually pretty intense." 
 A lot of readers will tell you that this is the beginning of the highlight of the series, books 3-6, and I couldn't agree more. Just thinking about where we started a mere three books ago is mind boggling - both the reader and the characters have come a long way from sheep herding. The stakes are high and they keep getting higher with every book, but we never feel out of our depth (...yet). I can hardly wait to start The Shadow Rising.

So many characters. Each time I read one of these books (which is one every January) I end up doing hours of research to try and remember all that happened in the books before this. I know the further I get along this will only grow, unless I just take time to read them all in a row. I do not thinking I could hand 11 more books this size in a row. Maybe I just haven't fallen in love with the series the way I do some others. I know some series I'll read every book in a year. 
 I almost feel like I'm hoping reading all these will give me more nerd cred, because, I love epic fantasy, but each time I read these books I started to think to myself, "maybe I don't like epic fantasy?" Which I know isn't true, because there are many great series out there of which I can't stop reading. 
 Is it getting repetitive though? They all set out different ways to complete different task, all to end up in the same place at the end for a big battle (TO END ALL BATTLES) only to find out, it really isn't the last battle, and there will be many many more. 
 I must say that I love some of the group dynamics. Tom and Matt most of all. I enjoyed all the gambling and all the luck involved, in Matt's story. I found that the most exciting part of this story. Matt's journey was the best. 
 Well I do look forward to the next one, at this rate I'll finish the series in 11 years. Not including prequels and the like. I'm sure as I get closer to the end I'll probably pick up the pace, but not anytime soon.

I found it difficult to keep up with the character arcs that Jordan wove in and out throughout this book. I had actually thought the focus was to be on Rand (as the Great Hunt certainly set the stage for) but a good deal of time was spent going back and forth amongst his comparisons in various states of dismay and drama. 
 No disrespect, but wasn't well laid out in my view and was somewhat confusing.

The Dragon Reborn is the third book in The Wheel of Time series. I like the third book better than the second one, mainly because the story has shifted from Rand to his companions, especially Mat. In the second book, Mat is no more than a background, an addition to other companion's storyline. So, it's a good thing to read more about Mat's actions. 
 Anyway, this book is a five stars rating for me, and I will begin the fourth book as soon as possible.

I struggled between two and three stars for this book, but I decided to round down. 
 What could have been an exciting (if not slightly illogical) 200 pages was stretched to nearly 700 pages, in what is the first filler book of the series. This is disheartening, considering it's only the third book in the Wheel of Time cycle. 
 If not for the existence of my book club, this read would have been very little fun, if any. The real joy of reading this book came from being able to craptalk the bad parts (which were aplenty). Our FB message thread was renamed "Jordan Bashing" on account of this. 
 That being said, I am still very interested in the characters of this series. They are rather one-dimensional and stodgy, but the first couple entries were enough to keep my interest in them going through this clunker of a novel. 
 And despite overall writing or editorial choices to make this book seem like useless filler, there are story elements that Jordan controls very well. It is a very readable book, if you can manage not to throw it against the wall a time or two. However, unless you're committing yourself to reading the WoT series, there are so many better fantasy books and series out there. 
 Go with one of them. 
 *Cough*Kingkiller Chronicles*Cough*

The pacing is better here than in TGH and the story is even better. The narrative is less 'epic' but somehow bigger: bigger thoughts, bigger feelings, wider imagination. All of the characters are advanced another degree and the world reaches a level of (seemingly) effortless detail that makes turning the pages a compulsive pleasure. Go pick up Eye of the World (Book 1) and introduce yourself to this extraordinary work of literature -- your imagination will thank you for the rest of your life :)

** spoiler alert ** 
 That's it. I'm done. The inconstant characters and sloppy plot lines have finally got to me. I gave every effort to like this heralded series but it's just too difficult. My last straw (spoiler alert!!!)...was when a character spends weeks tracking down and rescuing three friends... Then the friends smack their superior Magic on him because he wanted to know why they just physically beat a "seemingly" helpless woman. Um...where's the "thanks for putting up with weeks of shit and risking your life" . And... You just beat down a helpless old lady...what's he supposed to say??? And finally, you obtain great power and you abuse this "friend" with that power just because he spoke up about an old lady beat down...just because you "could" do it and it made you feel good??? How am I supposed to like these characters??!!?? Perhaps someday I'll try to pick this series up again...but for now, I'm not even going to read the end... only a handful of chapters to go. Why? Because I'm hoping this world ends in destruction and theses stupid characters die. Since there's about a dozen more books left in the series I don't think that's going to happen.
Ok, things got more interenting in this one, there are some nice fights and a really nice twist related to the dark one.

Classic Jordan work. Some of my regular gripes about Jordan are as follows: 
 All of his characters hate each other. There are a few exceptions but usually only briefly. It bugs me that none of his characters want to work together. And when they do work together they hate it. Its hard to get really attached to characters who are constantly at each others throats. Even Moiraine and Lan are now starting to hate each other more than like being bound. It would be nice to see at least some emotional loyalty between characters that isn't condescending. 
 There is an abundance of detail. Even at intense moments Jordan doesn't stop the flow of detail. A prime example, when a character has a sword to his throat and the offender asks the character a question, its practically an entire page of various thoughts and details and surrounding info and such before we get a response from the character. You can imagine that things progress very very slowly. 
 There are a million characters to keep track of, and Jordan keeps adding new ones. I can never keep track of all the names. I'm starting to get used to all the made up words that the Moiraine uses but only the most common ones. I really can't stand fake languages. I feel they add very little to the ambiance and add a lot of confusion. 
 With this in mind, Jordan is still an excellent writer. On the days I don't bike or jog and don't get the chance to listen to the book I find myself wanting to do that instead of watch TV. He is a very compelling story teller. So, despite all the shortcomings of his writing style I will continue to read his books. Well, at least listen to them. I don't think I'de have the patience to actually read them.
mechanical ,soulless

A few cool things happen. I have come to hate all the females in the series; if they all die in the next book that will be great. I like the character Mat has become even if most of the abilities he has just magically appeared out of nowhere with no previous hint that he had them.

I think it was about here that some slogging became evident. 
 I wrote a bunch about part 1, so read there.
I couldn't get into this book no matter how hard I tried. I wasn't interested in the characters or their plights. I may try again in the future.

Re-reread August 2015: Still feel the same. Book 1 was amazing, book 2 was comfortable, and book 3 is where he really starts to need an editor. 
 Reread June 2009: The weakest in the series yet, but still a strong book. This is where Jordan starts to get a little repetitive and I ended up skimming a little bit. Lots of braid pulling and worrying about male channeling, etc. 
 I did like the way the 4 story lines (Rand, Perrin, Mat, the 3 women) reconverged in this book. It was a well-woven plot to give each group an incentive to be in Tear and bring them all together . 
 There was one point in particular that bothered me: when the women (posing as full Sisters) are on the ship headed towards Tear and it gets hung up on the mud... why didn't they just channel the boat out of the mud? Move the mud, flood the water, move the ship, something. It really bothered me. Seems like a plot device just to get them on the ground to meet the Aiel and get into trouble.

The adventures continued, and it got more exciting. The 3 girls, Nynaeve, Egwene and Elayne, found themselves thrust deeper into the betrayals and secrets of the Aes Sedai. The Black Ajah was real and they had to track down 13 whom had been identified. 
 Nynaeve's power was growing with a remarkable speed, but she still could not control it. She could only unleash it if she was angry, which is an irony; considering she thought of herself as Wisdom, but her giving in to short-temper was not exactly close to being wise. 
 Egwene, on the other hand, had grown up here. Though she still got into catfight with Nynaeve from time to time, but unlike Nynaeve, Egwene knew when to back off. She also got more power in the dream world, which I think will be major point in the turn of the story in later sequel. 
 Elayne became more queen-like. Her knowledge in the old history was useful in their chase of Black Ajah. 
 In this third volume, finally their individual trait came out. So, I now can tell the difference between each girl. 
 Mat became my favorite here. He was funny. He seemed to complain a lot, yet I feel he enjoyed this adventure more than anyone else. In the beginning, he was healed by Aes Sedai and afterward, he wanted to go on his own and tried. But then, he could not disentangle himself from the thread of others. His travel with Thom through places, laying wagers with anybody who was willing to (and won big quite many times), finally took him met the others and saved them at the end. 
 Perrin, saved several times by his increasing ability in fighting, and communicating with his wolf brothers, still struggled hard to accept this ability of his. Unlike Mat who made use of his ability to saving people, Perrin tried hard to stop using his. It was painful and tiring for him, of course, and made him vulnerable at times, also. 
 Rand's story, was glimpsed through the dreams and tracks others got on him. It looks like he had partially accepted his fate as the Dragon Reborn. He announced himself, traveled to Tear, left many weird events along the trails, and claimed the Calandor at the end. 
 As in the first and second volume, here subplots and minor characters' stories were also told in length. I enjoyed all these as the parts necessary to the whole series. I mean, the series is consisted of 15 volume books with 700-800 pages each. The story was taking place at a vast world, in a fascinating time, with one age coming to an end. So, of course, there should be many characters and events involved to make it represent-able to the age and that world. All in all, it is a fascinating story with deep characterization. I now look forward to reading the 4th sequel.

The last time a read a book in this series was over a decade ago. I tried picking this volume up a time or two since and never made it very far before putting it down for something else that caught my interest more. For whatever reason I made it through rather quickly this time around. Overall a fairly fun read. I certainly had my fair share of fist-palming moments. Nearly every character is a bit of a hot head, and half of the problems everyone faces seem to come from their ever present, self imposed need to keep secrets from each-other. I mainly enjoyed Matt and Perrin's story lines in this one. Rand seemed more of a plot element than a character this time around, but that didn't really bother me much. The Three girls discovering their powers and whatnot was interesting, but I could have done with a little less of their constant bickering and inflated egos. I do plan on continuing with the series, and probably at a quicker pace, but with these big long juggernaut series I usually need a break in between books or all the little annoyances get the best of me.

I just wanted to show you, why I continued with all of this books - Matrim bloody Cauthon! 
 "Blood and bloody ashes." -Mat 
 "Dovie'andi se tovya sagain" 
 I'm no lord. I've more respect for myself than that. ~Mat 
 Bad habits pay off in the long run. -Mat Cauthon 
 I came to bloody rescue you. Burn me if I expected to be treated as if I'd come to steal a pie. -Mat Cauthon 
 "Sheepswallop and bloody buttered onions!" -- Mat (obviously) 
 Here's my top 5 Mat quotes. 
 1. When the poor blind fool they've chosen out for their Amyrlin gets here, I will do the talking. She can't be very bright, or they'd never have been able to shove her into the job. 
 2. Well, I'll not be the one to pull his bacon off the coals. He's the one who can channel. If he's put his head in a hornet's nest, he can bloody channel his way out of it. 
 3. And if she tries Mistress Snoot with me too often, I'll bloody well kick her! 
 4. I came to bloody rescue you. Burn me if I expected to be treated as if I'd come to steal a pie. 
 5. I'm a gambler, a farmboy, and I'm here to take command of your bloody army. 
 And the rest: 
 "Mat scowled. It seemed to him that when you got sick, you became invisible to women unless they were actually talking to you. And then they took at least ten years off your age." 
 "If you can't hide what you are going to do, do it so everybody thinks you are a fool." -Mat 
 "Discovering what Rand could do had been like finding out his best friend tortured small animals and killed babies."- Mat 
 "I read a book once." -Mat Cauthon 
 "It was a simple truth; the Creator made women so men would not find life too easy." - Matrim Cauthon 
 "Metaphor for. . ." Mat scowled. "Bloody ashes, woman. This isn't a metaphor for anything! It's just boots." 
 And his letter, that is from one future book, but I just wanted to show you all what kind of awesome guy Mat is!!! 
 "Your Royal Bloody Pain in My Back, 
 We're bloody waiting here to talk to you, and we're getting angry perturbed. (That means angry.) Thom says that you're a queen now, but I figure that changes nothing, sense you acted like a queen all the time anyway. Don't forget that I carried halled your pretty little backside out of a hole in Tear, but you acted like a queen then, so I guess I don't know why I'm suprised now that you act like one when you really are a queen. 
 So I'm thinking I should treat you like a bloody Queen and send you a bloody letter and all, speaking with high talk and getting your attention. I even used my ring as a signet, like it was paper proper. So here is my formal salutation. So BLOODY STOP TURNING ME AWAY so we can talk. I need your bellfounders. It's bloody important. 
 --Mat 
 p.s. Salutation means greeting. 
 p.p.s. Don't mind the scratched out words and bad spellings. I was going to rewrite this letter, but Thom is laffing so hard at me that I want to be done. 
 p.p.s. Don't mind me calling your backside pretty. I hardly ever spent any time looking at it, as I've an awareness that you'd pull my eyes out if you saw me. Besides, I'm married now, so that all doesn't matter." 
 And others: 
 "I wish Perrin/Matt/Rand were here. He knows what to say to women" 
 And his conversation with Rand in the last book: 
 "Mat: "What did you do to your hand, by the way?" 
 Rand: "What did you do to your eye?" 
 Mat: "A little accident with a corkscrew and thirteen angry innkeepers. The Hand?" 
 Rand: "Lost it capturing one of the Forsaken." 
 Mat: "Capturing? You're growing soft." 
 Rand: "Tell me you've done better." 
 Mat: "I killed a gholam." 
 Rand: "I freed Illian from Sammael." 
 Mat: "I married the Empress of the Seanchan." 
 Rand: "Mat, are you really trying to get into a bragging contest with the Dragon Reborn? . . . Besides, I cleansed Saidin. I win."" 
 Everything by Mat - who is the best bloody character I have ever read - Burn me if he isn't!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!! 
 :D

This was actually better than I remember it. I think I was really focused on Rand the first time I read it, and I didn't care for the fact that the main character was basically MIA for the entire book. But I realize now it was Jordan's way of showing how much Rand could influence events throughout the entire world without even having him in the narrative. We showed up one step behind him, just like the rest of the characters, but his presence was felt throughout the story. I can really appreciate this time around how creative that was.

I love this series and have decided to read it all again before I read the last one just to familiarise myself again. The characters are all starting to grow up and I like the romantic relationships which are developing between Rand and Elayne - curious!

Phew! Took a while to finish the third book, though it is smaller than the first two. It was better than the second book (The Great Hunt). Perrin & Moiraine have larger roles, which is good. Rand comes only in a few scenes, which is great. Mat and the Two Rivers ladies are as tiresome as in the earlier books. 
 The best thing about this book is that the main story moves, unlike the second one, which was virtually a side quest. 
 The WOT world and the story are really good. But the impact is somewhat lessened by the prevalence of repetitive interior monologue and inane dialogue, mostly by the Two Rivers folk. I wish the writing had been more concise. The characters of Perrin, Lan, Moiraine, and to some extent Mat & Thom, seem real and filled out. Egwene and Rand (and Nynaeve to some extent) feel at bit hollow. Events shape them. 
 I guess I would have likes the series more had I begun it at a younger age. But other authors took precedence.

If you had told me even 20% of the way through this book that it would manage to scrape two stars by the end, I would've laughed it off. It took SO LONG to get going, and then once it did get going I was still a little sour over suffering through the beginning. Despite narrowly escaping the One-Star Rule*, I need an indefinite hiatus from these. The writing and I just don't gel, and although Mat is becoming more and more interesting to me, nobody else is really grabbing me. I spend too much time bored, and these are far too long, for me to sink another book or two into the Wheel of Time right now. 
 Although I will give kudos for the departure from Rand as a central character. And another tip of the hat for the nice ending touch: "That wasn't the Big Bad, that was just a moderately large bad and really, we're not even sure how large." Added a much-needed layer of menace. 
 Also...need Egwene and Co. be kidnapped by EVERYBODY??!??!?!! 
 - - - - - 
 *One-Star Rule: If one of the books in a series gets a one-star rating that means I'm clearly not getting anything out of it, and am therefore exempt from finishing the series. (See: compulsive series finisher.) Applied thus far to: Dune, Sword of Truth. I have my suspicions that the Wheel of Time's day is coming, but as long as they keep scraping two stars I'll keep going.

I was excited to see the author start doing interesting things with the characters. However, I feel that the ending of the book was very disappointing. And, I am growing frustrated with waiting for these people to actually start using their powers. I will probably read more of this series, but for now, I'm done.

Come nei precedenti romanzi negli ultimi capitoli c'e il bossazzo finale e naturalmente uccidendolo non si risolve una minchia XD 
 Il resto del libro e tutto una corri qua e la a cavolo e succede poco o niente di rilevante per l'avanzamento della storia.

3.5/5 - When I was at Books-A-Million buying the series, a random man walked by and informed me that "it's the greatest series ever." I'm waiting to confirm that opinion until I'm done, but BAM stranger aside I have only heard good things about it. So, I decided to take the plunge even though it's a sprawling fourteen books, between 500-900 pages each. 
 Even though he's the main character, Rand is barely in Book Three at all. He sneaks away from the group and heads to Tear to prove himself. Meanwhile, Mat is taken to Tar Valon to finally be healed of the sickness from the dagger. Once he's better, Elayne gives Mat a letter to take to her mother, Queen Morgase, and he sneaks off to travel with Thom Merrilin. 
 Nynaeve, Egwene, and Elayne are tasked by the Amyrlin Seat to hunt down the Black Ajah (all Aes Sedai are divided into Ajah's, you can guess that the Black Ajah is the bad one) and their journey takes them to Tear. More under spoilers... They're captured in Tear but eventually rescued by Mat and a man named Juilian Sandar, he betrayed them while being influenced by Liandrin. 
 Meanwhile, Perrin travels with Moraine, Lan, and Loial to follow Rand. A girl named Faile joins them and she and Perrin immediately form a bond. She's hunting the Horn of Valere, unaware that it's already been found. They arrive in Tear in time to see that Rand is already there, too. He fights one of the Forsaken, whom Moraine destroys with balefire. Rand takes Callandor, a sword that is a powerful sa'angreal (a tool to help channel the One Power) and fights and destroys Ba'alzamon for the third time, although Moraine believes that this man wasn't a full representation of the Dark One and that he still lives. By taking the sword, Rand has fulfilled prophecy. 
 Random thoughts...(These were on my Book 1 & 2 Goodreads reviews, I reviewed 1-3 together on my blog so pardon the similarities. The rest in the series will be reviewed separately.) 
 Perrin's abilities are my favorite, even if they're not the most powerful. I was indifferent about Rand (until the end of book three) and I strongly disliked Mat for a while but Perrin is cool. His character development is the most steady, in my opinion. 
 Not all of the female Aes Sedai have a Warder, but if I were an Aes Sedai I totally would. Who doesn't want a strong warrior man who follows you around, guards your back, and keeps you company as you spend your days as badass sorcerer? 
 These books could easily lose 100+ pages each if they'd had a more thorough editor. Seriously, it reads "Moiraine looked coldly at Rand," and then a few paragraphs later, "Rand felt Moiraine's ice-like stare" constantly throughout the book. I am not stupid. Jordan seems to think I am and that I will forget things I JUST READ. I do not need to be beaten over the head with the same phrases over and over again. I love long books and I'm not intimidated by them, but there has to be a reason for it. 
 The One Power is very Yin and Yang. It has two halves that are only reached by either male or female channelers. I like that part, the dual forces have moments throughout the book where they clash or connect and the dynamic plays out well. However, I think Jordan tried too hard to create defined male and female characteristics in this series which resulted in stereotypes. The channeling women are untrustworthy and the channeling men are dangerous. The women have tempers, the men are constantly wondering why the women are so difficult, etc...it sometimes feels like I'm reading about adults who have a high school mentality. These people are powerful and cool otherwise; I wish they would stop exclaiming "Men!" or "Women!" and sighing that they will never understand the other. 
 I like the story and characters well enough that I can overlook the stereotypes, repetition, and Nynaeve's attitude. It'll take me a while to finish because of those issues, but I'll get it done.

The second book I'm reviewing this week is The Dragon Reborn by Robert Jordan. I had actually read this one before, but I'm re-reading it to participate in a Wheel of Time read-along. It was really fun to go back and read this book, especially since I haven't read it cover-to-cover in almost ten years. 
 I'm not going to say tons about this except that it's fantastic! The adventures of Rand al'Thor continue, taking him and his friends to Tear. More Forsaken show up, more information about the world and it's characters/people (including the big baddies and the Aiel) is revealed, and the ending is awesome. One of my personal favorites of the series. Because it's book 3, I wouldn't recommend picking it up until you've read the first two books, but it's definitely a great addition to the series. And once you read the end of book 3, well, you just have to go read book 4. :D 
 Jordan really finds his stride with the writing in this book and this is where most fans become pretty die-hard. Once you get to book 3, you'll probably finish the series. Just sayin.' We also get to spend more time with some of the supporting characters in this book, such as Perrin, Mat, Egwene, Elayne and Nynaeve. I really enjoyed that aspect of it. Overall, this is a great read and one that I thoroughly enjoyed reading. Again. :D

Big fan of the series still. 
 + Characters are all well written. They are evolving as the story grows, which in turn changes which one I ones I like/dislike. 
 + The different cultures are always one of my favorite things to read about in fantasy and this book has some good ones. 
 - I can see the problem with where to grow this story from here and am concerned with how well the next few books will continue to grow.
Thank god I'm finally finished. I've tried. But wheel of time... you and I are finished.

Somewhere around 3.5 stars 
 This was a step down from the second book, but still better than the first book. It's depressing because while this was the shortest of the three I've read so far, it felt so very long. So many inns and boats. So much traveling. Heavy sword in the stone influences. So much superfluous detail. 
 I don't really like how there's just this faceless mass of enemies burbling out of reach somewhere, and anytime the story needs some conflict we can just run into some Myrddraal or what have you. The only opposition that isn't unequivocally aligned with eeevil is the Children of Light, and they didn't feature much in this book. 
 A lot of the characters annoy me. I can't quite put my finger on it, but it feels as if nearly every interaction has this level of, I don't know, puerility. Almost like a kid aping how they think adults act and interact. I think it'll be awhile before I get around to the next book.
Definitely loving this series! I wish there would have been more from Rand's point of view in this book, but great character development of the other main characters. On to book 4!

Doing a slow reread of my favourite fantasy series. This one stands up exceptionally well and is still exciting. I'm just a fanboy going googaa all over again. There are 372,598 characters in the Wheel Of Time (unofficial Andy stat) and my ribs still get tickled by Jordan naming the most boring one Faile.

The Dragon has been REBORN!!!!!!!!!!!!!! what will the world do now, a man who can channel and has the sword that can help him destroy the world. Plus a side story of Perrin and a side story of matt my two favorite characters.
This series is awesome and this book could have easily been the end of the story. But, obviously, Jordan had more story to tell!
See review on #7.

*Probably closer to a 2.5 than a 3 
 I am... disappointed. Maybe also a little frustrated. There is so much potential in The Wheel of Time. The plot, while somewhat predictable, is engaging. The world, in growing, has started to become more realistic (as far as fantasies go). Mat has finally become an interesting character instead of being just a whiner! 
 But there are just so many flaws. And probably the worst among them is the writing itself. The prose is simply average, at best. (I suppose I should clarify here that this is purely my opinion, and I'm certain others may feel differently). Robert Jordan seems to describe things in the same way every time, and the writing serves to just.... be. There's no other purpose to his prose than to tell you what is happening at the moment. Jordan does seem to become more creative in the dream sequences and I wish that was applied throughout the entire novel. 
 Nearly as throwing was the repetition. My god the repetition. I can't stand the repetition. It just repeats over and over and over again. 
 Ok, I may be overselling it for the sake of style, but really, how many times do I need to hear how Nynaeve can't channel unless she's angry or that Egwene will not be captured again or that Mat/Perrin/Rand are better with women than the others... It's ridiculous how often the same basic lines repeat. It's incredibly frustrating and it brings me to my last point: The characters. 
 They don't feel real. They feel like cardboard cutouts. I know it is no fair to compare authors, but I think about a character like Shallan in Brandon Sanderson's Stormlight Archive, and I can't help but feel as though she compares favorably next to any of the female characters in Wheel of Time. She grows, she has realistic thoughts, she doesn't (incredibly minor spoiler to follow) attack her rescuer for simply asking questions. 
 Jordan's female characters are petulant and childish (minus Moraine, who is mysterious to the point where it is surprising whenever she speaks). His male characters are slightly more realistic, but are sometimes so slow on the uptake that I almost find myself rooting for Shai'tan. I'm not a writer, but the dialogue feels so stilted and wooden. 
 I want to like this series. I want to continue.... though I probably won't pick up the fourth book for a little while. I need a break and I need to cleanse my palette.

I'm shocked. I'm not really sure what to say. Well, that's not true, I have a lot to say, so here I go, reviewin' the big one. 
 I was looking forward to getting back into this series this year so much, only to find out that it's just been a colossal waste of my time. The first book had a great magical enticement for me mainly because it was something new, fresh. The start of a journey into the unknown is a concept that has always gotten me excited, and not just in fantasy. But it's as you continue down this "unknown" road that Robert Jordan has created that you start to see the flaws, the glaring problems which are absolutely everywhere. 
 The biggest issue that I have with Wheel of Time is everything about the characters. Seeing how they all react to one another becomes just like a really bad comedy show set in medieval times, so bad it becomes funny, but is a tragic thing since this is supposed to be a serious story. 
 Besides changes in what they are capable of (concerning magic and power), Rand, Mat and Perrin, the main males, have hardly changed and grown in character. And over the span of 2,000+ pages! No joke, it's straight mental torture. The characters' minds are all one-track and you never truly get to see any depth in them at all. They're all so concerned with themselves, of selfishly running away or ignoring the obvious that it becomes painful to read about what they do. And on the other side of the "bad characters" spectrum, we have one of the most annoying female characters I've ever read about, Nynaeve. I do wonder what drove Robert Jordan to write such a terrible person into this story. She has hardly grown up from when she left Emond's Field in book 1, because she's still disrespectful, hot-headed, she lacks self-control... and worst of all, her few redeeming qualities are overshadowed by her flaws. And since Robert Jordan jumps around from character arc to character arc intermittently (and stupidly often), he paradoxically writes so much but ends up saying so little. I believe it is because of this that we're not allowed enough time in a character's head to really understand their viewpoint and sympathize past their personality flaws. However, when we do get any of their thoughts, it's all simple rehash of "the same old, same old": flat, obvious dialogue lines that keep these characters shallow and uninteresting. Thanks, Jordan. 
 The characters also have this weird recurring problem with miscommunication. They all want to save the world (at least the good ones do) and help Rand, but somehow they miss the fact that cooperation should be involved. A lot of them make horrible decisions and don't know how to keep their petty emotions and words in check. Or in the Aes Sedais' case, being so overly cryptic, tight-lipped and inexplicably hostile that I actually feel sorry for them. It's mind-blowing that they can all be so sour and inhumane all the time. And so, as anyone could guess, all of these obstinate characters in the books lacking basic human relation skills leads to hurt feelings and unnecessary trouble, which should not be happening after this long of a time period since post-Emond's Field. 
 But perhaps the greatest miscommunication up until this point is the "relationship" between Rand and Egwene. They're both supposed to be in love, but ever since the first book they've been on incredibly shaky ground with each other--getting angry and not really being understanding--while they slowly drift further and further apart. Either Egwene says something dumb or callous, or Rand does and gets the obligatory "Men!" response popular with the hordes of women in this series. As such is the case, might as well have cut the romance from Wheel of Time if it was going to be this unrealistic. It just hurts the books terribly. And speaking of Rand, he's hardly even in this third book (go figure), but when he is around he's even more distant and shallow, an incredible feat of character regression that I can't even believe happened. 
 Another element of the crucial epic fantasy recipe is world-building. Well, Robert Jordan does poorly in that area, too. Just like the absurd length of this story, Robert Jordan's meticulous descriptions of anything he can think of goes on and on. A lot of things we've already heard described, too, like Perrin's broad shoulders and his axe for the umpteenth time, or the long-winded talk about the space Loial needs because he's so giant. These world-building descriptions also happen to pop out at bad times and ruin the flow of the story, instead of helping it along by keeping our interest. Don't even get me started on the ludicrous amount of "swear" words in these books, such as "Light!", "Burn me!", or good ol' "Blood and bloody ashes!" which all make me grind my teeth the more I have to read them. Honestly, if Robert Jordan simply cut down on repetition and detailing, I'd probably have enjoyed this much more. 
 I've also come to realize how lazy the plot is. "The Wheel weaves as the Wheel wills," the Aes Sedai say. And when absolutely everything, from Mat Cauthon choking on food to Rand al'Thor stubbing his toe, is chalked up to being this mysterious "Wheel's Will," there is hardly any room left for creativity on Jordan's part for some really great ideas and plot twists. Instead, I predicted the end of this book halfway through, and I bet I can predict the end of this series. This is an example of "The Chosen One" story gone horribly wrong, where predestination pretty much fouls up the whole experience for you. The action also heavily stagnates in this book. What happens instead is a boring lot of fretting, arguing, tomfoolery and incompetence beyond any logic. There are a few good moments in this book, like the surprising response of a minor character in a village in Chapter 11 (that's actually pretty bad that I found that a highlight), Faile (or her other ten names) being slightly interesting, and some thriller action parts all near the end. But those are all very minor and can't save this wreck of a book in the slightest. 
 Man, I really wanted to enjoy this, but it's just so dull and the characters are abysmal. Dropping this series feels almost surreal right now. Yet here I am with my head in my hands and laughing incredulously. Seeya, Robby J., you're off my Favorite Authors list.

An enjoyable book. It had a few spots in the middle where it slowed down. Honestly, I took a few too many days between finishing the book and writing this to give an honest appraisal of the book. I enjoyed it but it hasn't stuck with me and now I'm well into listening to the next book in the saga.

One thing that I found interesting about this book was the emphasis on characters. In Eye of the World, the emphasis was mostly on Rand, but we got a good feel for the whole group. Then in The Great Hunt, we saw much of the same: primary emphasis on Rand, but every character was developed. However, in The Dragon Reborn, despite what the title may lead one to believe, Rand was not the most prominent character and I LOVED IT. Robert Jordan finally gave us a more in depth look at Perrin, Nynaeve, Egwene, Elayne, and especially Mat. I really liked the way the characters developed and how their stories evolved.

** spoiler alert ** 
 Not a whole lot of action happens in this book, but several continuing plotlines are set up, and that's why I'm giving it 4 stars instead of just 3. Also, Robert Jordan's annoying habit of repeating some things in every book doesn't really kick off in this one, (such as re-explaining how the power works, who can use it, what the wheel of time is, and just about everything else really). Anyone who is reading this series should start with book 1, and by book 4 they should have a good idea of the rules of this world without having to be told again at the beginning of every book. Like I said, I didn't notice it as much in this one, but I sure picked up on it in the 4th and each successive volume. Anyway, the plotlines: 
 The Black Ajah is exposed and proven to actually exist, and the hunt for them by Egwene and friends commences. 
 While we don't meet all of the remaining Forsaken, it's clear that all of them are now free, and will be causing trouble. 
 We are introduced to the Grey Men who serve as assassins for the dark one. They are so ordinary looking that they walk around unnoticed by almost anyone, even when one is walking straight toward you with a knife drawn. 
 Egwene learns of her dreaming ability and begins to play around in Tel'aran'rhiod. 
 Faile (ugh, the bitchiest of all the protagonal bitches in this series) shows up, and her relationship with Perrin is set up. Meanwhile, Perrin becomes more immersed with his wolf side. 
 And the best! Mat starts to become the Mat I love later in the series. In the first 2 books he's a whiny little shit, and I really just want to smack the taste out of his mouth. But now we begin to see his awesomeness. He continually stays in trouble with just about everybody, but he kicks ass anyway. 
 We don't see Rand very much in this book, but it works here (unlike a later book in the series, if I recall). He runs off, but we get glimpses of him from Egwene's dreaming, and see that he's learning how to use his ability. Then at the end he finally proclaims himself as The Dragon Reborn, which is the main plotline of the entire series. 
 The Aiel show up, but it's cursory. We don't really learn much about them until the next book, but at least they're here now. 
 Another cursory glance: The Prophet. And really, there's not much more to say about him at this juncture, but he's here now, and he'll be making things exciting for people in the future. 
 I can't remember anything else right now. Like I said, this book doesn't have any epic battles or scenes that stand out against others in the series such as one in book 6, and another in book 11. However, there's a line in this book that I love. Moiraine comes in looking a bit haggard, (or as haggard as she ever gets which means that every hair is still in place, but she might have a worry line on her forehead), and she says "The Forsaken are loose, and one of them rules in Ilian." That's the stuff that makes goosebumps if you're really into this kind of shit, which I am. 
 Check it out, and enjoy.

De los tres primeros, el mas cansado. Me agrado ver un poco mas de desarrollo en Perrin y Mat, ademas de Egwene y Nynaeve. Y el final fue sumamente emocionante. Muchos personajes no terminan de caerme bien pero ya veremos que onda en el siguiente libro.

reference_books.title: The Casual Vacancy
reference_books.review_text: If you are looking for another hart-warming, exciting J.K.Rowling-novel, then you will be thoroughly disappointed. I found this one quite depressing. A bunch of entertwined sad lives, adults hating their spouses, all gossiping away, and a set of unruly teenagers set on (self-)destruction. And yet Rowling manages to make it feel as if nothing happens in the first 90% of the book. What's more, all the characters are so unlikeable or boring that I couldn't even care when something did happen. Definitely won't read this one again.

reference_books.title: Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?
reference_books.review_text: Clearly not my cup of tea. May well be one of the classics, but simply did not like the author's style nor found the story very intriguing.

reference_books.title: The Curious Incident of the Dog in the Night-Time
