I would give this 4,5 stars but more 4 than 5. I loved this though, I haven't read about schizophrenia before from a patient's view, and I think this was an excellent one. So sad, touching and beautiful, and so full of brilliant sentences that I had to underline some. One of my favorites this year.

While I understand the concept - from the prospective of someone suffering through/with mental illness and coming to terms with a terribly tradedy - I did not enjoy the format. The story looped around, sections were repeated and I found it difficult to follow without going back pages to catch the tiny thread. The final 1/3 of book was the most enlightening, but the journey there was unpleasant. 
 It would have been nice to have the voice of someone else, on the outside, explain the changes they saw in this deeply troubled young man. I wish I knew what they did to help him and themselves. I was seeking a better understanding, even if just a bit, of his illness and didn't get it.

It's good. Very assured debut. Powerful and very real voice. 
 Unfortunately for me though, I've read a number of books in the last year narrated by people with unique points of view (such as mental illness), so I don't think I was as affected by Matthew as I might otherwise have been. 
 I did still find Filer's writing strong and confident for a first novel, and did want to know what would happen to the man speaking to me through the book. 
 We know from the offset that Matthew's brother died as a child and that he feels responsible. It takes more than three quarters of the book to find out what happened, with insights into Matthew's adulthood and frequent tussles with his schizophrenia along the way. I found Matthew's daily life very interesting, his relationship with his grandmother touching, and comments on social care illuminating. I wasn't very shocked or moved by the revelations into Simon's death, rather anticlimactic actually, but Filer's ending was moving while leaving the reader wanting more. 
 It's lovely when a debut writer received accolades and awards over seasoned novelists, getting more names into the public eye. And Filer covers an important area that deserves ore recognition and discussion. 
 Lots to learn and technique to admire.

The Shock of the Fallwritten by Nathan Filer, a registered mental health nurse. This is part of what attracted me to the book; I was interested to see how having that experience of taking care of mentally ill patients day in, day out would help facilitate writing a book from the point of view of someone who often refers to himself as 'mental' and 'crazy.' The book follows the story of Matthew Homes, a teenager who struggles with mental illness and whose tragic past, including the untimely death of his big brother, Simon, continues to haunt him. 
 Perhaps because Matthew's trauma occurred when he was a young boy, and because it then influenced every part of his life, he speaks with quite a childish voice and uses simple, straightforward language. Matthew's story is written on a computer or sometimes a typewriter, and he always accompanies his own words with pictures and illustrations, much like a child. He identifies his illness almost as a another person or entity that shares and lives life with him. However, despite his childish manner of communicating, he has a belief in the theory that all the atoms in the universe have also been part something else entirely in the past - 
 These are the things we learnt. 
 We learnt about atoms. 
 This illness and me. 
 I was thirteen. 
 .... 
 "Billions of years ago exploding stars sent atoms hurtling through space and we've been recycling them on Earth ever since. Except for the occasional comet, meteor, some interstellar dust, we've used exactly the same atoms over and over since the Earth was formed. We eat them, we drink them, we breathe them, we are made of them. At this precise moment each of us is exchanging our atoms with everyone else, and not just with each other, but with other animals, trees, fungi, moulds -" 
 It is this belief in this rather sophisticated scientific theory that leads him to see - and feel - his brother Simon everywhere. He hears him in the wind, sees him in the air, and feels him nearby. To Matthew, Simon is never truly gone, because his atoms are everywhere, a wonderful coping mechanism but also a devastating side-effect to his illness. It also makes fascinating reading. 
 Matthew is quite an unreliable narrator, as is to be expected, but it's his outlook on this notion that is quite refreshing. He is aware that his own perceptions and memories can't be trusted, and he often points this out. He is fully aware and accepting that he is "mentally unwell" and understands that he needs to be careful not to relapse into bad habits or miss his medication. 
 I don't know why it was this day I decided to follow him. Perhaps it wasn't. Perhaps it was another day. 
 He often points out that getting the story exactly right doesn't matter, and it makes sense, especially in understanding the story. In order to understand the narrator and how he thinks and feels when he's battling schizophrenia, reality more often than not doesn't come into it. It's about understanding why he thinks, and feels, and remembers, and copes the way he does. If reality and sense came into it, this novel just wouldn't be what it is. The treat here is that Nathan Filer has helped us understand the human condition - and one human condition that is often under-represented and misunderstood. 
 Nathan Filer also does a beautiful job of creating the characters of Matthew Homes' parents. His mum and dad are obviously hit hard by the premature death of one of their sons and the slow deterioration of the other. I won't go into detail here about what happens with them in the novel - I don't want to give everything away in one review! - but it is worth reading the book for this exploration of the different ways in which one family copy with familial tragedy. 
 As is often needed with tragic stories, the narrative is punctuated throughout with humour and provides relief from the heartache and confusion. Matthew's frankness about himself is quite hilarious, and it keeps you going through a book that might otherwise be a bit too sad to bear. Hearing himself refer to where he lives as the 'Crazy Crazy NutsNuts ward' gives you that urge to cringe and laugh simultaneously - something special in and of itself. 
 Matthew...suffers from command hallucinations, which he attributes to a dead sibling. Crazy shit, eh? Problem is he's been known to interpret said hallucinations as an invite to off himself....he sits alone in his flat, tapping away endlessly on a typewriter his grandmother gave him, which if you think about it, is a bit mental in itself." 
 The book was so much more than I thought it would be - it was a perfectly balanced tale laced with humour, sadness, wit, and philosophical musing. The book forces laughter from your throat at the same time as breaking your heart, little by little. And while you're always on the outside of the story looking in, Nathan Filer is amazingly skilled at making you empathise with Matthew and see the world through his eyes - if only for a little while.

Oh, man. This book really got to me. It's been a long time since I read a book that I couldn't put down, and this was definitely one. The subject matter was close to me in more ways than one, so perhaps it made a stonger impact on me than it would on others, but i thought the writing was simple, but beautiful, and the story was very honest and heartbreaking, but hopeful.

One of those books where the back gives nothing away. So I read the first few chapters in the shop to be sure it was for me. I enjoyed it, and understand why the blurb doesn't give much away, but good as the book was I find myself unable to recommend it
brilliant. not my normal style, but it was brilliant. I laughed and I cried and I couldn't put it down.
Story could have been so much better. Liked that you felt how the main character was going crazy. However the story was too broken up and hard to follow for me.

Nathan Filer is a registered mental health nurse as well as a performance poet and his real-life experience is evident in this, his debut novel. The story is narrated by Matthew, a nineteen year old schizophrenic who recalls the sudden, tragic death of his older brother, Simon - a death which he believes he caused. 
 The use of mixed formats, different fonts interspersed with occasional line drawings cleverly mirrors the ebb and flow of Matthew's mental illness. Likewise, the narrative flits between different stages in his life, before Simon's death, after Simon's death, during hospital stays, independent living. This is an extremely honest account of one man's journey through mental illness but there is also humour and great insight from Matthew as he sees how his brother's death tore his family apart and left them adrift. 
 The characters are living, breathing creations, with their own foibles and imperfections. You see the heartache of Matthew's parents who, having lost one son, feel they are losing their only remaining child. His Mum, is at her wits end, making lots of noise whilst Dad retreats into silence. His grandmother, the wonderful Nanny Noo, accepts Matthew as he is, visiting him at his flat every other Thursday, never passing judgement. 
 "If it wasn't for Nanny Noo I wouldn't give a shit, but when somebody cares for you as much as she does, I know it's not nice to make them worry." 
 This is a beautifully written, moving story - the beauty is in the everyday detail of Matthew's life - from the fleeting memories of a holiday in France to the stultifying routine of an acute psychiatric ward - eat, sleep, smoke... It's a novel which will stay with me when others have disappeared into the ether - you won't forget Matthew in a hurry and you cannot fail to wish him well....or just to keep his head above water...
I gave up half way through. Crap.

** spoiler alert ** 
 I went into this book not knowing a thing about it. To be honest, had I known I would likely have avoided it. That is not to say that the story was bad but it is about a man that suffers from Schizophrenia and my dad also suffered from the illness and it is a trigger I tend to avoid. 
 The first part of the book you don't know that he suffers any mental health issues but the author wrote the character in a perfect way that made you understand that something isn't altogether right with him. His recollections of his childhood memories and even talking about current events in his life jump a lot so it is spotty in parts and in all honesty it reminded me of my own dad and the way he spoke to me. My dad also wrote a 'book' when he was ill and with that being in the book too also stuck with me. 
 Basically, I found that Nathan wrote the illness quite well and although there is a lot more to the illness and each person who suffers have different experiences it stayed true enough throughout the book.
Rich and moving and funny and compelling.

I found this book dull and I couldn't really connect with the style of writing. 
 Had to put this one down.

Mental illness is a hard thing to write about, especially if you're writing about it as an outsider. There are some very good insights in this novel and some parts are spot on but, overall, I think it fell short of achieving that in-the-mind-of-madness feeling it aimed for. Partly, I think, because it tried too hard. You don't need to scatter words about meaninglessly on a page to show that someone's thoughts are scattered; it's too... contrived. Also, if you tell the reader that someone is intelligent, and a good student, and that they've been writing their whole life, don't you dare make them a bad writer. Finally, there was no reward for finishing this book. It felt like it ended just because the author didn't really know where else to take it. This one left me feeling disappointed.

I really did not enjoy this book. It was a classic case of style over substance. First, I found the plot (what little there was) forced and believable. The characters were poorly drawn to the point of being almost cyphers - including the narrator. Over all, I found the book tedious and boring.

About 20-30 pages into the book, the narrator who sounds like a 9 year old, all of a sudden uses a word/concept that is quite unlike a 9 year old. There are quite a few instances like that in the book. I did not enjoy the style at all. As for the context, there are much better written books about psychiatric disorders. 
 I am sorry for the time I wasted finishing this book. I cannot believe it won the Costa Award!

Decent enough first person narrative from a schizophrenic ... Overall theme ; grief and bereavement firstly, mental health secondly 
 Very curious incident ...
This book gave me this quite unpleasant feeling. Like I was about to be dropped on the trailes under a train.
very different from anything ive ever read. at times i was a bit annoyed bc the narrator is unreliable and so i didnt know if i should trust him or not, but i really enjoyed this book!
I found this book had a very interesting narrative intertwined with memorable characters that exuded such honesty that I found the book really intriguing and life affirming.
Enjoyable coming-of-age story with deliciously meta elements. A sensitive portrayal of mental health issues - and sharp observations about mental health centres.

The Shock of the Fall by Nathan Filer, tells the story of Matthew and Simon, two brothers who are separated yet united by a tragic accident. Exploring themes of loss, grief and mental illness, the novel transports the reader directly into the mind of Matthew and his decent into madness as he confronts his role in the boyhood death of his older brother ten years earlier. 
 This is an extraordinary novel, and reminded me in parts of a wonderful book I read a number of years back, which has stayed with me ever since, called 'Carry Me Down'. 
 There are lots to grip you about The Shock of the Fall, firstly it's a very unusual narrative, but also the absolute ability on the part of Nathan Filer to be both funny and inventive, to touch your heart and mind, to deliver prose that you don't want to put down, that is equally moving, tragic, heartfelt, pure and memorable, and at the same time, feels very different to anything you have read before. 
 Acquired in a hotly-contested eleven way auction, The Shock of the Fall has been described as a brave and ground-breaking novel from an exciting new voice in fiction. Featuring a cast of expertly crafted characters, The Shock of the Fall, is quite simply one of those books that will stay with you. And, I wasn't one bit surprised to discover that Nathan Filer is a mental health nurse. The novel is littered with insight and is touchingly harrowing without ever falling into sweet sentiment. There is no room for sweet within the four hundred or so pages, poignancy, yes, human frailty, yes, sharp shocking reality, absolutely, YES. 
 It is clever, real, gripping, and pure. I'm already looking forward to his next book.

This book just didn't really do it for me and I honestly don't know why I kept reading. 
 I've read reviews on the cover and one said about the amazing build up to the big reveal at the end about what happened to Simon, that wasn't a build up,that was just dragged out until over 200 pages when you could already make a pretty good guess as to what happened Simon. 
 Deeply moving...no sorry it was bland and uninteresting,it didn't have me captivated or gripped or even interested in Matts story. 
 I liked Simon and the younger Matt and that's about it. 
 I did want to see happiness for smart but with a mental illness it doesn't work like that.

Really wanted to like this. So much to engage the reader emotionally: 19yr old schizophrenic Matt believes he caused the tragic death of his older brother Simon, who has Down's Syndrome. Yes, we are give a profound insight into mental illness and its treatment, since Filer is a mental health nurse. There are some fabulous moments and characters: Nanny Noo is great, and there are many bleak ironies. But the novel is full of gimmicks, almost like a check list of 'What I learned on my creative writing course'. Irritating rather than moving; pity.

THE SHOCK OF THE FALL by Nathan Filer 
 You may recall that a couple of months ago I reviewed SEATING ARRANGEMENTS by Maggie Shipstead (1 Aug). As it had won the Dylan Thomas Prize I was wary of the part poetry might play in the prose. I approached THE SHOCK OF THE FALL with a similar degree of trepidation since the author, Nathan Filer, is not merely a poet, he is a performance poet. For those of you unused to performance poetry, this involves physically acting in some way so as to compliment the words. And whereas Maggie Shipstead avoided any suggestion of poetry in her work, Nathan Filer does not although it's the performance element that's reflected here rather the poetic use of words. More of that later. 
 But first I want to tell you what the book is about because that may influence your decision as to whether to read it or not. It deals with the subject of mental illness and in this particular case, schizophrenia. The book is written in the first person so we get the inside line of what it must like to be schizophrenic. The narrator is Matthew Homes and we follow his journey beginning with his 'fall' as a young boy, the subsequent death of his elder brother Simon (whom he adores), his experiences in (and out) of mental institutions and his eventual release back into the community. It comes across as an accurate portrayal - it should do as Nathan Filer is not just a performance poet, he is also a registered mental health nurse. There are echoes of ONE FLEW OVER THE CUCKOO'S NEST here and Matthew's story will no doubt resonate with those who have suffered mental illness or been otherwise involved with it. It draws high praise from Jo Brand who was once a psychiatric nurse herself. 
 I am telling you this because the back cover blurb gives little in the way of clues as to the book's real intent ie. 
 I'll tell you what happened because it will be a good way to introduce my brother. His name's Simon. I think you're going to like him. I really do. But in a couple of pages he'll be dead. And he was never the same after that. 
 No hint of mental illness here - we have to read the endorsements for that. And excuse my cynicism, but I detect the influence of the Creative Writing MA Mr Filer attended here. As modern authors we are continually told how our first paragraph, even our first sentence, must instantly engage the reader. No longer do we have the luxury enjoyed by such literary greats as John Steinbeck who spent the first few pages of EAST OF EDEN in a lengthy description of the red soil of the Salinas Valley in California. He won The Nobel Prize for Literature - today his manuscript would be returned as unsuitable. So this back cover blurb isn't meant to tell us what the book is about, it's there to suck us in, hence my need to advise you. 
 But before my cynicism has chance to affect you, let me say that THE SHOCK OF THE FALL is an extremely well-written book. It certainly achieves what it sets out to do and the voice of Matthew Homes is very authentic. It warrants comparisons with THE CURIOUS INCIDENT OF THE DOG IN THE NIGHT-TIME (Mark Haddon) and THE UNIVERSE VERSUS ALEX WOODS (Gavin Extence) although this last is in my view a superior effort. 
 In fact, the similarities with THE CURIOUS INCIDENT bear further consideration and the more I think about it the more similar they become. Both deal with mental illness, autism and schizophrenia respectively. Both are first person narratives with much the same distinction of voice. Plus, (and this is my main point), they both use visual effects within the body of the work in order to enhance the words ie. this is the 'performance' element I talked of earlier. For example, page 8 of THE SHOCK is a sketch of the doll which is the subject of the first chapter. Filer uses the burial doll as the catalyst for the story in much the same way as Haddon uses the death of the dog. We also get lists and diagrams but Filer brings something new to the party by deliberately changing the font to signify the narrator's use of a typewriter instead of a computer at an appropriate point in the narrative. 
 So, this disruption of the written word with visual effects - is it a valid enhancement of the form? Or is it purely a gimmick? I can see how the purists might object. But although I may have traditionalist views, I am not a purist and I do not find these intrusions out of place. Reading is after all, a visual experience. In fact I do think they enhance the form of these particular books and add to our experience although if this were to become a trend throughout literature I think I might begin to smell a rat. 
 So, will the more avant-garde Creative Writing MAs soon be teaching us how to draw as 
 well as write? Let's wait and see.

Okay so if you don't know about this book it is about a young man dealing with mental illness, after his brother Simon died. The main character blames himself for his brother Simon's death. I thought this book was a nice light read, I liked the various set-ups of pages with scattered words however I felt like this book dealt with mental illness with a light hand, it was a nice portrayal but not very well done in my person opinion, this is coming from someone who has had a lot of experience around people with mental health issues. 
 I liked the story and how it made me feel happy, sad and angry but I was left rather disappointed. I think I need more books similar to this until I can be sure this book is a better or worse depiction of mental health. I like however that is was from a males point of view and dealt with mental illness, disabilities and death.
More like 2.5, really. It felt a bit thin to me, and it offered yet another take on an unreliable narrator with mental illness that didn't seem very original or add much to what's been done before.
Tragic and beautiful.
Painful to read, but extremely life affirming too.

I somehow started this book without realising it's about someone who lost his special needs sibling at a young age and struggled with his mental health throughout his youth. The similarity to my own life situation pretty much guarantees I can't give this one an objective review, but I did enjoy it. It's tragic, hopeful, emotional, etc.. A story with a real heart that felt very authentic.

I didn't actually finish this book, and was unable to get more than about halfway through it. Admittedly, I had high expectations that it didn't really deliver on. Suffice to say, I thought it'd give me a bit more than it did, but it ended up feeling a lot like One Flew Over The Cuckoo's Nest or Flowers of Algernon, but with more amateur writing and less moving plot. Was really hoping to like it, but it just didn't do it for me. Mental illness in novels is something I think needs to be approached in a very fresh, but deep, way, and this kind of fell through for me.

The Shock of the Fall ili Where the Moon isn't (ovaj drugi naslov je svakako bolji) je prica o Metjuu, koji je sve samo ne jos jedan od obicnih knjizevnih junaka. 
 Odmah u startu citaoci su svesni da on nije jednostavan, da je nesto drugacije u njemu, njegovom nacinu razmisljanja i da je pritisnut mnogim bolima, tugom i krivicom. 
 U prici koju on prica, tj. pise na kompjuteru ili pisacoj masini (sto je pisac ostvario promenom fonta), citaoci putuju napred-natrag kroz Metjuov zivot i postaju saputnici u njegovoj prici i njegovom zivotu a isto tako i njegovi sapatnici, jer ne mogu a da ne osete tu bol i krivicu koja mu pritiska ramena i srce. Sam glavni lik, Metju je odlican, a postoje i odlicne sporedne uloge, kao na primer Anabela, Sajmon i Metjuova (i Sajmonova) baka. Roman je uistinu prosaran zivopisnim likovima. 
 Osim toga, roman je prozet i odlicnim humorom (poprilicno crnim), cak i pored toga sto se bavi ozbiljnim problemima - opakom bolescu uma, detetom sa daunovim sindromom,... 
 Fajler ima dara za pisanje i odlicno je primenio malo drugaciji stil koji savrseno odgovara glavnom liku i njegovom problemu. Generalno nemam sta da zamerim knjizi, osim cinjenice da sam ipak ocekivao malo bombasticniji kraj. Kako sam se priblizavao kraju romana, nekako je sve ukazivalo na to kakav ce da bude zavrsetak. 
 Sve u svemu, jedna jaka cetvorka.

This book was a fascinating insight into an often misunderstood mental illness. It was beautiful and heart-wrenching in equal parts, with a very likeable main character. This is easily one of the best books I've read this year. I hope the author has written more since this publication (this is his first novel) so I can devour his back catalogue...

All the words used to describe this book (-from the reviews written on the cover-) are true. 
 Engaging. 
 Dark. 
 Touching. 
 Bittersweet. 
 Heartrending. 
 I don't know what else I can add. 
 The Shock of the Fall is different to anything I have read before. The narrator Matthew, is a schizophrenic and tells the story of his life in his own words. It is repetitive in parts, blunt, and moves forward and back in time. All evidence of his illness. He describes it as a 'cut and paste life'. 
 A compelling and thought provoking story I would highly recommend.

I really enjoyed this book. It was funny, touching, and a glimpse into schizophrenia from a surprisingly reliable narrator. 
 I highly recommend this book.

I spent half the time reading this confused, and the other half intrigued! I think on balance it was great...although at times the shifting of time back and forth wasn't easy to follow. An exploration into the mind of someone with a mental health disorder makes for uncomfortable reading at times but it was a fascinating read, if a little different to what I normally read 
 I was torn between 3 & 4 stars but in the end decided on 3 as I think if if been reading this between work and horses etc like most books I read instead of laying by the pool reading solidly, I think I would have struggled to keep going due to the confusion!
this took me way too long to read n idek understand why it was really really goodddd
I give up!

** spoiler alert ** 
 I'm not going to write an in depth review as I'm not entirely sure how I feel about this book. There were some elements which I thought were quite brilliant and others which I found irritating. 
 One irritating feature, as mentioned by someone else, is the orchestrated 'reveal' whereby we have to wait until almost the end of the book to find out the terrible secret about Matthew's dead brother which we guessed at right from the beginning. I don't see the point of this. Either have it as a genuine surprise, or fill us in straightaway. There were also occasional dips into sentimentality that annoyed me, for example, regarding the girl and her buried doll. (And - for those who have finished the book - why does Matthew take Simon to go and dig up the doll anyway?) There is also something very self-conscious about the writing. Obviously, it's Matthew writing and he's very self-conscious. But this device can become rather wearing. 
 BUT there is some brilliant writing and observation here too. The depiction of the mental health services is particularly good. You can see how the staff are so well-meaning and the structures in place designed to be helpful. And yet, Matthew's often damning reaction to them is very easy to understand. It makes you count yourself lucky. 
 The family relationships are well drawn and the perhaps difficult characterisation of Simon is particularly successful. His own mental and physical deficiencies are not patronised but dealt with honestly, recognising that he can be both loveable and infuriating. 
 Anyway, only two stars because, for all its worth, I've come away from this book feeling more irritated than enthused and perhaps that is in part down to the fact that I feel I am meant to appreciate its 'worthiness' in a didactic way. 
 There's my short review ;P

It was not a great book. The story jumped around so much I could not identify with any of the characters. I kept hoping for and surprise ending or some kind of paranormal activity. There isn't any. You can skip it.

If you plan on reading this book, and I recommend that you do, do not read the quotes on the inside of the cover. One of these quotes really spoiled a section of the book for me and I'm really surprised it was there. 
 This is a finely drawn observation of a difficult subject. The narrator is a sympathetic and hugely likeable character and I look forward to reading more by this author.

This is a touching novel about a young man coming to terms with his older brother's accidental death...and his role in it. It veers toward the gimmicky at times--the story is told in short and long spurts, aided by correspondence, drawings, in different type fonts--but the protagonist/narrator has been diagnosed with schizophrenia, so all of that sort of fits. His condition, and the jerky way he tells his story, also makes it hard to get a handle on him (we don't learn of his schizophrenia until toward the end of the book, although clues that he is very sick were certainly planted before then) and this lessens the story's eventual impact in a way. But it certainly deserves four stars.
What a wonderfully tragic book.

Another novel to prove, if proof was needed, how utterly heartless and without pity I am becoming. Sorry, Nathan Filer, I come to rain all over your parade. Well, quite a lot of it. 
 The blurb has these three little sentences: 
 There are books you can't stop reading, which keep you up all night 
 (Well, I actually was reading this most of last night, but that's because I had insomnia.) 
 There are books which let us into the hidden parts of life and make them vividly real. 
 (Referring to the world of the schizophrenic, since that's what this novel is all about. But I wouldn't call mentally ill young people and their lives in and out of institutions a hidden part of life , there are movies (Broken, Silver Linings Playbook, etc etc) and books ( Henry's Demons - recommended - and lots of others), it's not terra incognita. 
 There are books which, because of the sheer skill with which every word is chosen, linger in your mind for days. 
 (Wow, fire that blurb writer! For days you say?! Sheer skill? I suppose with not so much skill a book will only linger for minutes. So yeah, they still crank out this silly OTT hypegloop.) 
 THE BIG BLACK PLOT DEVICE 
 This book won the Costa first novel award, so what do I know. I was almost completely unthrilled. It was tiresome. I mean to say, there's this big thing which is hinted at in the first few pages and which hangs over the rest of novel like a Big Black Cloud About to Burst Forth With Torrential Rain. The schizophrenic brother whose impressionistic memoir/confession we are reading has in some way caused the death of his Down Syndrome brother (yes, this is a blighted family). Cornily, the Big Reveal of What Really Happened That Fateful Day is coughed up only on page 247. The fake suspense of waiting to find out what you figure out roughly from page 5 does not kill you. It just makes you think oh are they still using this plot device? They should really stop. 
 I thought I would only write a three line bah-humbug review, but the sheer skill with which every single word was chosen has made the crabbiness I felt linger in my mind for... hours. 
 I'D LIKE TO TEACH THE WORLD TO SING IN PERFECT HARMONY (BUT I DON'T THINK I'LL GET ROUND TO IT) 
 It says here - 
 The comedian Jo Brand has called The Shock of the Fall "one of the best books about mental illness" and judges for the Costa book awards said it was a novel "so good it will make you feel a better person". 
 Maybe it is, maybe it will. But I thought the bleak realism and painful memories of Matt's story did not then mean it was okay to ladle dollops of sentimental goop into the mix. It's strange how wildly different reactions to novels can be - look at the love-gush that puthered all over Donna Tartt's latest whopper, and look at this rather good review here. 
 SOMETHING I DID LIKE 
 You do get a very strong sense of the mental bind that some patients (or : "service users"!) get into once they're sucked into the mental health biz. The regime is almost designed to engender fear and distrust. They're confined to a facility. And drugs are administered to them, all of which have horrible side effects (even the drugs they give you to combat the side effects of the first drugs). And there's no choice in any of this. They have proved they're incapable of existing in the outside world in one way or another, so there they are, here's their diagnosis, there's the drugs (if you don't take those 6 pills we'll inject you) and there's your room. So, the patients become locked into a low-level interior guerrilla war against the people who are trying to help them. Inside their heads - as well as fighting their illness - every mental patient is either consciously or unconsciously Jack Nicholson in One Flew Over The Cuckoo's Nest. The staff are their enemies (even the nice ones). (Matt : I don't hate these people. I just hate not having the choice to get rid of them.) The terminology is dehumanising. Their lives are deserts of idle hours spent smoking with a guy who talks to his tattoos. Or daytime tv, your choice. 
 Last time I went into the office to borrow the Nursing Dictionary, I counted three mugs, a mouse mat, a bunch of pens, two Post-It note booklets and the wall clock - all sporting the brands of different medicines. It's like being in prison and having to look at adverts for fucking locks. 
 SOMETHING ELSE I LIKED 
 Matt is haunted by his dead brother 
 If the tap choked and spluttered before the water came, he was saying I'm lonely. When I opened a bottle of Dr Pepper and the caramel bubbles fizzed over the rim, he was asking me to come out and play. He could speak through an itch, the certainty of a sneeze, the after-taste of tablets, or the way sugar fell from a spoon. 
 No doubt at all, this book has its heart in the right place, unlike mine, which was abandoned a long time ago in a left luggage locker in a train station in a town whose name I no longer recall.

To explain exactly how I felt about this book would provide far too many spoilers which as a reader I would hate to do to someone planning on reading this beautiful book. I will simply say it deals with one very complex protagonist who has had his fair share of hardship in life. 
 Nathan Filer has written such a wonderful book and I wept at several parts in the story. This is primarily because I could empathize directly with the main character Matt. He is a unique young man and the way his story is told is very much like peeling the layers off a very thick onion and then trying to go back and out some of them back. He is a young man who has been wounded in many ways and will continue to be even after the book ends. I found myself routing for him as he faced his difficulties and tried to make some sense of where he found himself. This is a tough call because where he finds himself is not a place anyone else can truly understand. 
 Please give Nathan's book a chance, you won't regret it I promise.

I'm not sure what to make of this book. It started out reminding me of The Curious Incident of the Dog at Midnight, which I loved. But this book is so dark and so depressing and so entirely bleak and dispiriting that I couldn't finish it. The Curious Incident was hopeful. This is definitely not.
Difficult to get through and understand. Perhaps the writer was doing a stream of consciousness similar to flowers for Algernon, but the presentation was wrong.

book_b.title: Let's Pretend This Never Happened: A Mostly True Memoir
book_b.user_review: Laughed out loud the first few chapters, but after a while the anecdotes started to repeat themselves and got gradually less and less funny. I found it difficult to understand the reasonings of the storyteller and sadly, as this is an autobiography, can only hope the author's aim was to portray herself as someone who is capricious, foul-mouthed, insane, inconsiderate and impossible to live with.

sample_reviews.review_text:
** This book review, as well as many more, can also be found on my blog, The Baking Bookworm (www.thebakingbookworm.blogspot.ca). ** 
 My Review: I picked up this book recently from my local library right before a job interview. Trying to distract my nerves I sat there reading the book jacket I was quietly chuckling to myself and it honestly helped to reduce my nerves. I like funny reads. I do. But I also feel that they're really hard to write well. What is deemed "funny" means different things to different people and while I think that Jenny has a great sense of humour I don't necessarily think it came through well in this book. 
 There were some great, hilarious gems in this book but the overall feeling of chaos in her writing stifled those funny bits. It felt very disjointed -- like you were talking to a overly caffeinated person who would shoot out random stories that didn't necessarily have anything to do with each other. It often felt like she was just babbling and not caring about what she was talking about and after awhile that got frustrating. And don't get me started about the overused and excessively annoying footnotes! Gah! Enough already! I know you're funny Jenny! Show me! 
 Don't get me wrong, there were certain parts of stories where I did actually laugh out loud because Jenny is funny. But then she'd take too long to get to the end of the story and start to lose me. Or the story seemed much too unrealistic to be true and ... she'd start to lose me. Overall, I guess I just felt really lost. I read over half of the book before I finally called it quits because I just couldn't take any more of the rambling bedlam that is her memoire. 
 I think Jenny excels at writing funny little snippets (like on her blog, The Bloggess) but this full-fledged book didn't showcase her best comedic assets. With better editing and a more polished feel I think this could have been amazing. Unfortunately her frantic way of storytelling just isn't for me, I guess. I'll stick to reading her blog. 
 My Rating: 0 (didn't finish it)

The read was definitely a train-wreck. I good train wreck at times definitely, but a train-wreck nonetheless. The funny thing is that Jenny would probably take this as a compliment. It was great to hear Jenny's story and it gave so much honest perspective on the most interesting experiences. Throughout the book, I wondered if she would still be with her husband by the end. She must have guessed that because she addressed in the epilogue and made it clear that sometimes what people perceive as imperfection or "weird" is actually just a fraction of the silent majority's reality.
I bought it because Jen Lancaster wrote on her blog that it's funny. Meh. It was an ok, quick and easy read for a hot and lazy summer weekend but it did not make me laugh.

This is an incredible book. Its "laugh out loud while rolling on the floor" funny. The author is vulgar, opinionated and offensive, but she is never condescending to the reader. Her writing reminds me of Lewis Grizzard, who was a brilliant storyteller. 
 If you are offended by profanity or overt references to reproductive organs in contexts you would never dream of, stay away from the book. 
 If you want to read writing that is heartfelt and can make you laugh at things the would normally have you crying, this book is well worth the cost and time.
Hilarious. The author narrates herself and is very funny. Anyone looking for a light listen (but who is not offended by strong language) should try this.

I was unfamiliar with The Bloggess before this book started popping up in all the summer "Must Read" lists, but the buzz surrounding this one was enough to convince me to give Jenny Lawson a shot. In the end, I'm kind of underwhelmed. She started out strong; her childhood stories were flat-out hysterical. Reading about her father waking Jenny up with a puppet fashioned out of a dead squirrel had me laughing so hard I couldn't barely breathe. It's not necessarily new territory - the wacky parents are a staple of the humor memoir - but Lawson related the antics with a wry tone that killed me. 
 And then she grew up, and the stories became less funny than "Look at how weird I am, you guys. Ohmigosh, I'm so weird." Maybe I'm being a little cynical but once the perspective shifted to her life as a wife, mother, HR specialist and socially awkward blogger, I got bored. I didn't feel like there was anything particularly unique about Lawson's story and the tales of her arguments with her husband and her inability to moderate her anxiety as she met with other bloggers for a spa weekend weren't amusing. It struck me as someone trying too hard to be funny and quirky without any idea of the point she was trying to make.

Jenny Lawson is a blogger. This book consists of stories of her life. Her family did not have much money as she was growing up in Texas. She has an... unusual... father. She and her sister grew up with lots of animals around, wild and domestic, dead and alive (her father is a taxidermist). She suffers from social anxiety. Her husband's family has money and is quite different from her own, so she struggles a little bit to fit in with them. 
 I had no idea who she was, but I saw some good reviews for the book, so I thought I'd give it a try. I found this so funny! I laughed out loud plenty of times, and the one chapter that had me laughing so hard I was crying and it was hard to breathe, and I couldn't stop for some time, was the one that described the 5 foot tall metal chicken she brought home. In particular, it was her husband's reaction that got me going. It was the best 15th anniversary ever! Oh, and there are photos to go with the stories, so you know they really happened!

I couldn't/didn't finish this. Who ever said this was up there with Tina Fey and David Sedaris is smoking crack; or has never read either of them. She is in serious need of an editor. It's over written and she's trying way to hard which just made it terribly annoying. I'm baffled how this became a best seller.

If you want to laugh so hard you cry or pee your pants then this is your book. I have never in my life enjoyed a "funny" book as much as this one. It never bores you, or makes you wish you hadn't bought it. It was a hysterical, tear jerking, pee your pants, not for the faint at heart or the easily offended kind of person. I think Jenny and I are related somewhere in our family tree because this book made me think of my own family and childhood and makes me happy to see there are other families like mine. Be proud of yourself and your abnormal family and enjoy more than a wee chuckle.

Hysterically funny, laugh out loud hilarious!! 
 5 out of 5, no question! 
 Love her blog and her book was just wonderful...! 
 Rude, crass, un-explainable at times but truly wonderful.

I really enjoyed this book. I wasn't quite sure what to expect as I had already read Jenny Lawson's second book. While this is a autobiography as well this focuses more on Lawson's childhood/growing up. It is interesting to see how she handled things before coming to terms with her mental illness. 
 All that being the case the book is not as cheerful or funny as furiously happy. However, there are still some hilarious stories. I also think it makes Furiously Happy even better since it helps to frame who Lawson is as a person.
I don't think I've ever laughed out loud to a book as much as I did with this one!

Wow! This is a bizarre but an awesome memoir! I've never read a memoir like it, Jenny Lawson really puts it all out there -the cursing, threats, the insane stories that can't possibly be true but totally did happen, and off topic remarks... now that's a memoir! It's not your stereotypical memoir... Jenny Lawson shares a variety of events, some are a retell of an event, from her blog, a conversation she had with someone, a side comment in a footnote (even a few from the editor), the variety of writing in this book makes it really interesting to read. I recommend it to anyone who are open-minded and appreciate good humor.

Hated this book because it had so much potential and yet fell so far short. Yes, its funny at times, very funny, but the book reads like workshop free-writing exercise (poor editing) and lacks depth. and can I just say I saw this in hardcover selling at Target for $20 or $25. Mindboggling.

There were some chapters that made me laugh so hard that tears came to my eyes. 
 If you appreciate the absurdities of life, you will find many moments in this book that will fit the bill. 
 Jenny is a great story teller and shares experiences from her childhood up until her current life, which is apparently filled with scorpions, rattlesnakes, vultures, and chupacabras, or perhaps not. 
 My attempts to share would pale in comparison unless I took passages out word for word. I wanted to space the book out over a period of time, but I couldn't put it down. The laughter was great and I thank her for writing this book! 
 While the taxidermy would take a bit of getting used to, I think I would benefit from hanging around with her. 
 Plus, she's a 'Toid like me! (People who live with rheumatoid arthritis I fondly call 'Toids. We are a fine, but gnarled group.) 
 Update (5/27/12) - A friend I've known since high school came to visit me. As we rode back to my house from the airport, she said, "I went to see an author speak. I don't know if you've heard of her. Her name is Jenny..." and I yelled out, "LAWSON?" 
 My friend brought me an autographed copy of this hilarious book, so I can read bits of it whenever I want! What a great gift!

I can honestly say that I laughed so hard I cried. And then I even cried some for real because thru all the F bombs and the jokes and quick wit there was some really deep stuff in there too. 
 The book is not for the faint of heart. If you are easily offended I wouldn't recommend it at all. Just warning you. I did the audio which is read by Jenny (I feel like we are on a first name basis after listening) and I highly recommend doing the audio. I don't know that I would have enjoyed it as much. 
 Favorite quotes - 
 "In short? It is exhausting being me. Pretending to be normal is draining and requires amazing amounts of energy and Xanax." 
 "I'm simply too unstable to know how pants work today."

Over Winter Break, I was lamenting my lack of fiction reading. I searched and couldn't find exactly what I wanted. It turns out what I wanted and needed was this book. 
 I laughed aloud with other people in the room (not just so they'd ask, "What's so funny?"). More importantly, I laughed aloud with no one else in the room and found myself chuckling later as I remembered a passage. 
 While the main thrust of the book is humor, Lawson also lets herself have moments of sincerity and emotion that are made all-the-more poignant by the funny surrounding them. I'll probably re-read this book in a bit the same way I return to comedy albums or Monty Python sketches. 
 It is smart, funny, perfectly offensive and made my day. I wish there was more of it to read.
Hilarious at points, slow at others, and totally strange all the way through. It promises to be everything it is!
This book had some funny bits in it... but mostly it just came off as "look at me! I had a crazy childhood! I am excited!" Gave up 20% through.
Pretty funny, but also very spazzy......
just read it... that is the only way you can understand.
One chapter, "The Psychopath On the Other Side Of the Bathroom Door," made me laugh so hard I cried. I couldn't breathe. It was that funny.
This was like reading someone's journal... With no thought as to what was going to come next.. Random and not enjoyable to read..

I never want to read a book written by a blogger again. This book should have had an editor. If it did indeed have an editor, that editor should be fired. This book is rambling and point-free, like a blog. It is, though, a good airplane read, in that it's a quick read, and should be left on the plane. 
 I am in need of aspirin.
I snorted, I cried, I laughed so hard I could barely breath. I enjoyed every page of this book and am so sad there are no more to read. I want to be Jenny's best friend.
I wanted to like this book but I am just not a fan of it. I skipped parts of the book because they were just so boring or unbelievable.
Didn't hit the right tone with me, all the tangents and asides were annoying.

I LOVED this book. It is hard to believe that these things happened to her, but I was in stitches laughing. I thoroughly enjoyed her storytelling and her sense of humor in each experience. Even when they were sad stories, Jenny Lawson somehow made it ok to laugh. I'm sure my husband is glad I am done with this book, I lost count of the eye rolls he gave me for laughing out loud.

Ugh. Yeah, I get it. Jenny Lawson has had an out-there life. No really, she is weirder than you. I don't think I need to waste any more time hearing how truly special and hilarious she is, or how she is unable to write coherently because of all her years vomit-blogging. She has enough people who love her and will validate her. I bet if I were hearing this in person, I would be laughing, or if it were a tv show. But I read Infinite Jest this year,and I just keep thinking scornfully that DFW did it so much better. Even though this will throw me further behind far behind of reading for 2013, I don't want to waste more time on this.

This book goes on my very short I-Couldn't-Even-Finish-It list. I made it to pp. 125. Maybe it's because I also spent my high school years and some college in small west Texas towns, but I didn't think her stories were particularly funny. I also felt like she could have used some serious editing - not the awful attempting-to-be-funny fake editors notes at the bottom of many pages. I loved Tina Fey and Mindy Kaling's books, and also really liked Lena Dunham, Amy Poehler, and Andy Cohen's memoirs. I WOULD not put this book in the same category.

I don't think I can finish this one. Maybe it's better as a blog in spurts. After the first third of the book all I can think was, "I get it. Someone told you that you were funny and a little quirky. Now how are you going up fill up an entire book?" When I read her blog I laugh. I just didn't think it translates to an entire book of material.
If there was nothing else to read and I wanted some diversion, then I might finish this. But this author tries awfully hard to be a wise-ass and that gets wearing.

I loved this book through the entire beginning, straight up to her marriage. Then it regressed into blog form. 
 This writer is hilarious. And most of her readers are from the blog. I've read one of her blog posts (the giant chicken lawn ornament) and loved it. But this book could've been crafted and wonderful. Instead it ended up kind of sloppy and not all that interesting. I can't really blame the editor either because like I said, most of these readers came from the blog and they probably liked it just fine. 
 It all went south when I reached the Spartan cheerleaders bit. And then the bloggers' retreat. Ugh. Just not book-worthy material. But I'd try reading her again. And I envy her raccoons-in-jams childhood.

Oh Jenny you're so fine,..... If you are intelligent, want to laugh out loud and aren't easily offended, this is the book for you. Probably the single funniest book I've EVER read. I want to read it again, but this time with a highlighter to mark some of the many memorable passages. Not to be missed by anyone with a twisted sense of humor and an intellect to match.

Really funny! Like reading about my Texan counterpart. Not that our lives are similar or anything, because my dad didn't have a taxidermy shop and I don't have arthritis or a kid or a husband but still Lawson is probably the Texan counterpart of me, you and maybe everybody, somehow. 
 Except maybe other Texans as they have no need for a Texan counterpart. 
 I found myself really liking Jenny Lawson. She is funny, charming, intelligent, etc. She is also a blogger though, and it shows. Not that there is anything wrong with that (I mean, hey!) but the entire book was like a very, very long blogpost. Which is fine!
This wasn't for me - wasn't funny to me, and I found myself quickly skimming.
Jenny Lawson makes me feel like everything will be alright. I haven't laughed or cried so hard at a book in a long while.

Her successful blog format didn't translate well to a book for me. I appreciated her highlighting and educating me on her mental disorder, but her constant manic book was exhausting and wore on me. All that being said, I think I'd love her blog and I'm going to check it out.
Seriously funny.
Gee I laughed a lot and thought a lot reading this book.

I tried to give this book a chance. It annoyed me so much in the first chapter by calling Laura Ingalls Wilder a "liar" and a bad autobiographer (!) that I almost tossed it aside. Int he second chapter it annoyed me so much more by being a great load of meaningless babble without any focus that I did toss it aside. Reading it is like listening to a person try to tell a story who keeps going off on tangents and can't really get the story out. This book isn't like the work of David Sedaris. Anyhow. On to the next.

I will admit that I laughed out loud on more than a few occasions when reading this book, but the author is really crazy and a lot of the time I just felt sorry for her, though I wouldn't be surprised if that's what she's after. A little sophomoric for my taste, but I do enjoy a book that makes me laugh.

The fact that I forgot to write a review for this, makes me said. If you haven't checked out the Blogess, aka Jenny Lawson, you are missing out on endless humor and amazing stories. Jenny has a way of telling tales that leaves you laughing for hours and hours on end... Once you read them, you are not likely to forget them at all! One amazing laugh after another, this book is worth every penny and I am just dying for news of her second novel
Not a fan. Too much cursing.

Meh. I felt this book was vastly disturbing. My daughter had recommended it saying it was hysterical. I, however, found nothing hysterical about this poor girl having to have grown up in a deeply disturbed poor family. I managed to read it through to the end, but that is about all I have to say about it.
Some funny parts but makes too much use of the word vagina. Pretty elementary
Started out as incredibly funny but the charm rapidly wore off and it deteriorated into incredibly annoying.

Jenny Lawson is HILARIOUS! She is quirky in the most creepy yet lovable way, and she makes me feel I'm not the only weirdo out there. 
 After reading beforehand her second book "Furiously Happy", I loved hearing about Jenny's childhood and adolescent and about her first steps in her life with Victor. Together, I feel "Let's Pretend This Never Happened" and "Furiously happy" complete each other to tell a fuller story, the first mainly about Lawson's past and the latter about her present. 
 My only regret is that now I have to wait for Lawson to write another book until I can find myself in the uncomfortable situation of laughing my face off in a middle of a crowded public bus.
a constant struggle to finish---parts were funny but not the best
Funny, though rambling. The raccoon in jams was pretty cute.

reference_books.title: The Chemist
reference_books.review_text:
2 stars 
 She used to work for the U.S. government, but very few people ever knew that. An expert in her field, she was one of the darkest secrets of an agency so clandestine it doesn't even have a name. And when they decided she was a liability, they came for her without warning. 
 The Chemist begins with a strong storyline and promising premise. An ex-agent hiding from government because they wanted to get rid of her. I mean, it's gonna be a thrilling journey right? 
 Until the heroine met with her love interest, that promising premise seems like a dream that never come true. 
 Stephenie Meyer is known for her ability to write addictive romance, like Twilight Saga and The Host. However, The Chemist wasted two half of the book with them hiding from the government in order to build the unnecessary romance between the heroine and her love interest, if anything it felt forced. I can't believe I'm saying this, but if we took out all the romance aspect of this book, it would have been a great book. Because nothing worse than an unconvincing romance. 
 I am so disappointed because this book was one of my highly anticipated book to read in 2016.

sample_reviews.review_text: Loved the first half, hated the second, so I rounded up my rating to a 3. Insert sad face here.

** spoiler alert ** 
 DNF @36% 
 Ok sorry I just can't do it. I honestly just cannot get over how these two got together, among other stupid things in the plot. 
 How am I supposed to believe that this guy, who at the time all we know about him is that he's an arsehole that yells at his employees and constantly looks like he's pissed off, magically falls head over heels for some girl he's never actually met. I know, because she sent him photos of her tits, arse and legs FOR GOD KNOWS WHAT REASON??? 
 So let me just back pedal a bit. It stars out on a train. This chick notices some really angry dude yelling at an employee on the phone and thinks he's a (very good looking) arsehole. Fair enough. Then somehow he drops his phone and she picks it up. Instead of returning it she goes through it, looks at pictures etc. after a couple of days she shows up to his building to return it, yet he refuses to speak to her. So what does she do? She sends him photos of her cleavage, arse and legs. Because that will teach him! WHAT THE ACTUAL FUCK?! Oh but she's sure to leave her face out of the pictures because she doesn't want him to recognise her. Then they go back and forth texting each other when finally he convinces her to go on a date with him "because he wants more with her". Makes no sense. Like no FUCKING sense. 
 And as if the authors realise "hey wait, we need to make the readers like this guy and make him relatable" they throw in the fact that his mother dies. But don't worry, in case you missed it the first time it was stated, it will continue to come up every 10 pages. 'Oh you have a dog? Yeah it was named after the character on my mums favourite show which happens to be a soap opera which I secretly love because I watched it with her on her death bed and now I still watch it because it makes me feel closer to her'. 
 Yeah no, I can't do it. I just don't understand how so many people love this book? It makes me think I'm missing something (apart from 64% of the story).

I didn't like it and nor did I dislike it. It was just meh, hence the three stars. Two stars seemed too harsh for something that wasn't unpleasant for me to read so I went with three even though its I've given better books that rating. The characters were likeable and their chemistry was great, the back and forth was fun as well. I just didn't really connect to either of them. And then there was the twist which was so stupid, actually on reflection one of the worst romance 'misunderstandings'. That's it, I'm demoting this to two stars.

3.5 Stars 
 These authors sure know how to right 'em sexy and steamy! And by that I mean the story, the hero and the heroine, the chemistry - all sexy and steamy. At times the story verged into territory that was far too cheesy for this reader, but for the most part, I liked this one. 
 Thumbs UP 
 The stories hero, Graham, was a wealthy, arrogant, prick! He was crude, rude, and far too full of himself - and I loved him. The guy was a total caveman. He knew what he wanted (Soraya) and he took it. Underneath his asshole persona, he was just a guy with a shitty past looking for someone to share his life with and love. He was really quite sweet. 
 Soraya was a spunky heroine, who was stubborn but not too much so, who spoke her mind and didn't pull any punches. But she was also thoughtful, caring, and kind (not to mention, a tease). She was an easy character to like. 
 I flippin loved the way these two met! The lost phone, the stalking, the secret stares in train cars... It was all so fun and I could have easily read a hundred more pages about these two trying to play dumb and act like they didn't know who the other was. I especially liked that Soraya didn't make herself known straight away, because a desperate Graham, was very entertaining. 
 The story had some unexpected twists I didn't see coming, which added to the stories drama and made for entertaining (and frustrating) reading. 
 Thumbs DOWN 
 Unfortunately, this book had a storyline that was almost exactly the same as another book I read just a few days ago. Thus, when the surprise drama sprung up in this story, I wasn't very impressed. The shock of it was lost on me and I couldn't help but compare the two stories, which was distracting. 
 I felt that these two (especially Graham) fell for each other way too quickly. Insta-love-city. 
 There were some moments in the story that were far too melodramatic and cheesy for me. The tattoo that Soraya got was ri-god-damn-diculous! I mean sure, get his name, that's fine - Tit-for-tatt and all that... but to get his daughters name tattooed on her as well? Not only was that weird, but it was also seriously over-stepping. After all, he didn't even have his daughters name on him and she BARELY knew the girl. By my count, they had met less than a handful of times before she got the tatt, and they weren't even in a stable relationship at the time! Silly, silly girl. 
 Final Thoughts 
 I rely on these authors books when I want something quick and easy to read, with an alpha-male hero and plenty of steam. They have yet to disappoint. I wouldn't say this book was perfect, but it was still pretty damn entertaining! I look forward to whatever these ladies come out with next.

2 1/2 stars for this one. It's a story line that I've read many times before. The couple sucks at communicating and one person takes it upon themselves to decide what's best for the relationship without consulting the other person. No thank you.

The idea that any self respecting guy would put up with the kind of treatment she dished out was VERY unlikely. MAYBE I could see a really self hating, unattractive guy with a severe inferiority complex would put up with the way she treats him....but the book describes a confident, intelligent( well it TRIES to paint him as intelligent...) man. No man like that would deal with a stalker harridan like Soraya. She is a mean mouthed, self impressed, shallow, uninteresting bully.
The high ratings drew me in so while I take a break from the heavy books I've been reading, I read this one and it was fun to say the least.

 Until the shitty ex and secret baby was thrown in and then everything spiraled into a TBQ Rage Fest more than anything else. 
 You can read my full ranty review HERE.

Gorgeous rich prick who turns into a super great boyfriend to a girl who is not his type, blah blah blah.....Boooorrriiinnggg!
4.5 stars :)

3.5 Stars, I really struggled if I should rate this 3 (even though it's 3.5 or 4 even though it's 3.5 and I decided with 3.) 
 This book was great, interesting, engaging until it hit stupidity. 
 I had just read The Baller by Vi Keeland and I found some of the dialogue in this book to be the same at The Baller, which got annoying. Luckily it didn't last that long. 
 Soraya is a funky Italian girl who is riding the train to work, and over hears this "stuck-up suit" yelling at the poor unfortunate person on the other line of his cell phone. She makes snap judgements about him which don't really pan out in her mind. He gets up to leave and uh oh he dropped his cell phone. Lucky for Soraya she finds it and even more lucky for her he doesn't have a password on his phone! (who in this age doesn't have a password?) There aren't many pictures, and there are a lot of contacts. Soraya decides to hold on to the phone for a while, as well as text a contact, Ben and call a contact, Avery, who promptly tells her to toss the phone into the Hudson. Bitter much? 
 Soraya eventually drops off the phone to give to Mr. Morgan the owner of the phone, but he's an asshole and refuses to see her. So she takes a few select photos of herself and adds her number to it so he can thank her. And the rest takes off from there. 
 The book moves along nicely, I felt it was going at the right pace and everything. Graham (Mr. Morgan) is an asshole, doesn't care about the people around him because he's working so hard. See his ex-fiance went and hooked up with his BFF and several years ago his mother died, and they were close. Her death wrecked him and thus he was a closed off asshole due to these issues. 
 The book though, while it had it's good parts also had its share of equally bad parts, and characters that were not fleshed out. I understand they weren't the focus of the story, but honestly the way they were or how they were developed they could have just been left behind. 
 Now here are my issues, and in order to explain my issues I will need to spoil some of the plot, so here I'll use spoiler tags, You've been warned. 
 Genevieve the ex fiance ends up marrying Liam, the bff. Shortly after their hook up she turns up pregnant. Graham thought the child was Liam's until Liam's untimely demise via heart attack at age 31. He happens upon Chloe, the daughter, where she looks like a spitting image of Graham's late mother and thus he begins to wonder if Chloe is his. Clearly the resemblance is too much so yes she is his. Genevieve, the bitch, wanted both Graham and Liam, and the best of both worlds. She wasn't sure who the father could be, but really she knew because she was 2 months along when Liam and her were only 1 month into their sordid relationship. This throws a monkey wrench into Graham and Soraya's relationship. 
 See when Soraya was a kid her father (and the details are murky at best) had an affair? with Theresa. Theresa had her own children that Soraya's father took up for. There was this rose event at high school that Theresa's daughter also went to. Soraya got all dressed up hoping her father would come for her and instead found him giving roses to the step sister who's name isn't important. This crushed Soraya and made her feel like Theresa was a homewrecker. Great. So now that Graham has a child, she feels that she is going to be a home wrecker for Chloe and that she should gracefully bow out. Really I'm not making this up! Genevieve and Graham aren't even together, she cheated on him AND lied/never told him he had a child for 4 years and basically he missed his daughter's life due to this but in Soraya's deluded mind she thinks they should be a family *eye roll* 
 Soraya works at an Ask column in the paper and writes to her boss "Ask Ida" about her relationship with Graham, and the response is utterly stupid. I can't see that any columnist in their right mind would give the advice that was given to Soraya! It's crazy, it's stupid, and it's just absurd. One comment in the response was "Give him back his family..." and to "Give him the impression there is someone else". Soraya knows it will KILL Graham but she does this anyways. She devises a plan with her BFF. 
 Now prior to this we meet Soraya's BFF Tig, and his wife Delia they run a tattoo shop, Tig doing the tattoos and Delia doing the piercings. They are flat, we don't know how they got together other than they were childhood sweethearts we don't know much about them as far as character developments go. 
 Now instead of asking her about this plan or how happy she is, or how stupid she's being they immediately support her decision. Ok the point of being a BFF is to also look out for your friend's well being, if you're their bff you should also tell them how stupid they are being. Tig and Delia know exactly why Soraya is doing this, but none of them talk her out of it. WHY? Why couldn't she help Graham with Chloe? Why not? They never touched on this. This is where the story goes completely down hill for me. I was super angry and super pissed by this turn of events. Why do something so stupid and so damaging?? It made no sense. 
 Never once did Soraya think she could be Chloe's step parent if Graham and her ever got married, she never thought once about being an active participant in their lives! It was super stupid. 
 THIS TURN OF EVENTS TRULY RUINED THE BOOK! This book was easily edging 4-5 stars but nope. This down graded it to 3.5 the reason it's not a true 3 is because up until that point I was fine. 
 Also Soraya's father made ZERO sense, his responses made zero sense and did nothing for the clarity of the story. I've had better stories and I'm disappointed in the way this ended up. The ending was quick and tied up nicely, but I'd have really liked for the conflict to have been better, more important and difficult to resolve. I'd like to have seen them have to work through their problems. I'd like to have seen the events happen, but this was meh.

WOW! This is a great fast read for me, my best romance read in like forever, I love the way Vi Keeland captured the character and the way they met is so amazing, who would have taught you'll meet your true love on a train. Since i pretty much can't review without spoilers here it goes. 
 The story is about Soraya an Italian lady and Graham a hot, arrogant businessman. Graham lost his phone on the train and she found it and when she tracked him to return the phone to him at his office he was arrogant and refused to see her, She took a pic of her tits, rearview and feet without her face and sent it to his phone and wrote your mother should be ashamed before giving the phone to his receptionist. When he saw the pics he was curious about what she looked like and texted her,They started texing regularly until he saw the same tattoo that was on the feet in the pic on a lady in the train, he just knew that was where she got the phone. 
 They finally met and started dating, just when things started going well he found out he has a daughter with his ex who cheated on him and married his best friend. It disturb his relationship with Soraya and she felt like a homewrecker was taking a chance from a little girl at being happy, because her father left her mom when she was younger and it was hard for her,So she pretended to cheat on Graham so he'll live her and get back with his ex in order for his daughter to be happy. 
 He was devastated but did not get back with his ex till he found out that Soraya lied about cheating on him through an advice column where she works, He tracked Soraya down and they got back together and lived happily ever after,HOPEFULLY cause she got pregnant and they had a son Lorenzo who is absolutely adorable.
Entertaining, quick read. Love some bits and bobs of it, but some things were straight weird !(eg the first conversation between MBP and grandma about Soraya, what?)

Vi Keeland et Penelope Ward forment un duo diabolique. Elles ont une ecriture plutot differente mais tres complementaire et elles peuvent se rejoindre sur quelques points forts communs comme les dialogues et cela donne cette romance sans pretention mais reussie de bout en bout. En toute honnetete, il y a quelques faiblesses mais tellement de passages reussis a la perfection qu'on devore cette petite perle de la romance contemporaine. 
 Les deux complices n'en sont pas a leur coup d'essais. Elles avaient deja ecrit un excellent livre, Cocky Bastard, auquel d'ailleurs elles font un clin d'oeil tres amusant dans le roman ( il y a meme un autre clin d'oeil a Step-brother de Penelope Ward). Elle reitere ici l'exploit avec une histoire totalement nouvelle. Le roman est de plus independant, ne fait partie d'aucune suite et c'est tres bien comme ca. Et ca commence sur les chapeaux de roue avec une scene d'entree brillantissime et une idee de genie. 
 Graham J. Morgan est un connard de la pire espece dans les criteres de Soraya. Un matin dans le train, en route pour son travail au coeur de New York, Soraya va le decouvrir braillant des ordres dans un telephone. sample_reviews.review_text: I absolutely couldn't get through this book. I am reading it now for one month, and I couldn't get further than chapter 15. Normally, I like biographies, but I don't know why I don't like this one. I didn't even bother to finish it. It's not a page turner like other biographies are.

Penny, a blogger, goes to New York and meets a boy with secrets. Cliched coming-of-age plot ensues. 
 I found the characters were very much cardboard-cutouts. Penny is described as the clumsiest, quirkiest, most awkward teenager ever, she has a fake, vain ex-bestfriend and then she falls in love with a sweet, older boy with a chiseled jawline. Where have I seen these characters before?? Oh, right, in all of the YA reads. 
 The plot seemed formulaic, and the romance occurred as fast as the romance in The Sun Is Also a Star, except without as much buildup. The Brooklyn Boy, Noah, is very good-looking, but seems to be hiding things. Penny is hiding her online blog from everyone else as well. Of course, both secrets come to light by the end of the novel, but they weren't enough to add suspense to the storyline. Also, the click as Pen and Noah stare into each other's eyes, as well as their adventure through NY, was unoriginal. 
 I found the writing to be gushy and corny, and there were too many excess exclamation points. It was not mature enough for me. 
 Sometimes, the narration sounded more like a blog than a novel. This wouldn't be a bad thing if I wanted to read Zoella's blog, but I wanted a cute, fast YA novel. 
 At the very least, Zoe Sugg offers very meaningful advice to younger kids. She addresses everything, from embarassing situations to fears, growing out of friends to finding boyfriends, dealing with panic attacks to setting goals. 
 Don't get me wrong, I will probably continue to watch Zoella's YouTube videos because she is great on camera; her talent just doesn't translate onto paper. I can see how it would appeal to younger audiences who relate to Pen, or who are huge Zoella fans. Not my favourite series, but I'm still going to finish it. Product knowledge!!

 I thought it would be another fluffy YA novel, but Girl Online is infused with modern references (Frozen's Let It Go, Twitter, Tumblr, Facebook, among others) and also realistic struggles (Penny's panic attacks). It really surprised me.

 Well, well, well. I know there's not-so-great writing; I know this book is literally a million tropes; I know that I cringed at basically every other page. But did I still somehow like parts of it? 
 ............Yes. 
 I guess I'm a sucker for any romance, cheesy, corny, or bad-written. That's not to say I actually liked it; that's not to say I think it's amazing. But I still kind of liked it. 
 l i k e s: 
 -gay best friend, Elliot: the only representation in this book, but it's better than nothing? 
 -famous-and-regular person have a romance! trope. now I know why I like the movie Starstuck so much. 
 -I know this book didn't have the best representation ever, but I've never read a book with it before: panic attacks. 
 -the pacing! nothing was extremely dragged out. 
 -this book is good for young girls who are trying to figure out their worth and what they deserve. i liked the whole finding-yourself aspect. 
 d i s l i k e s: 
 -can I just say everything else? 
 -tropes, tropes. So. Many. TROPES. a couple are bound to happen in every book, but really? the protagonist is a clumsy red-haired girl who ~everyone can relate to~. do I need to continue? 
 -trying to be relatable. come on, NO ONE calls anyone else the "Walking Selfie". 
 -the writing. I'm aware this is written by a ghostwriter (at least, I'm pretty sure), but there was no originality. I probably could've written something highly similar in vocabulary and description when I was 9. 
 -the plot. okay, okay, it's a contemporary and those usually have one plot, but this was just so. straightforward. I have no desire to read the sequel at ALL, because it's probably as lacking in character development for anyone but the main character and no originality. 
 In conclusion: I like Zoe Sugg, Zoella, whatever. I do not like 90% of the things of her book.

AUDIOBOOK REVIEW: 5+++++ STARS 
 I am not overrating this book/audiobook at all. It really was amazing. I loved everything about this book. Firstly, the narrator, Hannah Tointon, has a beautiful voice with the most amazing British accent ever that fitted perfectly with Penny and all the characters in the book. In addition, her narration was flawless, perfect pace, perfect pronunciation, I could understand everything she said in her British accent - Sometimes it's hard for me to understand it. While the audiobook was playing, I was getting into the story, into Penny's teenage mind/life and made me fall in love with her, her friends -the real ones, her family and the most amazing boy in the world, Noah. 
 Zoe Sugg made an amazing work with this book. It's her first book and I'm so happy I had the opportunity to read/listen to it as soon as it was published. Her writing style is so cool and funny. I loved the sound effects along the audiobook of when Penny was typing when she was writing posts in her blog, or when she was typing in her phone when she was texting, or even better, how her phone buzzed when she got notifications!! It was awesome. It's the first time I listen to an audiobook with that kind of effects and I totally loved it. 
 Gir Online's plot was definitely the best. I was captivated by Penny's adolescent life, her insecurities and her never-ending problems. I loved how she sorted with everything, with the help of her best friend, Elliot -Who I totally love and his idea of Ocean Strong, best idea ever; her parents -Their job was the best; and the help of Noah *sigh*. He was the best. I fell in love with him along with Penny. I loved every moment they shared together, the picnics, the Magical Mystery Day *grinning like an idiot*, the lunch at the artist building... Everything they did together was great. I felt like a teenager all over again, the first love, the first kiss, the first heart break *sad*.... Ii could feel everything that Penny was feeling... Everything was so happy, angsty, sad, and funny to read. I loved it because it was all REAL and awesome. 
 I could talk about this book for ever: I loved Penny's blog, I loved her blog followers, I loved Noah's sister -the cutest thing, I loved Penny's brother, I loved Noah's G-ma, I loved Princess Autumn, I loved New York through Penny's eyes and.... I hated her classmates, especially Megan *shakes head*. I could go on and on with the list of things I loved about Girl Online, but you all better get a copy of the audiobook -Yes, audiobook, you need to live the full experience with the narration and the sound effects, and enjoy Penny's adventure in this book. 
 I totally loved the ending of this book. I felt so anxious when the drama was happening and I thought this book was going to end in a cliffhanger -because of the drama and because I found out that there is going to a second book in the series *happy dance*, but thank God it has a HEA!!!
