Five years ago, in the thick of my fanfiction phase, I read this amazing gem of a fic called TheCherryOnTop. It was about this girl who anonymously runs a gossip blog about her schoolfellows and teachers, gets tricked into admitting her identity by a guy who eventually falls for her. I was so inspired by it that i went and read ALL the Gossip Girl books along with Meg Cabot's kiddy romances and Alyson Noel's Kiss and Blog, but never EVER have I read anything that could top that fic. 
 So when I read the blurb, I was actually very excited. Even after reading really bad reviews about it, I held out hope. Maybe this would be it, I told myself. Maybe people just don't like this kind of stuff anymore. A real life blogger is writing this. It can't be that BAD. Alas, all those reviews were not wrong. 
 Zoe Sugg's book was two dimensional, lacking depth or continuity, had all the cliches including gay best friend, bitchy best friend turned enemy and love at first sight along with awful and flimsy characterization. Too mainstream! Too cliche! Too trite! Too tried! Too sappy! Too blah! One second, Ollie's this completely obnoxious dim wit the heroine likes to call with complete and utter contempt 'the walking selfie' and the other he turns into this hunkalicious surfer boy. One second heroine has an insufferable inferiority complex and the other she's completely over it. Say what? 
 And just WHAT the HELL was all that 'cute!' with Cindy and Jim! As if Sugg had no other distinguishing adjectives to make the speech more american. Frankly, it was the absolute worst part! It made me cringe and it made me angry! 
 The panic attacks were made out to be such a huge deal in chapter one but were only used to facilitate the authors convenience throughout the rest of the book. Plus there was this giant loophole where Penny is completely terrified of air planes yet she's totally fine on elevators which are smaller, more constricting and closer to a car phobe's worst nightmare then planes. 
 There was this AWFUL use of metaphors and analogies. The writing was choppy and stiff. The dialogue was cringe worthy and the characterization was just bleak. 
 Penny had the mindset of a two dimensional toddler. In retrospect, instead of a toddler, Bella was written as a teenage drama queen wild child. And the time they break out the L word I wanted to RIP my hair out! Facepalm times TRILLION!!!! HOW WHY WHY WHYYYYYYYYYYYY!!!!!! I reaaally wanted to bitch slap someone into the next century! Barf barf barf! INCONSISTENT! There was NO conflict at ALL. the minor one that was there was played up to be waaaay bigger than it actually was and solidified Penny's stupidity. 
 In the end this was a love story between penny and her blog. A needlessly long soap opera. Tbh I would have taken the celeb watch deal. Goody two shoes was so blah! Also, Penny was constantly 'engulfed by sorrow' over the slightest of things. And I think sorrow is too large an adjective to describe teenage boy drama angst. 
 Bottom line: I hated Penny AND the story line. Therefore I couldn't get myself invested. Sorry, not sorry. I was forced to conclude that Sugg knows no adjectives other than cute adorable and lovely. I'm even starting to believe that Alyson Noel went somewhere with kiss and blog - which I LOATH - after reading this piece of garbage.

Apparently, Zoella, YouTube beauty vlogger, has decided to write and publish a book, a YA fiction book at that, and with over a million subscribers, she has been able to do just that. Girl Online has had record sales in its first, comparable to those of Harry Potter, but of course there's a catch. This book was ghostwritten, meaning that while Zoe might have had the idea, there was a person (or a group of people) behind the scenes actually putting the sentences together. To be quite honest, I didn't know ghost writing was a frequented route for many authors, but it only makes sense when so many celebrities have their own book. I admit I was hesitant to read it. The plot seemed uninteresting and the fact that Zoe didn't write the book herself and was taking credit for it is oddly unnerving. 
 I will admit that after reading this book I am pleasantly surprised. I think this would make a good coming to age book for girls between the ages of 11 and 15, any younger and you might not understand the "coming to age" part of the book, and any older you might look too much into the plot and characters, finding the obvious gaps between this story and reality. 
 Even as I type this, I'm still conflicted about how I feel. Whilst I read it, emotions of giddiness and adorableness bubbled up inside me, due to the romance BUT the sharp deviations from reality really brought the book down for me. Do I recommend it? I have no idea. It's definitely not a bad read, but the lack of realism may be a turn off for some people.

 Where do I begin with Girl Online? 
 I love Zoe (or Zoella, as she's known on Youtube) and I love Young Adult. But there's something about Girl Online that irked me. It wasn't that the book was ghostwritten and it wasn't that she's a youtuber-turned-author. As skeptical as I was, I wanted to like it, I wanted to read it and form my own opinion. But finishing Girl Online was a struggle. 
 Even days after finishing it, I can't put a finger as to why I didn't enjoy it as much. Girl Online was an okay read; it has its funny moments and in parts, it resonated with me but it came off as too juvenile for my taste. Penny behaves like someone who is much younger than 15 and its funny when Noah's little sister comes off as more "adult" than she is. Girl Online is probably (and definitely) catered to the younger audiences (my library catalogues this as one for 10-year-olds and above). That, is my problem, not the book. So for that, I can't fault it. 
 Girl Online reflects much of Zoe's real life and though it is fictional, you do get to see bit and pieces of her life through Penny. One of the few things that both Zoe and Penny have in common are their blogs, them living in Brighton and of course fairy lights. Penny also suffers from panic attacks, something that Zoe herself has struggled with for many years. 
 The book is filled with sentences that aren't necessary and doesn't push the story arc forward. Its filled with silly little thoughts and descriptions that made the book seen more juvenile and childish. And don't get me started on the insta-love. Penny falls in love with Noah in a span of 48 hours or less. Its ridiculous how crazy-in-love they are when they barely knew each other. Penny recognises this and so does her best friend Elliot, but Penny chooses to ignore this fact. She chooses to ignore the fact that she doesn't even know his last name or background other than he's presumably a rockstar and his grandmother is a fantastic caterer. Instead she's off making plans to make this relationship work long distance. 
 Girl Online is somewhat predictable. I could guess Noah's secret from the way he was being so shady about things, though I have to admit that the last couple of chapters were more interesting than the rest. That was the real highlight of the book -- the drama -- and its a shame that it ended too quick and began too late. 
 Again, I am not the target audience of this book. Its incredibly fluffy and better suited for those much younger than me. This book isn't incredible; it is flawed and could have been better. It isn't a "how-to-deal-with-your-anxiety" book either. It shifted to "girl-falling-in-love" with anxiety on the sidelines. 
 I tried, and as much as I love her, its not something I would necessarily recommend. Maybe for the younger folks, perhaps. Okay to read, but probably not a must on your bookshelves.

I will be the honest person here. 
 I must say that I've been watching Zoella vids for a while now and I truly feel her close to my heart. I won't say that I think that she is a genius, doing an extraordinary things, because no matter how much I like her, I don't think that this applies to her. There is something else I love about Zoe - I believe she is one ordinary girl that has the unique charm in herself, that does things with dedications and I just adore that about herself. She doesn't claim to be something she is not, she is down to earth, she had her struggles and she fought her demons. And most of all - I love that Zoe's work gathers people together and makes them feel special. At least that's how she made me feel and it wouldn't be a lie if I say that I couldn't be more grateful to her because of all those times she made me smile and she was a friend to me, even though she doesn't know about my existence. 
 So, as a person that loves the girl she is, I gave her book a go. As a bookworm I won't argue that her book is a phenomenon and I choose to be honest, writing this review with clear mind. 
 The thing I loved about Girl Online is that it speaks to me and my experience as I've suffered a panic attacks before and I know the horrible consequences that follow them. There is one extremely true quote in her book that even made me tear up. It goes: 
 As my fear of panic attacks gets bigger and bigger, it seems to be making my world feel smaller and smaller. 
 I felt sympathy for the main heroine, I felt her embarrassment, her fear, her weakness, her determination, her hope, her wanting-to-get-the-best-of-life urge. And that's what I liked about the book. That's what I loved about it. Because only a person that had those panic attacks and that knows all about them and the desperation and the hope, gets to be the judge here. The others would've only imagined. And believe me you wouldn't be even close. 
 The thing that I didn't like about the book was the slowly way the story was expanding and the pointless at times descriptions. The rest of the story was revealing the regular relationships that teenage girl has with people in her teenage world. Nothing new here, nothing that unusual. And yet that's the thing that made the book interesting I guess. From time to time we all need to remember how it was our life back in the high school. 
 As a reader - I give 3 stars. 
 As a human - several times above that.

In the end, I went with three stars because I 'liked it', but I didn't 'really like it'. 
 I loved the premise - the bit on the blurb that says 'I have this dream that, secretly, all teenage girls feel exactly like me'. I read the first few pages of the book and it echoed this sentiment. It even got an extra layer of complexity from her panic attacks. (I found out about it because of something I've subscribed to, I'm not sure what, I like getting emails telling me about newly published works.) 
 I was really impressed by how polished the book seemed for a first-time author. 
 Later, I found out it was ghost-written. This made me less impressed, but I was still looking forward to reading a book about young adults bonding together in a time when the Internet looms threateningly on the horizon as they tenderly piece together notions of who they are and whether or not they're okay with it. The idea that there is hope for those straddling the years between 'kids', 'teenagers', and 'young adults'. 
 Unfortunately, the book is *much, much* more of a romance than it is any of those things. Yes, there's online scandals, and fights with friends, and the realisation that the world doesn't end when some small (or even quite large) bad thing happens. But the number of pages dedicated to describing romantic picnics and fluttery butterfly feelings (and an 18 year old that spent an hour with her in a basement alone under the table on cushions and happy feels and there was nothing other than kissing? hmm..) was too high for me when I was looking for inspirational insights into the world of a young girl who suffers from panic attacks. 
 Edit: Scanning through, there are some great other reviews for this book that sum up why it didn't work for me. It wasn't just that it was a romance when I was expecting something else. It was that the romance kind of made me cringe. There are lots of pages about 'finding your soul mate'. For 16, she isn't *terribly* bright (who lurks on the internet and doesn't know a bit more about the world?) and yet this 18 year old is *deeply* attracted to her. It's written in first person present-tense, so there can't really be any space for self-analysis, but as soon as you *actively* think things like "I know I just can't tell my parents" and "why would X be the case?" it means you're thinking it and doesn't that mean you're going to keep thinking about it a few moments longer rather than move instantly onto the next thought...?

If Zoe Sugg herself had written the book herself, it's hideousness might have been understood. Apparently you don't need talent to be hired as a ghostwriter. Shame on everyone involved, especially the people who made this book more popular than Harry Potter. Shame on you.

RATING: 5 out of 5 stars 
 SUMMARY: Ponyboy Curtis' life is not easy. Not only is he a greaser in a soc world. His parents are dead and his brothers are doing the best they can to raise him. His friends are being jumped and attacked. One day, chaos occurs and Ponyboy has to find a way to live with it. 
 REVIEW: I understand when people criticize the male voice of Ponyboy because what 14 year old boy talks about how cute his brothers look all the time. However, that doesn't bother me in the slightest. I've read this book multiple times and it still hits me in the core. It is so sad and honest. I've spent years avoiding this book, and I'm not quite sure why. Maybe because some of the descriptions made it sound kind of hokey, like West Side Story set in Oklahoma. 
 In some ways, this book helped to start the modern YA fiction movement, both because the author was so young when it was first written, and because it was a realistic novel, which most older YA fiction was not. 
 In fact, the least realistic part of the story was that Ponyboy and Sodapop [their real names] apparently weren't the cause of their parents' death. I know that if I'd been stuck with a name like that, I'd have at least considered strangling my parents... 
 Still, the story focuses on the concept that class differences, rather than the more commonly portrayed ethnic differences, can be at the heart of gangs and conflict. In that slightly-more-innocent time of the 1960s, the older, less structured gangs were still around, with groups of teens fighting it out over who got to hang out at the local park or drive-in. 
 In this case, the "greasers," who were basically anybody poor and who adopted the slicked-back hair and the Fonzie lifestyle, were fighting it out with the Socs [I think it's pronounced "soshes], who were basically bored rich kids who wanted to be thugs, just because. 
 The title of the book may derive from the way that the Greasers are on the outside looking in, or it may be based on how the narrator character and some of his friends are not really a part of the stereotypes which surround them, and are thus also "outsiders". There are a number of ways to look at it, and any of them work. 
 The only weakness in the book is that we never got to really understand the Socs or their penchant for bored violence. We just see the tragic results of their actions. The Greasers are much better explained, and easier to understand.

 I sometimes forget how much I like this novel. This is the first time I've read it since my very first graduate class in YAL, about 13 years ago, so there was a lot I didn't remember. Hinton's book, written when she was a Tulsa teenager, is considered one of the landmark publications in young adult literature, and rightly so. Prior to Hinton, almost no authors for children/young adults were writing about "serious" topics such as gangs, difficult home lives, and death. The fact that Hinton approached these subjects (in this, and her other early novels) in a straight-forward manner, without interjecting moral lessons, and did it through a first person POV, I think, is significant. Told through the eyes of Ponyboy, this tale of class warfare, between the Greasers and the Socs, still holds water today. 
 I see this book taught all over the place; had we remained in Oklahoma for our daughter's middle school years, she would have read this book. It's become a staple in secondary curricula, yet also one of the most challenged books around. It's also interesting that the entire book is supposedly written as a school assignment, revealed only at the conclusion. The role of education in the novel, and the novel's adoption by schools for instructional use, seem to be intertwined. If the "way out," for Ponyboy at novel's end, is to simply study harder, and possibly leave for college some day, then that says something about the power of the individual to overcome obstacles and odds. But what does that do, if anything, for the "hundreds and hundreds of boys" to whom Ponyboy refers at the end of the book, and the social class they represent? I love when books can appear relatively simple on the surface, and present just a good read, yet offer a lot more to readers who want to dig deeper. Reading Hinton again, I'm reminded of how well she presents both options to her audience.

 Two*Way Street by Lauren Barnholdt is another book from my Contemporary YA novels list. To be honest, I wasn't really planning on reading this one but then again I went to the 33rd Manila International Book Fair which was held last September 12-16, 2012 at the SMX Convention Center and got this one along with two other Contemporary YA's. It tells about the two sides of a break-up. Let's face it, there is always two sides when it comes to break-up's. The story is told in Jordan and Courtney's perspectives who also happens to be the main characters of the story. 
 To start with, it's set set somewhere across America since the characters are on a road trip. And yes, they are ex's. I found Courtney a little immature to be perfectly honest. Yes, he broke her heart blah blah blah but I think she could have handled it differently. She seriously didn't have to try so hard just to show Jordan that she thought he was an asshole and all. Plus, the fact that every little thing somehow affected her. Seriously, I just didn't get her. All she did was try so hard to pretend that she doesn't care but somehow made it so obvious that she does. Don't get me wrong though I did enjoy reading her chapters even if she was annoying at times. I actually understood her in some ways. 
 Then there's Jordan. I love Jordan. I enjoyed reading his POV's more than Courtney's actually. The fact that he did what he did because he loved her. I'm not saying that what he did was right but to actually do something like that for the girl that you love is really something. I didn't think he was an asshole or anything. His patience towards Courtney's attitude is something. And I could say this with all my heart, HE IS A TRULY PATIENT MAN. He babysat Courtney along the way. 
 Overall, I enjoyed reading this book. I did finish it in one night. It's a quick and light read and if you're into road trips and romance then this one is definitely for you. I did think that everything could have been resolved if only Jordan opted to tell the truth even if it wasn't his truth to tell. Well, technically it is his truth as well since he was there when everything happened. Anyway, it is a good story. I enjoyed reading it a lot. No cheesy lines that make you want to throw up. I'm giving this a 4/5 rating though. Minus one star just because Courtney annoyed me a bit.

 What. The. Fuck. I'm not sure I've ever read a bigger piece of trash in my life. How anyone could get away with writing this is utterly beyond me. I actually had to take notes on everything that was wrong with this book, just so I didn't lose track. Let's start at the beginning, shall we? 
 First, everyone, and I mean everyone, in this book is fucking psychotic. All of them. It's a completely unrealistic portrayal of high school/college students. High school and college students do not spend all of their time fucking and drinking. They don't. I don't know how long ago Barnholdt was in high school and college, or what her social life was like when she was there, but for some reason I have a feeling she wishes this was what college and high school were like, not what they were actually like. Is there sex and partying in high school and college? Yeah, sure. But people do not spend every night of the week attending multiple parties. Especially when they're stellar students, like Courtney and Jordan supposedly are, because you actually can't be a stellar student and still have time to spend every night hooking up and drinking. Trust me, I know. And they all, even the adults, run around sharing secrets and blackmailing people. What? And let's not forget that not a single parent cares that their children, who are underage (Courtney is 17) are running around at all hours of the night with people they have never met before, and they encourage this behavior. 
 Then there are Courtney and Jordan themselves. We are supposed to believe that they had a wonderful, beautiful relationship, that they never fought, and it's wonderful that they got back together. Uhm, no. Not at all. Courtney, for starters, is psycho. She believes her ex-boyfriend is a liar and a cheat, even when she knew he wasn't lying to her or cheating on her. Her relationship with him revolves heavily around the use of Myspace, which is definitely not the way to have a successful, healthy relationship. She also automatically assumes that every girl who isn't a virgin is a slut. Myspace Girl is a slut because Jordan likes her. Any girl who ever bats an eyelash at Jordan, even before Courtney liked him, is a slut. But this logic does not apply to Jordan, even though he apparently hooks up with girls left and right. Barnholdt apparently still lives in an age where only women can be sluts, and men who sleep around are to be congratulated for their actions because it makes them even more desirable. And can I mention how Courtney thinks that girls who are desirable, but are honest and never cheat on their boyfriends are "the worst kind of girls"? What the fuck is that about? Apparently Courtney thinks that lying and cheating are desirable qualities in a girlfriend?! 
 Now let's talk about Jordan. Jordan, as mentioned before, is the type of guy who hooks up with a different girl every night of the week. He also deeply regrets not having the appropriate amount of time to gel his hair in the morning. He likes his rap "hard and dirty" and thinks Courtney, who he is in love with, is dressed like a slut because she's wearing shorts and a tank top in Florida in the middle of the fucking summer. Let me repeat that. She's a slut because she's wearing shorts and a tank top in Florida, one of the hottest, most humid places in the country. God forgive her for not wearing a full-length skirt and a bonnet to cover her hair! He also thinks that, if a girl shows any interest in him at all after they hook up, she is automatically psychotic; heaven forbid that a woman expects a guy she's been intimate with to treat her like an actual human being and not like a disposable fuck toy! We're apparently also supposed to think Jordan is edgy or something because he bought pot for a party once. No. That is not edgy, that's just stupid and a waste of money. We're supposed to like him because he cries over his breakup with Courtney, but that was all because he was a complete idiot in the first place, so I don't pity him at all. He broke up with her, after all, and for what was literally no reason. 
 Oh, and the "big secret" of the breakup is hardly a secret at all, and not nearly juicy enough to justify all of the sheer stupidity, slut-shaming, and overall misogyny of this book. And the writing sucks. How many times can you use "totally" in one sentence? And at least learn to keep your character details straight, because Courtney is some kind of stellar student one moment, is in all AP classes, and the next she can't solve a single math problem on her own.

 This book is the companion novel to Right of Way. I didn't enjoy Right of Way, but I had this book lying around on my shelf and I thought, maybe I should try this out. I am so glad I did because it was really good, much better than Right of Way. The characters were awesome, the plot was okay and the pace was great. I couldn't stop reading, I finished this book on Wednesday. But I didn't update my status because I wanted to write a review but there was so much homework, so I am writing this review now. :) 
 "In my mind, I still think of him as being a cheater. Otherwise he just met some girl he liked better, and it's not as dramatic." 
 This book is about a girl named Courtney who is going to go to college. Her boyfriend Jordan dumped her a few weeks ago for a girl he met online. Back when Jordan and Courtney were dating, they made plans to go on a road trip together to college. Courtney thought that since they broke up, they won't go together, it's too late to make any changes. On the road trip, it's obviously awkward but Courtney feels as if Jordan is hiding something. Told in both Jordan and Courtney's point of view, this book will have you laughing til the very end. 
 "I'm too quiet. But I'm really not quiet. I just tend to come across that way to new people because I don't like to talk first." 
 In my opinion, I believe you should read this book before you read Right of Way because Right of Way has spoilers. I knew some of the things that would happen and it was really annoying. But other then that, I think this book was really good. The plot was a little weak though and I wasn't a huge fan of it. But the characters were much better than the characters from Right of Way. 
 "You should never start thinking about 'what might have been,' and you should also never start thinking about another boy when you're heartbroken over someone else." 
 Although I wasn't a huge fan of Jordan, he was much better compared to Jace in Right of Way. Courtney was waaay better than Peyton from Right of Way though. Their relationship made sense and I found both characters really funny. B.J is the best, even though he could be a little awkward at times. It was really annoying when Courtney and Jordan would catfight about everything. 
 But at the same time, I did find it really funny. I wish I could love this book more, but I didn't love every aspect of it. Sometimes, Courtney was a bit over dramatic and I felt that Jordan could've been a little more logical. But other than that, they were great and I enjoyed the whole road trip. 
 I was happy with the ending of this book and I recommend you read this. I don't recommend Right of Way, I was so hyped up to read it and then I was so upset because it was not what I expected. But overall, this book passed and I did enjoy it. But if you want a really good road-trip, summer read, READ AMY AND ROGER'S EPIC DETOUR!!!!!!

 I had really high expectations for this book, but I think that's just because it sounded really good and I've read one of Lauren Barnholdt's other books. This book definitely didn't meet those expectations. 
 The thing that bothered me the most was probably just the way it was written. The book jumped around too much - it started off on the day of the trip, and then not too much later it was 100 days before the trip in Jordan's point of view, and then it was day one of the trip in Courtney's point of view, then 94 days before the trip, then 90 days before the trip, and so on. I get that Barnholdt wanted to show how Jordan and Courtney's relationship came to be, but honestly, it was too much skipping around for me. 
 Another thing I didn't like - the characters. Since the POV's switched off between Jordan and Courtney through the book, we get to see both their viewpoints of each other. Jordan's view of Courtney was so off most of the time that it simply made me angry. And his thoughts weren't that interesting, either. Both characters seemed so vapid and shallow at times that I didn't want to keep reading. And their friends? Don't even get me started on them. 
 The plot was probably the best part of this book, and even that didn't interest me very much. Jordan's big "secret" about why he broke up with Courtney wasn't even as mysterious as I was anticipating. And you find out the reason fairly quickly - no suspense. 
 Overall: While Barnholdt's writing may appeal to some, this book just wasn't for me. I can't think of a single good thing to say about it, other than the concept is an interesting idea: going on a roadtrip with the boy who just dumped you. I just wish Barnholdt had done a better job with it. I feel like I'm being unnaturally harsh, but I can't give it more than 1 star.

Un livre que je deconseille. 
 Je ne sais pas, j'ai peut etre vraiment passe l'age de certains livres young adult, mais celui la, c'est vraiment pas possible. 
 Tres mal ecrit, langage ultra juvenile, reflexions superficielles, histoire sans aucun axe dramatique valable, des personnages caricaturaux, dans le pire de ce que l'adolescence propose. 
 Completement leurree par le pitch, que je trouvais vraiment bien : une fille qui doit se taper un road trip avec son ex, qui a du rompre avec elle pour des raisons qu'on ignore. 
 En fait, l'histoire ne tient pas la route (c'est le cas de le dire) : le road trip aurait largement pu etre evite, le secret est bidon, la relation entre les deux mal decrite (on comprends pas ce qu'ils font ensemble, ou est l'amour?) 
 Je crois que le pire c'est quand dans un flashback (flash-back qui d'ailleurs ralentissent considerablement l'histoire et sont tres mal amenes) Elle veut faire l'amour avec lui, et lui refuse en disant qu'il veut pas de relations longues, et elle qui dit "bon ben oublie ca, on fait comme si de rien n'etait" ==> pathetique). 
 Les passage sur Myspace sont anachroniques et font du mal a l'histoire (qui en avait pas besoin). 
 La fin se finit de facon abrupte, comme si l'auteur avait autre chose a faire (la cuisine? le menage des chambres des petits?) bref, nul.
